docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Learners leave able to run the plan, implement, review loop in the CLI. They know what to approve, how context works, and when to reach for the IDE instead.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 What the CLI is, install, sign in 0:08 to 0:15 Interactive vs copilot -p 0:15 to 0:25 Plan mode and the core loop (demo) 0:25 to 0:33 Slash commands that matter 0:33 to 0:45 Permissions and context 0:45 to 0:55 Resume, CLI vs IDE, pros and cons, advanced slides 0:55 to 1:00 Lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Install the CLI and sign in. Run copilot --version.
  • Copy lab/starter/agent-tasks to a scratch folder. Run npm install and npm test. Expect 4 passing and 3 failing.
  • Run the lab once. Keep lab/solution/agent-tasks open to compare.
  • Check the current Copilot CLI docs for command or flag changes. The CLI changes fast.
  • Learners need Node.js 22 or later, Git, and Copilot access. If someone can't sign in, pair them with a neighbor and keep going.

docs.title: What the CLI is (0:00 to 0:08)
docs.text:
• It is an agent in the terminal, not a chat box. It reads files, edits them, and runs commands.
  • Install with npm, Homebrew, or WinGet. The first run asks for sign-in and folder trust.
  • Trust lets Copilot read and act in that folder. Say it plainly: trust only your own folders.

docs.title: Interactive vs copilot -p (0:08 to 0:15)
docs.text:
• Interactive is a conversation you steer. -p answers once and exits.
  • In -p mode nobody can answer a permission prompt. Allow tools up front with --allow-tool, or the command is refused.
  • Show both with the same question. Mention that -p suits scripts and CI.

docs.title: Plan mode and the core loop (0:15 to 0:25)
docs.text:
Demo on a project other than the lab, or the starter in a scratch copy. Use a small bug that spans two files.

  1. Press Shift+Tab to reach plan mode. Prompt: the bug, the test that shows it, and "smallest fix, don't change tests".
  2. Read the plan aloud. Find one thing wrong or too big. Ask for a change.
  3. Approve. Allow the first edit once. Allow npm test for the session.
  4. Run /diff. Run /review. Read one finding and decide.

Say why: a mistake costs one sentence to fix in a plan and ten minutes to fix in code.

docs.title: Slash commands that matter (0:25 to 0:33)
docs.text: Show each in 30 seconds: /help, /model, /context, /compact, /diff, /review, /resume, /skills, /mcp. Say that /skills and /mcp come back in M3 sessions. Don't show more commands. Learners can find them with /help.

docs.title: Permissions and context (0:33 to 0:45)
docs.text:
Permissions.

  • Allow once, allow for the session, deny. Explain when each fits.
  • --allow-tool and --deny-tool set the same rules from the command line.
  • Tell the story: /allow-all is fast until the first surprise command.
  • Rule of thumb: allow for the session only what you could describe from memory, like npm test.

Context.

  • @file for one prompt. Instructions for every session.
  • Write a short instructions file live: how to test, one scope rule.
  • /context shows how full the window is. /compact summarizes it.

docs.title: Resume, CLI vs IDE, advanced (0:45 to 0:55)
docs.text:
• copilot --continue reopens the latest session. /resume picks one.
  • Resumed sessions carry old context. Use /clear or /new when the task changes.
  • Walk the CLI vs IDE table. Ask: "Where would you fix a bug on a remote box?"
  • Advanced slides take one minute each. Say what it is, say the tradeoff, point to the stretch task.

docs.title: Pros, cons, tips
docs.text:
Pros Cons Works anywhere a terminal works, including SSH No inline completions Scriptable with -p Text-only diffs Plan mode catches mistakes early Permission prompts need attention Shares repo instructions with the IDE Long sessions drift

Tips

  • Ask for a plan before any change across several files.
  • Name files with @ instead of describing them.
  • Commit before a large task. git diff then shows only Copilot's work.
  • Run the tests yourself. Don't trust "all tests pass" in a summary.
  • Put repeated advice in the instructions file.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Approving without reading. Read the command.
  • Using /allow-all to silence prompts. Allow the one command for the session instead.
  • Approving a plan you skimmed. Check it against the code.
  • Letting Copilot change the tests to make them pass. Say it in the instructions.
  • One endless session. Start a new one per task. Use /compact in between.
  • Vague instructions. "Write good code" does nothing. "Run npm test" does.
  • Trusting /review blindly. It finds real issues and false ones.

docs.title: Lab notes
docs.text:
• Part 1: Cap sign-in problems at five minutes. Pair learners who are blocked.
  • Part 2: Learners often skip the flag and wonder why the command is refused. That is the lesson.
  • Part 4: Plans vary by model. Expect different wording. The three causes are:
  • GET /tasks filter uses !== instead of ===.
  • GET /tasks/:id compares a number with a string. It needs parseInt.
  • PUT /tasks/:id spreads the old task last, so the update is lost. Swap the order.
  • Part 5: If a learner's run asks fewer prompts than the others, check their /permissions or copilot config.
  • Part 8: Accept any answer with a concrete reason.
  • Part 9: Fleet and Autopilot results vary. Treat them as a demo of the tradeoff, not a pass or fail.

docs.text: The fixed project is in lab/solution/agent-tasks/. The reference instructions are in .github/copilot-instructions.md there.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Agent mode lets Copilot in VS Code work through a task on its own. It reads files, edits several of them, runs commands, reads the output, and keeps going until the task is done or it needs you.

You learn how Ask, Edit, Agent, and Plan modes differ, what tools agent mode uses, and how to steer it. Then you build one multi-file feature in a small Node.js project: plan first, review the diff, ask for a fix, and hand a TODO comment to the cloud agent.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Pick the right mode for a task: Ask, Edit, Agent, or Plan.
  • Name the tools agent mode uses: read, search, edit, terminal, and MCP.
  • Steer agent mode: plan first, review diffs, undo with checkpoints, approve terminal commands.
  • Explain how agent mode differs from the Copilot CLI (M2-01) and the cloud agent (M3-02).
  • Compare Ask and Agent output on the same prompt.
  • Delegate a TODO comment to the cloud agent from the editor.
  • Spot the common mistakes: vague prompts, skipped review, and blanket auto-approval.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
VS Code with GitHub Copilot Chat, Node.js 20 or later, and Git. The TODO step also needs the GitHub Pull Requests extension and a GitHub repository you own with the cloud agent enabled.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Starter project lab/starter/notes-api/ Finished project lab/solution/notes-api/

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• Ask, Edit, Agent, and Plan modes
  • Tools: read, search, edit, terminal, MCP
  • Steering: plan first, review diffs, checkpoints, command approval
  • Trust: what the agent can touch and what you must read
  • Agent mode vs the CLI and the cloud agent
  • TODO code actions
  • Pros, cons, tips, and common mistakes

docs.title: Plan first, review the diff, stay in charge
docs.text: Session M2-02 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Four modes 10 min What agent mode can touch 12 min Steering 13 min Agent mode vs CLI vs cloud agent 8 min Demo 12 min Pros, cons, mistakes 5 min

docs.title: Four modes
docs.text:
Mode What it does Changes files? Ask Answers questions about your code No Edit Edits the files you pick, in one pass Yes, only those Agent Finds files, edits, runs commands, loops Yes, and runs things Plan Researches and writes a plan No, until you approve

Pick the smallest mode that does the job. Current VS Code lists Ask, Agent, and Plan. Check what your picker shows for Edit.

docs.title: What agent mode does
docs.text:
You: prompt
  → Copilot picks a tool and asks the editor to run it
  → the editor runs it and returns the result
  → Copilot reads the result and picks the next tool
  → ... until done, or it asks you

A tool is an action the editor can run for the model.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool kind Examples Read Open a file, list a folder Search Find text or symbols in the workspace Edit Change or create files Terminal Run npm test, git status MCP Tools from servers you add: issues, databases, docs

Open the tools picker in chat to see and switch them off.

docs.title: Trust: what it can touch
docs.text:
• Your files. It edits them directly. Git is your safety net.
  • Your terminal. Commands run as you. Each one asks first.
  • MCP servers. They can reach outside systems with your credentials.
  • Text it reads. A file or web page can contain instructions. Treat it as untrusted.

You are the review step. Nothing else is.

docs.title: Steering
docs.text:
1. Plan first. Use Plan mode, or say "plan, don't edit yet".
  2. Be specific. Goal, files, how to check it.
  3. Watch the tool calls. Stop it if it wanders.
  4. Review every diff. Keep or undo per file.
  5. Undo with checkpoints. Restore chat to an earlier point.
  6. Read terminal commands before you allow them.

docs.title: Terminal approval
docs.text:
Agent mode asks before it runs a command. You can:

  • Allow once.
  • Allow a command prefix for this session, or always.
  • Auto-approve chosen commands with chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove.

Tip: auto-approve npm test. Keep asking for anything that deletes, installs, or pushes.

Menu labels vary by version. Check the current docs.

docs.title: Agent mode, CLI, cloud agent
docs.text: IDE agent mode Copilot CLI (M2-01) Cloud agent (M3-02) Runs Your machine, in VS Code Your machine, in a terminal GitHub, in its own environment You are Watching, in the editor Watching, in the terminal Away until the PR Result Edits in your working tree Edits in your working tree A pull request Best for Feature work with diff review Terminal tasks, scripts Well-defined tasks you can hand off

docs.title: TODO code action
docs.text:
// TODO: Add GET /export that returns all notes as CSV.

With the GitHub Pull Requests extension, a lightbulb appears. Pick Delegate to coding agent. The cloud agent opens a pull request.

Good for small, well-described tasks. You review the PR.

docs.title: Demo
docs.text:
Same prompt, two modes. Then agent mode with a plan.

  • Ask: explains what to change.
  • Agent: changes it and runs the tests.

Watch the tool calls, then the diff.

docs.title: Pros and cons
docs.text: Pros Cons Multi-file changes in one go Can edit more than you wanted Runs tests and fixes failures Long runs are hard to review Sees your real project Wrong assumptions hide in big diffs Easy to undo Slower than a quick Ask

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Vague prompt. "Add tags" gets guesses. Name the behavior.
  • No plan. Big tasks drift.
  • Skipping the diff. Accepting all without reading.
  • Blanket auto-approve. One bad command costs more than the clicks.
  • Giant tasks. Split them.
  • No tests. The agent has nothing to check against.

docs.title: Session M2-02 lab: Add a feature with agent mode
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: Your notes-api with the tags feature, a short Ask vs Agent comparison, and a TODO delegated to the cloud agent

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You start with a small, working notes API and add tags to it. You do it once in Ask mode to see what it gives you, then in Agent mode with a plan first. You review the diff, ask for a fix, and hand a TODO comment to the cloud agent.

Part Work Time 1 Set up the project 10 min 2 Ask vs Agent on the same prompt 20 min 3 Plan first 15 min 4 Build in agent mode 25 min 5 Review the diff and undo 20 min 6 Ask for a fix 10 min 7 Delegate a TODO 15 min 8 Compare and wrap up 5 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need VS Code with GitHub Copilot Chat, Node.js 20 or later, and Git. Mode names and buttons change between VS Code releases. If something differs from this guide, check the current VS Code docs.

docs.title: Part 1: Set up the project
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-02
cp -R sessions/session-m2-02-agent-mode-ide/lab/starter/notes-api ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-02/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-02/notes-api
git init -q && git add -A && git commit -qm "Start"
npm install && npm test
code .

Four tests pass. Open src/routes/notes.js, src/store.js, and src/validate.js and read them for two minutes.

In Copilot Chat, open the mode picker and the tools picker. Note which modes you have and which tool groups you can switch off.

Checkpoint: npm test passes and you can see the mode and tools pickers.

docs.title: Part 2: Ask vs Agent on the same prompt
docs.text:
Use this prompt in both modes. It is specific on purpose.

Add tags to notes. A note gets an optional `tags` list of up to 5 strings,
each 1 to 20 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. The list defaults to
empty. Accept tags on create and update, validate them, and add a `?tag=`
filter to GET /api/notes. Add tests and update the README.
  1. Set the mode to Ask and send it. Read the answer. Don't apply anything.
  2. Run git status. Nothing should have changed.
  3. Open a new chat, switch to Agent, and send the same prompt. Let it start, but when it asks to run a command, stop here. Read the command, then click Cancel or don't allow it.
  4. Run git restore . && git clean -fd to return to the starting point.

Answer in comparison.md (3 to 5 lines):

  • What did Ask give you that you could act on?
  • What did Agent do that Ask couldn't?
  • Which files did each one mention or touch?

Checkpoint: comparison.md exists, and git status is clean.

docs.title: Part 3: Plan first
docs.text:
Open a new chat. Switch to Plan mode if your build has it. If not, use Agent mode and start with "Plan only. Don't edit any files."

Send the same prompt. When the plan comes back, read it and edit it. Pick at least one change:

  • Add "validate tags in src/validate.js, not in the route".
  • Add "write tests before changing the code".
  • Remove a step you don't want.

Tell Copilot to use the revised plan.

Checkpoint: you changed the plan before any file was edited.

docs.title: Part 4: Build in agent mode
docs.text:
If you used Plan mode, start the plan from there. Otherwise tell Agent mode to go ahead with the plan.

While it works:

  • Expand the tool calls. Note which files it reads and searches before it edits.
  • Read each terminal command before you allow it. Allow npm test. If it wants to install a package or delete files, say no and ask why.
  • Let it run the tests and react to any failure.

Checkpoint: Agent reports the tests pass, and npm test also passes when you run it yourself.

docs.title: Part 5: Review the diff and undo
docs.text:
Open Source Control and read the diff file by file. For each file, ask:

  • Does this change belong to the request?
  • Is anything missing, such as a test for a bad tag or an update to the README?
  • Did it touch something you didn't ask for?

Write down one thing you would change. Then:

  1. In chat, find the checkpoint for your request and restore it. Check that your files go back to the starting point.
  2. Redo the request, or use the redo option, to get the changes back.
  3. Keep the changes with the keep or accept control, file by file.

Commit when you're happy: git add -A && git commit -m "Add tags".

Checkpoint: you read every changed file, and you used restore at least once.

docs.title: Part 6: Ask for a fix
docs.text:
Change a requirement. Tags like Work and work should be the same tag. Ask in the same chat:

Tags should be case-insensitive. Normalize them to lowercase when a note
is created or updated, and make ?tag= match case-insensitively. Add a test.
Run npm test.

Check the new diff. Did it change validate.js to reject uppercase tags? That conflicts with the new rule. If it did, say what is wrong and ask it to fix that.

Checkpoint: a note created with ["Work"] is stored as ["work"], ?tag=WORK finds it, and the tests pass.

docs.title: Part 7: Delegate a TODO
docs.text:
src/routes/notes.js ends with a TODO comment:

// TODO: Add GET /export that returns all notes as CSV ...

You need the GitHub Pull Requests extension and a GitHub repository you own with the cloud agent enabled. Never use a repository that holds real work or data.

  1. Create a private repo and push your project to it.
  2. Put the cursor on the TODO comment. Open the lightbulb (code action) and choose Delegate to coding agent. Newer versions may say "cloud agent".
  3. If asked about local changes, push them so the agent starts from your current code.
  4. Open the pull request link Copilot gives you. Don't wait for it to finish. Come back in Part 8 or after the lab.

If you can't use the cloud agent, read the lightbulb options and note what they offer. Skip the rest of this part.

Checkpoint: a cloud agent session exists for your repo, or you noted why you skipped.

docs.title: Part 8: Compare and wrap up
docs.text:
Add three lines to comparison.md:

  • What did planning first change?
  • What would you do differently with the same prompt next time?
  • Which of these would you give to the CLI, to agent mode, and to the cloud agent? Give one reason each.

If the cloud agent pull request is ready, review it like any other pull request.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. Your notes-api with the tags feature and passing tests, including the case-insensitive fix.
  2. comparison.md with your Ask vs Agent notes and your closing lines.
  3. The cloud agent session or pull request from the TODO, or a note on why you skipped it.

Compare with lab/solution/notes-api/. The solution doesn't include the lowercase fix or the CSV export, so your code may go further.

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Learners leave knowing which mode to use, what agent mode can touch, how to steer it, and how it differs from the CLI and the cloud agent.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:10 Four modes 0:10 to 0:22 What agent mode can touch 0:22 to 0:35 Steering 0:35 to 0:43 Agent mode vs CLI vs cloud agent 0:43 to 0:55 Demo 0:55 to 1:00 Pros, cons, mistakes, lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Use a current VS Code with GitHub Copilot Chat. Mode names and settings change often, so open the mode picker and check what you see.
  • Run the lab once on a scratch copy of lab/starter/notes-api/. Keep lab/solution/notes-api/ open for comparison.
  • For the TODO demo, push the scratch copy to a private repo you own. Install the GitHub Pull Requests extension and check that the lightbulb shows Delegate to coding agent. If it doesn't, check that the cloud agent is enabled for the repo and for your plan.
  • Have a small MCP server ready only if you want to show an MCP tool. It is not needed for the lab.

docs.title: Four modes (0:00 to 0:10)
docs.text:
Mode Use it when Ask You want an answer, an explanation, or a review of an idea. Nothing changes. Edit You know which files to change and want a quick, contained edit. Agent The task spans files and needs commands, such as running tests. Plan The task is big or unclear. You want a reviewed plan before any edit.

Key line: pick the smallest mode that does the job. Ask is cheaper to review than Agent.

Edit mode and the mode list have changed between VS Code releases. Show what your build offers. Tell learners to check the current docs if their picker differs.

docs.title: What agent mode can touch (0:10 to 0:22)
docs.text:
Tool use in plain words: the model can't open a file or run a command. It asks the editor to do it, the editor does it, and the result goes back to the model. Agent mode repeats this until the task is done.

Walk through the tool kinds: read, search, edit, terminal, MCP. Open the tools picker and switch one off to show you control the list.

Trust in plain words: what the agent can change or reach without asking you.

  • Files: edited in place. Git makes it recoverable.
  • Terminal: commands run with your permissions. VS Code asks first.
  • MCP: servers can reach other systems. Add only servers you trust.
  • Untrusted text: a README, issue, or web page can contain instructions aimed at the model. This is prompt injection. Tell learners to read what the agent fetched, not just what it wrote.

docs.title: Steering (0:22 to 0:35)
docs.text:
1. Plan first. Use Plan mode, or write "Plan only. Don't edit files." Edit the plan, then say go.
  2. Write a good prompt. Goal, the behavior you want, where to work, how to check it ("run npm test").
  3. Watch the tool calls. Expand them. If it reads the wrong files, stop and redirect.
  4. Review the diff. Open each changed file. Keep or undo per file or per change.
  5. Checkpoints. Chat keeps a restore point for each request. Restore to go back and try another prompt. Check the current docs for the exact UI.
  6. Terminal approval. Read each command. Allow once for unfamiliar ones. Auto-approving a safe command like npm test is reasonable. Auto-approving everything is the mistake. Setting names change, so look them up in the docs.

Say this once: tests are the agent's feedback. A project with tests gets better results.

docs.title: Agent mode vs CLI vs cloud agent (0:35 to 0:43)
docs.text:
IDE agent mode Copilot CLI (M2-01) Cloud agent (M3-02) Where it runs Your machine, in VS Code Your machine, in a terminal GitHub's environment Your role Watch and review as it works Watch and review as it works Review the pull request Output Edits in your working tree Edits in your working tree A branch and a pull request Strength Diff view, checkpoints, editor context Scripts, terminal tasks, any editor Hand-off while you do other work

The loop is the same in all three. The place and your involvement change. Rule of thumb: start in the IDE for work you want to watch. Use the cloud agent for tasks you can describe fully and review later.

docs.title: Demo (0:43 to 0:55)
docs.text:
Use lab/starter/notes-api/.

  1. Open Chat in Ask mode. Paste the lab prompt. Read the answer. Nothing changes on disk.
  2. Switch to Agent mode in a new chat with the same prompt. Expand the tool calls. Approve npm test when asked.
  3. Open the diff. Point out one thing the plan or Ask answer didn't mention.
  4. Restore the checkpoint to show undo.
  5. Put your cursor on the TODO in src/routes/notes.js, open the lightbulb, and show Delegate to coding agent. Don't wait for the PR.

docs.title: Pros, cons, and tips
docs.text:
Pros Cons Handles multi-file changes in one request Can change more than you asked Runs tests and reacts to failures Long runs make big diffs Works on your real project and context Can build on a wrong assumption Every change is visible and undoable Slower than Ask for small questions

Tips

  • Say what "done" means: "all tests pass, README updated".
  • Ask for a plan, then edit the plan, then go.
  • Commit before a big run. Git is the real undo.
  • Give a short list of files to start from with #file references.
  • Keep requests small. Two small runs beat one huge one.
  • Add repository instructions (M1-03) for conventions it keeps getting wrong.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Vague prompt. "Add tags" leaves the agent to guess limits and format.
  • Skipping the plan on a task that touches five files.
  • Accepting all without reading the diff.
  • Auto-approving every command.
  • Doing everything in one chat. Long chats lose focus. Start a new one per task.
  • Using Agent for a question. Use Ask.
  • No tests, so neither of you can tell if it worked.

docs.title: Lab notes
docs.text:
• The Ask vs Agent comparison is qualitative. Ask learners what each output gave them and what it left out. Don't count messages or edits.
  • Part 6 changes a requirement on purpose (lowercase tags). It shows how to steer after a diff.
  • Part 7 needs a GitHub repo. Learners without one read the lightbulb step and skip the PR.
  • The finished project is lab/solution/notes-api/. Learners' code will differ. Compare behavior and tests, not lines.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Copilot only knows what is in its context window: the limited space that holds your prompt, instructions, files, and the conversation. Good results depend on filling it with the right material.

This session covers the ways to supply context and when to use each: Copilot Spaces, repository instructions, path-specific instructions, prompt files, custom agents, skills, memory, and @-mentions. In the lab you build a real Space, write an instructions file, and run the same task four times to see what each one changes.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain what a context window is and why more context isn't always better.
  • Explain what a Copilot Space is: its sources, how they refresh, who can see it, and how to share it.
  • Write .github/copilot-instructions.md and a path-specific .instructions.md file with an applyTo pattern.
  • Choose between a Space, instructions, a prompt file, a custom agent, a skill, memory, and an @-mention.
  • Run a controlled before-and-after comparison of context mechanisms.
  • Spot stale sources, context overload, and sensitive data in shared context.

docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Starter project and scorecard lab/starter/ Reference instructions, Space setup, expected results lab/solution/

docs.text:
• Context windows and curation
  • Copilot Spaces: sources, refresh, sharing, visibility
  • .github/copilot-instructions.md and .instructions.md with applyTo
  • Prompt files, custom agents, skills, and memory
  • @-mentions and file context
  • Comparison table, pros, cons, tips, and common mistakes
  • Optional: /env and /instructions in the Copilot CLI

docs.title: Give Copilot the right material, and only that
docs.text: Session M2-03 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Context windows 8 min Copilot Spaces 15 min The other mechanisms 15 min Which one when 8 min Demo: same task, three contexts 9 min Pros, cons, tips, mistakes 5 min

docs.title: Context window
docs.text:
The context window is everything the model can see for one reply.

  • your prompt and the chat so far
  • instructions Copilot adds for you
  • files, snippets, and Space sources
  • tool results

It has a size limit. Anything outside it doesn't exist for the model.

docs.title: Why curation matters
docs.text:
• Missing context: Copilot guesses. Guesses look confident.
  • Too much context: the answer gets vague, slower, and more expensive.
  • Wrong context: Copilot follows it faithfully.

Goal: the smallest set of sources that makes the task answerable.

docs.title: What is a Copilot Space?
docs.text:
A named, saved collection of context that you ask questions against.

  • Sources: files, folders, repositories, pull requests, issues, uploads, pasted text
  • Instructions: a few lines on the Space's job and limits
  • Lives on GitHub, outside any chat history

Reach it in Copilot Chat on github.com, or in an IDE or the CLI through the GitHub MCP server.

docs.title: Sources and refresh
docs.text:
Source How it loads File Whole file, in the window, every question Repository Searched. Only relevant parts come back Pull request, issue Linked by URL Upload, pasted text Static. It never updates

GitHub files follow the main branch. Push to main and the Space updates.

docs.title: Who can see a Space
docs.text:
Owner Sharing options Personal Private, specific people, or public (view-only) Organization Org members as admin, editor, or viewer, or no access

Viewers only see sources they can access. Sharing a Space doesn't open the repository.

Mixing private and multi-org sources can break chat. Check the current docs.

docs.title: Spaces: where and what it costs
docs.text:
• Any Copilot plan, including Free
  • Questions count as Copilot Chat requests
  • IDE and CLI access needs the GitHub MCP server with the copilot_spaces toolset
  • In the IDE, whole-repository and uploaded sources aren't available

Check current docs. This area changes.

docs.title: Repository instructions
docs.text:
.github/copilot-instructions.md

  • Added to every request in the repository
  • Short rules for style, build, test, and what to avoid
  • Lives in git, so the team shares it

Also read by Copilot: AGENTS.md, and user-level files in ~/.copilot/.

docs.title: Path-specific instructions
docs.text:
.github/instructions/routes.instructions.md

---
applyTo: "src/routes/**/*.js"
---

Register fixed paths before `/:id` routes.
  • Loads only when Copilot works on a matching file
  • Comma-separate globs: **/*.ts,**/*.tsx
  • Keeps the always-on file small

docs.title: Prompt files
docs.text:
.github/prompts/low-stock.prompt.md

  • A saved prompt you run on purpose, usually as a slash command
  • Good for a task you repeat: review, scaffold, write docs
  • Support differs by tool. Check the docs for yours.

Instructions are always on. A prompt file runs when you call it.

docs.title: Custom agents and skills
docs.text:
Gives Copilot Loads Custom agent (.agent.md) A role with its own tools and rules When you pick it or it's delegated to Skill (SKILL.md) A repeatable workflow When your request matches its description

Both are covered in Module 3. Here, know where they sit.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Copilot can remember facts from past work.

  • Repository facts: conventions, commands. Shared with people who can use Memory in that repository.
  • User preferences: how you like to work. Follow you across repositories.

Copilot writes them, not you. Review and delete what's wrong.

Available on paid plans. Check the docs for your surface.

docs.title: @-mentions and file context
docs.text:
The quickest context: point at it.

  • Attach a file, selection, or folder in chat
  • In the CLI, @path/to/file
  • In the IDE, #file and open tabs

Good for one task. Gone when the chat ends.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Mechanism Scope Loads Best for Space Anyone you share it with You ask in it Reference docs and specs Repo instructions Whole repository Always House rules Path instructions Matching files When working on them Rules for one area Prompt file Repository or user You run it Repeated tasks Custom agent Repository or user You pick it A role and tool set Skill Repository or user Matches the request A workflow with files Memory Repo or you Automatically Learned facts @-mention This chat You attach it One-off context

docs.title: Which one when
docs.text:
You want to... Use Answer questions from your spec and docs Space Enforce "ES modules, node:test" everywhere Repo instructions Apply a rule only to src/routes/ Path instructions Rerun the same review prompt Prompt file Look at one file right now @-mention

Facts the code lacks go to a Space. Habits for every task go to instructions.

docs.title: Demo: one task, three contexts
docs.text:
Task: add GET /api/products/low-stock with tests.

  1. No context
  2. With the Space
  3. With instructions

We score each on the same checklist.

docs.title: Pros and cons of a Space
docs.text: Pros Cons Context outlives chat Stale if sources aren't kept up Shareable Too much context hurts answers Follows main A bad push changes answers Right sources, not the whole repo Sensitive data can leak to viewers

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start with 3 to 5 sources.
  • Prefer files for key docs. Use a repository for big doc trees.
  • Write Space instructions as the job and its limits.
  • Keep instructions under about a page. Cut what code already shows.
  • Test any context with a question you know the answer to.
  • Date-check sources the way you'd date-check docs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Adding a whole repository "just in case" Add the files that matter One giant instructions file Split with applyTo Instructions that contradict the code Fix the instruction or the code Secrets or customer data in a shared Space Synthetic or public data only Uploads that go stale Link GitHub files instead Blaming the model for missing facts Check what context it had

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Build a Space. Write instructions. Run one task four times.

Part Time Set up 15 min Build the Space 25 min No context, then Space 25 min Write instructions 20 min Instructions, then both 25 min Compare 10 min

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-03 lab: Build a Space, then compare context
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: One working Copilot Space, a short instructions file, and a filled-in comparison of four runs of the same task

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You add one endpoint to a small Storefront API four times. Each run gets different context. You score the results and see which mechanism supplied what.

Part Work Time 1 Set up the project and a private repository 15 min 2 Build the Space 25 min 3 Run the task with no context, then with the Space 25 min 4 Write the instructions 20 min 5 Run with instructions, then with both 25 min 6 Compare and decide 10 min

Stretch tasks at the end are optional and sit outside the 2 hours.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • a GitHub account with Copilot, and access to Copilot Spaces;
  • the standalone Copilot CLI from Session M2-01;
  • Git, the gh CLI (signed in), and Node.js 18 or later.

Use only the synthetic Storefront files in this lab. Put them in a private repository on your personal account. Don't add real company code or data to the Space.

docs.title: Part 1: Set up
docs.text:
Make two copies of the project. The full copy goes to GitHub and feeds the Space. The bare copy has only src/ and package.json. You run every task in the bare copy, so Copilot can't read the docs on its own.

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-03
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-03
cp -R <path-to-repo>/sessions/session-m2-03-spaces-and-context/lab/starter/ecommerce-project storefront-api
cp <path-to-repo>/sessions/session-m2-03-spaces-and-context/lab/starter/context-comparison.md .

cd storefront-api
git init -q -b main && git add -A && git commit -qm "Start"
gh repo create storefront-api-lab --private --source . --push

cd ..
mkdir bare-api && cp -R storefront-api/src storefront-api/package.json bare-api/
cd bare-api
npm install
printf 'node_modules\n' > .gitignore
git init -q -b main && git add -A && git commit -qm "Bare start"

Open storefront-api/docs/api-spec.md and read the Low-stock report section. Your task needs that behavior, and the code doesn't contain it.

Checkpoint: storefront-api-lab exists on GitHub with docs/ on main. bare-api has no docs/ folder.

docs.title: Part 2: Build the Space
docs.text:
Go to github.com/copilot/spaces.

  1. Click Create space. Name it Storefront API reference. Choose your personal account as owner.
  2. Add Instructions. Paste the text from lab/solution/space-setup.md, or write your own in five lines or fewer.
  3. Click Add sources, then Add files and repositories. Pick storefront-api-lab and add these four files, not the repository:
  4. docs/api-spec.md
  5. docs/architecture.md
  6. src/models/product.js
  7. src/routes/products.js
  8. Leave the Space private.

Why files and not the repository? Copilot loads a file into the context window in full, for every question. It searches a repository and pulls only what looks relevant. For a few key documents, files are more predictable. For a large docs tree, a repository is the better source.

docs.title: Test the Space
docs.text:
Ask in the Space chat:

What is the default low-stock threshold, and which products does the report exclude?

You should get a threshold of 10, with inactive and discontinued products excluded, taken from api-spec.md.

docs.title: Watch a source refresh
docs.text:
GitHub files in a Space follow the main branch of their repository. Check it:

  1. In storefront-api, change the default threshold in docs/api-spec.md from 10 to 20. Commit and push to main.
  2. Ask the same question in the Space. The change may take a moment to show up. If it doesn't, check the current docs.
  3. Change the threshold back to 10 and push again.

This helps when docs change. It hurts when someone pushes a bad change. A Space is only as current and as correct as main.

Checkpoint: The Space answers from the spec, and you saw one answer change after a push.

docs.title: Part 3: Run the task twice
docs.text:
Use this exact prompt every time:

Add GET /api/products/low-stock that lists products running low on stock.
Put it in its own route file and add tests. Run the tests.

For each run: branch from main, start a fresh Copilot session, paste the prompt, save the diff, and go back to main.

docs.title: Run 1: no context
docs.text:
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-03/bare-api
git switch -c run-1-none
copilot

Paste the prompt. Allow file writes and npm commands when asked. When it finishes, exit and save the result:

git add -A && git commit -qm "Run 1" && git diff main > ../run-1.diff
git switch main

docs.title: Run 2: with the Space
docs.text:
The CLI's built-in GitHub MCP server doesn't include Spaces tools by default. Enable them for the session:

git switch -c run-2-space
copilot --add-github-mcp-toolset copilot_spaces

Paste the prompt with one extra line:

Use my Copilot Space "Storefront API reference" for behavior and conventions.

Look for a get_copilot_space tool call. If Copilot doesn't make one, repeat the request and name the Space owner.

Save the diff as run-2.diff the same way, then git switch main.

If your CLI can't reach Spaces, check the current docs. As a fallback, ask the prompt in the Space chat on github.com and paste the code it returns into the bare copy. The surface differs, so note that in your comparison.

Checkpoint: You have run-1.diff and run-2.diff. Fill in the first two columns of context-comparison.md.

docs.title: Part 4: Write the instructions
docs.text:
Instructions load every time, without you asking. Keep them short, so they don't crowd out the task.

In bare-api, create two files. Write them yourself first. Open lab/solution/.github/ only to compare.

.github/copilot-instructions.md applies to the whole repository. Include:

  • language style: ES modules, file naming;
  • how responses and errors are shaped;
  • how to test: the framework, how to start the app, the command to run;
  • one thing to avoid, such as new dependencies.

Aim for 12 lines or fewer. Use short imperative bullets. Skip anything the code already shows clearly.

.github/instructions/routes.instructions.md applies only to matching files. It needs frontmatter:

---
applyTo: "src/routes/**/*.js"
---

Add two or three rules that matter only in route files. applyTo takes glob patterns, such as src/routes/**/*.js or **/*.ts,**/*.tsx.

Commit both files on main:

git add -A && git commit -qm "Add instructions"

Checkpoint: Two files under .github/, committed on main. Neither repeats the low-stock spec.

docs.title: Part 5: Run with instructions, then with both
Run 3: instructions only
docs.text:
git switch -c run-3-instructions
copilot

Paste the plain prompt, with no Space line. Save run-3.diff and git switch main.

docs.title: Run 4: instructions and Space
docs.text:
git switch -c run-4-both
copilot --add-github-mcp-toolset copilot_spaces

Paste the prompt with the Space line. Save run-4.diff and git switch main.

Checkpoint: Four diffs. Fill in the last two columns of your comparison.

docs.title: Part 6: Compare and decide
docs.text:
Fill in the last two sections of context-comparison.md:

  1. What changed between runs. Name one behavior the Space fixed and one the instructions fixed.
  2. Which context would you keep. For each line below, pick Space, repository instructions, path-specific instructions, prompt file, or nothing:
  3. "Our API returns { data } envelopes."
  4. "The spec for the low-stock report."
  5. "Use node:test in this repo."
  6. "Summarize this stack trace."
  7. "Review a PR with our checklist, when I ask."

Compare your table with lab/solution/expected-comparison.md. Model output varies, so your runs may differ. Rerun a prompt if a result looks odd.

docs.title: Stretch tasks
docs.text:
Pick one if you finish early.

  • See what the CLI loaded. Run /instructions in the Copilot CLI to list the instruction files it found, and switch one off. Run /env to see what else is loaded. Check the current CLI docs for details.
  • Prompt file. In VS Code, create .github/prompts/low-stock-report.prompt.md that holds the task prompt, and run it from chat. Prompt-file support differs by tool and VS Code version, so check the current docs. If it doesn't run, skip this task.
  • Stale instruction. Add a rule to routes.instructions.md that contradicts the code, such as "use CommonJS". Rerun and see what happens. Delete it.
  • Share a Space. Create a Space under an organization you can use and compare its sharing options with your personal one.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. A private storefront-api-lab repository and a Space with four file sources and short instructions.
  2. .github/copilot-instructions.md and one .instructions.md file with an applyTo pattern.
  3. Four diffs (run-1.diff to run-4.diff).
  4. A filled-in context-comparison.md, including your choices from Part 6.

  • Adding custom instructions for Copilot CLI

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-03 trainer guide: Copilot Spaces & context management
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Learners leave knowing what each context mechanism is, when to use it, and how to tell from a result which one is missing.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 Context windows and curation 0:08 to 0:23 Copilot Spaces 0:23 to 0:38 The other mechanisms 0:38 to 0:46 Which one when 0:46 to 0:55 Demo: same task, three contexts 0:55 to 1:00 Pros, cons, tips, mistakes, lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Run the lab once. Keep your Space, your bare-api copy, and lab/solution/ open.
  • Check the Spaces toolset works in your CLI: copilot --add-github-mcp-toolset copilot_spaces, then ask for your Space by name.
  • Have the demo repository pushed to a private repository on your personal account.
  • Open the current Spaces and custom instructions docs. Details change often.

docs.title: Context windows and curation (0:00 to 0:08)
docs.text:
• The context window is everything the model sees for one reply: prompt, chat history, instructions, attached files, tool output. It has a size limit.
  • The model has no other memory of your project. If it isn't in the window, it guesses.
  • Three failures: missing context (confident guesses), too much (vague, slower, costs more), wrong (followed faithfully).
  • Goal: the smallest set of sources that makes the task answerable.

Ask: "What would a new teammate need on day one for this task?" That list is your context.

docs.title: Copilot Spaces (0:08 to 0:23)
docs.text:
What it is. A named collection of sources plus short instructions that you ask questions against. It lives on GitHub, not in chat history.

Sources. Files, folders, whole repositories, pull requests, issues, uploaded files, pasted text.

  • An attached file loads in full on every question.
  • An attached repository is searched. Only relevant parts come back.
  • For a few key documents, use files. For a large docs tree, use the repository.

How sources refresh. GitHub files and other GitHub sources follow the main branch. A push to main updates the Space. Uploads and pasted text don't change on their own.

Who can see it.

  • Personal Space: private, shared with named users, or public. Public Spaces are view-only by default.
  • Organization Space: org members get admin, editor, or viewer, or no access.
  • Viewers only see sources they can already access. Sharing a Space doesn't grant repository access.
  • Spaces that mix private and multi-organization sources may not work in chat. Check the docs.

Where you use it. Copilot Chat on github.com. IDE and CLI access goes through the GitHub MCP server with the copilot_spaces toolset, which isn't on by default. In the IDE, whole-repository and uploaded sources aren't available. Check the current docs.

Cost. Questions in a Space count as Copilot Chat usage.

Show: create a Space live, add two files, ask a question whose answer is only in them.

docs.title: The other mechanisms (0:23 to 0:38)
docs.text:
Go through them in this order. One minute of "what", one of "when".

Mechanism Where it lives What it is Repository instructions .github/copilot-instructions.md Always-on rules for the repository Path-specific instructions .github/instructions/*.instructions.md with applyTo Rules that load only for matching files Prompt file .github/prompts/*.prompt.md A saved prompt you run on purpose Custom agent .github/agents/*.agent.md A role with its own tools and rules (M3-04) Skill SKILL.md in a skills folder A workflow loaded when the request matches (M3-05) Memory Managed by Copilot Facts and preferences Copilot learned @-mention, file context Your chat Files you point at for one task

Key points:

  • Instructions are short and always on. About a page at most. Skip what the code already shows.
  • applyTo takes globs, comma-separated: **/*.ts,**/*.tsx. Use it to keep the main file small.
  • The CLI also reads AGENTS.md and user-level files in ~/.copilot/. Don't write conflicting rules in several files. Copilot combines them and defines no precedence.
  • Prompt files differ by tool. GitHub lists VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, and Xcode. The CLI docs don't list them, so check /help in your version. VS Code docs now tie prompt files to the Local harness and suggest skills for new work.
  • Memory is written by Copilot, not you. Repository facts are shared with people who can use Memory there. User preferences follow you. Show learners where to review and delete.
  • @-mention is the cheapest option. It doesn't last past the chat.

docs.title: Which one when (0:38 to 0:46)
docs.text:
Ask the room to sort five needs, then reveal.

Need Use Answer questions from the spec and design docs Space "ES modules and node:test" everywhere Repository instructions A rule only for src/routes/ Path-specific instructions Rerun the same review prompt Prompt file Look at one file right now @-mention

Rule of thumb: facts the code lacks go to a Space. Habits for every task go to instructions.

docs.title: Demo: same task, three contexts (0:46 to 0:55)
docs.text:
Use the lab task. Work in bare-api on a branch per run.

  1. Run with no context. Read the diff. Point out the guessed threshold and the test framework.
  2. Run with the Space. Show the get_copilot_space call. Point out the spec rules in the code.
  3. Run with instructions. Point out node:test and the error shape.

Keep a scorecard on screen. Say out loud which mechanism caused each change. If a run goes odd, say that model output varies and move on.

docs.title: Pros, cons, tips (0:55 to 1:00)
docs.text:
Pros of curated context: right answers on the first try, shareable, lives in git or on GitHub, saves repeated prompting.

Cons and risks:

  • Stale sources. A Space follows main, so it can also follow a bad change. Uploads never refresh.
  • Too much context. Whole repositories and long instruction files dilute the answer.
  • Sensitive data. Viewers see what the Space contains. Keep secrets, customer data, and real internal code out unless you know the audience.
  • Silent failure. A missing source doesn't raise an error. The answer is just worse.
  • Conflicting files. Several instruction files can disagree.

Tips:

  • Start with 3 to 5 sources.
  • Test a new Space with a question whose answer you know.
  • Write instructions as short commands, one idea each.
  • Put a rule in the narrowest place that works.
  • Review Spaces and instructions when the code changes.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Open lab/README.md. Tell learners to save each diff, because the comparison depends on them. Tell them the CLI needs the copilot_spaces flag for runs 2 and 4. Stretch tasks hold the CLI diagnostics and prompt files.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Adding the whole repository "just in case" Add the files the task needs One long instructions file Move area-specific rules to .instructions.md with applyTo applyTo glob matches nothing Test with the file you expect it to match Run 2 never calls the Space Start the CLI with --add-github-mcp-toolset copilot_spaces and name the Space Comparing runs from the same session Start a fresh session each time Instructions repeat the spec Put facts in the Space and habits in instructions Judging from one run Rerun once if a result looks odd Secrets in a Space Use synthetic data only

docs.title: Answer key for lab Part 6
docs.text:
Line Best home "Our API returns { data } envelopes." Repository instructions (and it's in the architecture doc for the Space) "The spec for the low-stock report." Space "Use node:test in this repo." Repository instructions "Summarize this stack trace." Nothing. Paste it. "Review a PR with our checklist, when I ask." Prompt file

Accept other answers if the reasoning holds.
