docs.title: Session M2-04: Copilot for code review & pull requests
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Copilot in Practice Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-03 Duration: 3 hours (1 hr trainer content + 2 hr lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Follow one pull request from change brief to final human decision. Inspect a flawed change, run /review and /security-review on its local diff, and compare those findings with Copilot PR review. Then correct the code and resolve a conflict. Keep the completed review template and the test output.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Generate PR summaries and review comments with Copilot
  • Configure automatic Copilot reviews for a repository or organization
  • Judge Copilot review quality and blind spots
  • Run general and security review on a local patch before committing
  • Triage unsupported claims and check fixes with regression tests
  • Resolve a merge conflict manually and keep both branches' intended behavior

docs.title: Session materials
docs.text: Resource Location Lab exercises lab/ Lab starter files lab/starter/ Lab solution files lab/solution/

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• PR summaries and commit message generation
  • Copilot code review, manual and automatic
  • Local /review and /security-review, then review of the correction diff
  • Review comments with one-click fixes
  • Manual merge conflict resolution and tests
  • Quality gates and team adoption

docs.title: Diffs, test results, and human judgment
Review is a human responsibility
docs.text:
Automation raises questions. A reviewer decides whether a change is correct, safe, maintainable, and in scope.

Issue and acceptance criteria
        ↓
Proposed change and checks
        ↓
Human review
        ↓
Accept, request revision, or implement manually

docs.title: Review rubric
docs.text:
• Correctness against acceptance criteria
  • Tests and check results
  • Security, dependency, and permission implications
  • Scope and maintainability
  • Repository conventions and human approval

docs.title: Conflict-resolution exercise
docs.text:
1. Read both branch intentions.
  2. Write the merged behavior and tests before editing.
  3. Resolve the conflict manually in the sandbox.
  4. Run checks and request review.

docs.title: Review the same diff through separate passes
docs.text:
1. Record the human verdict before assisted review.
  2. Leave the patch uncommitted and run /review.
  3. Run /security-review against that same local patch.
  4. Triage both outputs, then commit and request Copilot PR review.
  5. Repeat the local commands on the correction diff before committing fixes.

Keep the original verdict. Record no-findings results.

docs.title: A finding needs support
docs.text:
Claim Check Exposed password field Inspect the actual response and add a regression test Database compromise The mock route never executes SQL; reject that claim Leaked credential The strings are fake and unused; reject a live-leak claim Pagination defect Check page-one behavior separately from security review

Record: review source, file/line, impact, check, and triage decision.

docs.title: Local review vs PR review
docs.text:
/review, /security-review Copilot PR review Runs In the Copilot CLI, in your repo On GitHub Examines Staged and unstaged changes The pushed PR diff Shows Findings in your terminal; read-only Comments on the PR, some with suggested fixes Use Private first pass before you commit The pass teammates see

Their findings overlap but differ. Triage both. Neither approves.

docs.title: Security review has a narrow scope
docs.text:
/security-review examines current local changes. It's read-only and doesn't replace repository security scanning.

A clean result doesn't make a change secure. The human reviewer decides.

docs.title: Agenda and time plan
docs.text: Time Topic 0:00 Review workflow and roles 0:08 Summaries and descriptions 0:18 Local commands and PR review 0:28 Defect and triage demo 0:43 Suggestions and conflicts 0:51 Limits and adoption 0:58 Lab handoff and Q&A

docs.title: Copilot across a PR lifecycle
docs.text:
Issue and acceptance criteria
          ↓
Branch and bounded commits
          ↓
Draft summary and PR description
          ↓
Automated checks + Copilot first pass
          ↓
Human review and author response
          ↓
Approval, revision, or close

docs.title: Commit messages and PR descriptions
docs.text:
Copilot drafts text from the visible change. In the lab, you draft one from a staged diff and delete what the diff doesn't show. Authors check that:

  • the user-visible behavior is accurate;
  • tests and results aren't invented;
  • breaking changes and migrations are named;
  • security and dependency implications are named;
  • issue links and acceptance criteria match the work.

A polished summary can still be wrong.

docs.title: A reviewable PR template
docs.text:
## Problem
What user-visible problem does this solve?

## Change
List the bounded implementation choices.

## Validation
- [ ] Focused tests
- [ ] Existing checks
- [ ] Manual edge case

## Risk and rollback
Name data, dependency, security, and recovery considerations.

docs.title: Requesting Copilot review
docs.text:
1. Check that the PR is ready for a first pass.
  2. Request the Copilot review from the PR.
  3. Treat the comments as hypotheses.
  4. Resolve them, reject them with a reason, or implement a checked fix.
  5. Request human review with the diff, findings, and check results.

Copilot review doesn't replace required reviewers.

docs.title: Automatic review configuration
docs.text:
You can configure automatic review at repository or organization scope.

Before enabling:

  • choose eligible repositories;
  • decide who triages comments;
  • keep branch protection and required human approvals;
  • watch noise, missed findings, and review delay;
  • know how to turn it off.

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text:
Gate Checks Ready for first pass Clear description, focused diff, tests available Ready for human review Checks pass; AI comments triaged Ready for approval Acceptance criteria met; risks reviewed Ready for merge Required approvals and branch protections satisfied

Copilot review comes before human approval. It never replaces it.

docs.title: Demo PR: intentional defect
docs.text:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

The requirement says suspended users must never view invoices.

if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;

Ask which tests should accompany this suggestion.

docs.title: Demo narrative: complete lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Open the issue and read acceptance criteria aloud.
  2. Inspect the focused branch diff before generated prose.
  3. Generate or improve the PR description; correct unsupported claims.
  4. Run required checks and request Copilot review.
  5. Classify each comment: valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Apply one checked fix and add a regression test.
  7. Request human review and record the final decision.

docs.title: Reviewing suggested fixes
docs.text:
Before applying:

  • restate the finding in your own words;
  • reproduce the defect or find the violated requirement;
  • inspect the complete patch, not only highlighted lines;
  • add a test that fails before the fix;
  • run broader checks in proportion to the risk.

One-click application saves typing. The reviewer still decides.

docs.title: What review may catch
docs.text:
• localized correctness issues;
  • missing error handling or tests;
  • suspicious patterns visible in the diff;
  • inconsistent naming or repository conventions.

docs.title: What it may miss
docs.text:
• unstated product intent;
  • cross-system behavior absent from context;
  • runtime, operational, or legal risk;
  • subtle authorization and data-boundary flaws;
  • plausible but misleading changes.

docs.title: Merge conflict resolution
docs.text:
Base behavior + branch A intent + branch B intent
                        ↓
              write merged acceptance criteria
                        ↓
                resolve conflict in sandbox
                        ↓
                 run tests and human review

Don't blindly choose "ours" or "theirs."

docs.title: Adoption patterns
docs.text:
Start: Optional first-pass review on a few repositories.

Measure: Actionable findings, false positives, review time, rework, and defects that reach users.

Adapt: Tune scope, guidance, and escalation.

Expand: Only when quality and developer experience hold up.

Know how to pause reviews for a repository that needs an exception.

docs.title: Facilitation prompts
docs.text:
• Which comment needs domain expertise to evaluate?
  • Which code reference or test would resolve an uncertain comment?
  • Which repositories should not use automatic review?
  • How will the team detect over-reliance?

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
You will:

  1. follow one pull request from a flawed change brief;
  2. classify human and Copilot findings;
  3. apply only fixes supported by code references or test results;
  4. resolve the prepared conflict without losing either branch goal;
  5. record the final human decision.

Deliverable: The completed fix evaluation template, the corrected project with passing tests, and the conflict result.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Check generated summaries against the diff.
  2. AI review is a first pass. A human decides.
  3. Suggested fixes need reproduction, inspection, and tests.
  4. Conflict resolution starts from the intended merged behavior.
  5. Measure adoption and keep it reversible.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Which review decision needs a human, and what should they check?

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-04 lab: Code review workflows
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A completed fix-evaluation-template.md, a corrected project with passing tests, and a resolved conflict

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Review a deliberately flawed change. Support each comment with a code reference or test result, apply targeted fixes, and decide whether to accept the change. Compare your own review with Copilot-assisted review. Use only synthetic data.

Exercise Topic Time 1 Human, code, and security review of one diff 40 min 2 Validate and correct the starter project 35 min 3 Resolve a conflict and check the result 25 min 4 Review the results and make a final decision 20 min

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• the standalone Copilot CLI with /review and /security-review (check /help);
  • Copilot pull-request review;
  • an empty private GitHub repository you can push to (create one with gh repo create --private, or use the one the trainer gives you);
  • Git, the authenticated GitHub CLI (gh auth status), Node.js, and npm.

docs.title: What the review commands do
docs.text:
/review and /security-review Copilot PR review Where In your Copilot CLI session, in your working repository On GitHub, on the pull request What it examines Your staged and unstaged changes, before you commit The PR diff, after you push Output Findings in the terminal. Both commands only read; they don't edit files. Review comments on the PR, some with a suggested fix to apply Focus /review: correctness and missing tests. /security-review: high-confidence vulnerabilities in the change. General review of the PR. You can also set it to run automatically.

Committing the patch removes it from /review's scope. Local findings are private and quick, so use them before you push. PR review is the one your teammates see. Neither approves anything.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Starter assets:

  • lab/starter/review-project/: Express API under review, with src/api.js, src/utils.js, and Jest/Supertest tests in tests/api.test.js
  • lab/starter/code-changes.md: intentionally flawed changes to review
  • lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md: structured review worksheet
  • lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md: finding, fix, and test record
  • lab/starter/conflict-scenario/: manual merge-conflict scenario (README.md, utils-with-conflict.js)

Create a workspace outside the curriculum folder:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04
cp -R lab/starter/review-project ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04/review-project
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04/review-project
npm install
npm test
git init
printf 'node_modules/\n' > .gitignore
git add .gitignore package.json package-lock.json src tests
git commit -m "Record review baseline"
git branch -M main
git switch -c feature/add-user-management

Expected: npm install adds no new dependencies and npm test reports that the existing API tests pass.

If install or tests fail: Fix the environment. Don't change package versions to hide a failure.

Add your private repository as origin and push the baseline:

git remote add origin <private-training-repository-url>
git push -u origin main

The baseline must be the same commit locally and remotely, so the PR contains only the intended change. If the remote already has commits, use an empty repository. Never force-push or push the intentional defects to a public repository.

No private repository? Skip step 11 of Exercise 1 and compare /review with /security-review instead.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Review one diff through three passes (40 minutes)
Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the change brief. Open lab/starter/code-changes.md. It lists changes to src/api.js and src/utils.js, each with an intended defect.

  2. Open lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md. Use its one triage table for human, local, and PR findings. Each row names a file or function and the code or test output that supports it.

  3. Read the baseline. Open src/api.js, src/utils.js, and tests/api.test.js. Note the existing behavior so you can separate it from introduced defects.

  4. Apply the change brief on feature/add-user-management. Keep the changes uncommitted until both local reviews finish. Compare git diff -- src/api.js src/utils.js with the brief. Add no unrelated features.

  5. Run the existing checks.

npm test

Some tests may still pass because the defects aren't fully covered. Note the output and any missing coverage.

  1. Review the change yourself first. Write your initial verdict in the template and add your two most important findings to the triage table with Human as the source. Use partner-review-checklist.md for prompts if you want them.

  2. Run the general code review. Start copilot in the working repository:

/review Review the current changes to src/api.js and src/utils.js for
correctness and missing tests. Cite file and line references. Review only;
do not edit files.
  1. Run the security review on the same diff:
/security-review

Both commands review staged and unstaged changes. Committing the patch first removes it from that scope. (With a clean tree, /security-review reviews the branch diff instead.)

  1. Triage both outputs in the template. Leave your human findings unchanged. Accept, reject, or leave each finding unresolved, with a reason. If a review reports no findings, write that in the Review runs table.

The search route builds SQL text but connects to no database, so reject a claim that the lab proves database compromise. Synthetic key-shaped strings aren't a leaked real credential. Keep actual data exposure separate from unsafe patterns and maintainability suggestions.

  1. Draft the commit message and PR description with Copilot. Stage the two files, then in copilot:

    Write a commit message and a PR description (problem, change, validation,
risk) for the staged diff. Use only what the diff shows.

    Compare every claim with the diff. Delete any test result or benefit the diff doesn't show. Commit with the corrected message.

  2. Open the training PR. Push to your private remote and open a PR:

    git push -u origin feature/add-user-management
gh pr create --base main --title "Review synthetic user management" \
  --body "Training-only change. Contains intentional defects; do not merge."

    Request Copilot review from the PR page. In the template, record one finding that differs from the local results. Don't merge the flawed change.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
• Which findings block approval, and which are suggestions only?
  • Which defects did the existing tests miss?
  • What did /review, /security-review, and PR review each report, and what did only one of them find?
  • What changed after the assisted review?
  • Which claim rests on actual behavior rather than an assumed backend?

docs.title: Exercise 2: Validate and correct the starter project (35 minutes)
docs.text: Fix the defects with the smallest safe changes, then show the corrected project meets the review criteria.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Prioritize blocking findings. Start with issues that leak sensitive data, allow injection, crash the server, or return incorrect behavior. List each defect, its file, and the check you will run.

  2. Fix input handling in src/api.js. Replace unsafe string interpolation and fragile parsing with validated inputs and safe response shapes. The endpoint should handle empty, missing, malformed, and valid inputs predictably. Show the error responses in tests or manual requests.

  3. Fix sensitive response data. Remove password-like or token-like fields from responses. The JSON should show only fields the API contract needs.

  4. Fix pagination in src/utils.js. Page 1 starts with the first item, and boundary cases return predictable results. A focused test or Node.js check covers page 1, page 2, and empty collections.

  5. Add or update focused tests in tests/api.test.js for the behavior the original suite missed. New tests fail before the fix and pass after it.

  6. Run checks again.

npm test

All tests should pass. If one fails, record the failing assertion and correct only the related implementation or test expectation.

  1. Update the triage rows in fix-evaluation-template.md. Add the fix and regression test to each accepted finding. Record residual risk in its Human decision section.

  2. Review the correction diff before committing. Rerun /review and /security-review on it and compare with the initial findings. Rerun npm test, then commit and push only the reviewed fixes to the same PR (or just commit if you have no remote). A clean automated review doesn't approve the PR.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
• Every blocking finding maps to a focused fix.
  • New tests cover the missed behavior.
  • npm test passes.
  • The fix evaluation names residual risk.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Resolve a conflict (25 minutes)
docs.text: Resolve a merge conflict so both branches' intended behavior survives.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario. Open lab/starter/conflict-scenario/README.md. Two branches modify src/utils.js: one adds date formatting, the other changes price formatting.

  2. Open the conflicting source, lab/starter/conflict-scenario/utils-with-conflict.js. Find the conflicting region and state what each side does.

  3. Write the merged behavior before editing:

Preserve formatDate for date display and preserve formatPrice with an explicit
currency parameter. Existing callers should continue to work or be updated
intentionally.

  1. Resolve the conflict manually. Remove the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers, keep both valid behaviors, and avoid unrelated formatting changes.

  2. Add focused tests for date formatting, default currency, supplied currency, and unchanged helpers.

  3. Run the project test command and save the output.

  4. Peer review the resolution. Ask a partner to review only the resolution and tests. They should be able to say why both branch goals appear in the result.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
• No conflict markers remain.
  • Both branch goals appear in the resolved behavior.
  • Tests cover date and currency formatting.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Review the code and test results (20 minutes)
docs.text: Use the code and test results to make your final decision. An automated suggestion alone isn't enough.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Select one blocking finding from Exercise 1 (security, correctness, or reliability). It needs a file reference, impact, and acceptance criterion.

  2. Check its triage row. Add any missing before/after behavior, test names, or command output. A reviewer should reproduce the result from your notes.

  3. Classify remaining risk:

Risk type Question Data Did the change expose or process restricted data? Dependency Did the change add or update packages? Permission Did the workflow need a new permission? Security Did validation, error handling, or secrets handling change? Quality Do the tests and review results support the decision?

  1. Complete Human decision in fix-evaluation-template.md. Choose approve, request changes, or pause, and explain why. Someone reading it should understand the decision without seeing your lab conversation.

  2. Compare your initial review with the local and PR results. In the triage table, mark differences, false positives, and any finding that changed your verdict. Keep your original findings.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
• The decision is approve, request changes, or pause.
  • The rationale cites findings, fixes, and check results.
  • You accepted automated findings only after reviewing them.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. fix-evaluation-template.md, completed. It holds your initial verdict, the review runs, the triage table, test results, remaining risk, and decision.
  2. The corrected project, with npm test passing.
  3. The resolved conflict and its test output.
  4. The PR link, if you opened one.

Don't merge the training PR.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-04: Code review workflows
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Before teaching
docs.text: Prepare a small synthetic pull request, a reviewer, and a test command. Check that CLI /review, /security-review, and Copilot PR review work for you. Learners create their own empty private repository for the PR step. If they can't, they skip that step.

docs.title: Session objective
docs.text: Show learners how to use automated findings in a review. Learners check the diff, tests, and comments before they decide.

docs.title: Minute-mapped delivery plan (60 minutes)
docs.text:
Time Segment Result 0:00 to 0:08 Review roles Author, automation, checks, and reviewer roles are named. 0:08 to 0:18 PR summaries and review contracts Learners compare generated prose with the diff. 0:18 to 0:28 Local commands and PR review The group tells diff review from PR review. 0:28 to 0:43 Intentional-defect and triage demo Findings connect to behavior. Unsupported exploit claims are rejected. 0:43 to 0:51 Suggested fixes and conflicts Learners preserve intent before editing. 0:51 to 0:58 Limits, adoption, and Q&A Learners decide where people must review. 0:58 to 1:00 Close and lab handoff Reviewer roles are assigned.

The lab allocates 40/35/25/20 minutes to its four exercises.

docs.title: Segment 1: Review is an accountable decision (0:00 to 0:08)
Talking points
docs.text:
1. The author explains intent and supplies the diff and test output.
  2. Automated checks report results.
  3. Assisted review suggests issues to investigate.
  4. A human reviewer weighs intent, results, and risk.
  5. Branch rules and required approvals still apply.
  6. A generated summary, comment, or fix is never proof by itself.

Ask: "Who can explain why this change should merge?" The answer is the author and reviewer, backed by the diff and test output.

docs.title: Segment 2: Review contract and PR description (0:08 to 0:18)
docs.text:
Display:

## Problem
Suspended users must not view invoices.

## Change
Add an explicit suspended-status denial before role and ownership checks.

## Validation
- [ ] suspended administrator is denied
- [ ] suspended owner is denied
- [ ] active administrator is allowed
- [ ] active owner is allowed

## Risk and rollback
Authorization behavior changes only for suspended users; revert the bounded commit if needed.

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• Compare every generated statement with the diff.
  • Don't claim a test ran unless command output exists.
  • Name breaking behavior, dependencies, permissions, and data implications.
  • Keep the PR small enough to reconstruct intent.

docs.title: Mini-exercise
docs.text:
Read: "Improves invoice security and all tests pass."

Ask learners to find the unsupported claims. "Improves" needs defined behavior. "All tests pass" needs named command output.

docs.title: Segment 3: Review request and quality gates (0:18 to 0:28)
docs.text:
Open the small synthetic diff. Prepare the human-only review worksheet before opening assisted review.

Gate Result Ready for independent critique Clear intent, a small diff, and focused checks. Ready for assisted review The learner has written an initial verdict and the findings that matter most. Ready for human review Local and PR findings are classified and checks reported. Ready for approval A human reviewer has checked acceptance criteria and risks. Ready for merge Required approvals and repository protections are satisfied.

Before the assisted prompt, have learners write their initial verdict and their two important findings in lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md, with Human as the source. Afterward, they compare missed findings, false positives, and anything that changed the final decision.

docs.title: What the local commands run
docs.text:
Say this before the demo:

  • /review and /security-review run inside the Copilot CLI session, on the working repository on your machine. They read your staged and unstaged changes before any commit or push. Nothing appears on GitHub.
  • /review looks for correctness problems and missing tests. /security-review looks only for high-confidence vulnerabilities in that patch. Both only read; they don't edit files.
  • Copilot PR review runs on GitHub against the pushed PR diff. It leaves comments in the PR, some with a suggested fix, and can run automatically. Teammates see it.
  • Use the local commands for a private first pass. Use PR review where the team already reviews. Their findings overlap but differ, so triage both. Neither approves a change.

docs.title: Demonstrate the two local commands
docs.text:
Use a fresh Git repository with a committed baseline. Apply the synthetic changes from code-changes.md and leave them uncommitted.

/review Review the current changes for correctness and missing tests. Cite files
and lines. Review only; do not edit.

Then run:

/security-review

Both commands must see the same staged or unstaged patch. Committing it first leaves nothing for /review to examine, and /security-review falls back to the branch diff. Keep the output even if there are no findings. Check git diff afterward; review should not change the project.

Use the triage table in fix-evaluation-template.md. Each accepted finding needs a source, a claimed impact, and a reproduction or code reference. The mock search route doesn't execute SQL, and the training strings aren't live credentials, so don't teach them as proven exploits. Show the password exposure defect separately by inspecting the response.

After the local review, have learners stage the patch and ask Copilot to draft the commit message and PR description from the diff. They delete any claim the diff doesn't show. Then they push, request Copilot PR review, and compare results. Repeat both local commands on the uncommitted correction diff before they commit fixes.

docs.title: Scripted demo: Suspended invoice viewer (0:28 to 0:43)
docs.text: Use synthetic code with a local authorization defect to show the review steps.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use a disposable JavaScript file:

export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

Requirement:

Suspended users must never view invoices.
Active administrators and active invoice owners may view an invoice.
Other users may not view it.

Prepare four cases: suspended administrator, suspended owner, active administrator, and unrelated active user.

docs.title: Assisted-review prompt
docs.text:
Review only canViewInvoice against the stated requirement.
Return one file-specific finding with observed behavior, impact, and a test idea.
Do not propose unrelated refactoring.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the requirement before the implementation.
  2. Ask learners to predict each case.
  3. Run a prepared test or trace the cases manually.
  4. Request the assisted review of this function only.
  5. Classify the response as valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Restate the valid finding:
Observed: suspended administrators and owners currently return true.
Required: suspended users must always return false.
Decision: request changes and add regression coverage.
  1. Add or display a failing suspended-administrator test.
  2. Apply the smallest proposed fix:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}
  1. Run all four focused cases and inspect the complete diff.
  2. Ask the human reviewer to choose approve, request changes, or pause.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
• The suspended cases fail before the fix and return false after it.
  • Active administrator behavior stays true. An unrelated active user stays denied.
  • The diff contains one guard plus focused test changes.
  • The final decision cites the requirement and test results.

docs.title: Questions to ask
docs.text:
• Does the guard run before role and ownership checks?
  • Did any unrelated behavior change?
  • Does the review comment separate observation from assumption?

docs.title: Fallback worksheet
docs.text:
If the assisted review is unavailable or misses the defect, learners complete this table, write a review comment, a minimal patch, and test names. A peer makes the final decision.

User state Role/ownership Before Required Decision Suspended Admin true false Block Suspended Owner true false Block Active Admin true true Preserve Active Neither false false Preserve

If the assisted review invents broader policy, mark the comment uncertain or out of scope. If a suggested fix rewrites unrelated code, reject it and use the guard only.

docs.title: Segment 5: Suggested fixes and conflict intent (0:43 to 0:51)
Before applying a suggested fix
docs.text:
1. Restate the finding yourself.
  2. Reproduce the defect or find the violated criterion.
  3. Inspect the entire patch.
  4. Add a test that fails before the fix when practical.
  5. Run broader checks in proportion to risk.

docs.title: Conflict micro-exercise
docs.text:
Present:

Branch A adds formatDate.
Branch B adds an explicit currency parameter to formatPrice.

Before editing, learners write:

Preserve date formatting and price formatting with explicit currency.
Keep existing callers working or update them intentionally.

Ask for four checks: no conflict markers, a date example, a default currency example, and an explicit currency example.

Learners resolve the lab conflict manually, run tests, and review the result.

docs.title: Segment 6: Limits and adoption (0:51 to 0:58)
docs.text:
Assisted review may find local correctness issues, missing tests, error-handling problems, or convention mismatches.

It may miss unstated product intent, cross-system behavior, subtle authorization issues, operational risk, or plausible but misleading changes.

To adopt it, start with a small set of repositories. Track actionable findings, noise, rework, delays, and escaped defects. Decide who triages and how to pause automatic review.

docs.title: "Can Copilot approve a PR?"
docs.text: Not by default. Copilot reviews don't count toward required approvals unless an admin turns on Copilot approvals in the repository, organization, and enterprise settings. Required human reviewers and branch rules still apply.

docs.title: "Should we apply every suggested fix?"
docs.text: No. Reproduce the issue, inspect the complete patch, add a focused test, and accept only the smallest correct change.

docs.title: "What if human and assisted reviews disagree?"
docs.text: Return to the requirements, diff, and test output. Ask a domain owner if that doesn't settle it.

docs.title: "Can automatic review replace branch protection?"
docs.text: No. Keep required human review.

docs.title: "Why review a generated PR description?"
docs.text: It can invent results, omit risk, or misread intent. Compare every claim with the diff and command output.

docs.title: "Is security review covered by this feature?"
docs.text: /review checks general code issues. /security-review targets high-confidence vulnerabilities in current changes. It's a focused, read-only check. It doesn't replace code scanning, secret scanning, or dependency checks. Check /help in your Copilot CLI version before teaching.

docs.title: "Which repositories should enable automatic review?"
docs.text: Start with a few low-risk repositories. Define exclusions, owners, and a way to turn it off.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Reviewing the summary before the diff Read intent, diff, and checks first. Applying a patch from the highlighted lines only Inspect the entire proposed patch. Approving because checks pass Review coverage, intent, risk, and scope. Choosing "ours" in a conflict without thought Write the merged behavior before editing. Claiming tests passed without output Name and rerun the command.

docs.title: Closing and lab handoff (0:58 to 1:00)
docs.text:
Use automation as a first pass. Check its findings against the intended behavior, diff, and test output. The reviewer decides.

Open lab/README.md and assign author and reviewer roles. Learners use code-changes.md, fix-evaluation-template.md, the local review project, and the conflict scenario. partner-review-checklist.md is optional. The demo worksheet doesn't replace the learner pull-request workflow.

Remind learners not to commit the initial patch before the local reviews.

docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 2: Copilot in Practice

Difficulty: Intermediate

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04

Duration: 180 minutes (1 hour trainer content, 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The GitHub Copilot app is a desktop app for directing coding agents. It is built on the Copilot CLI and adds a session list, isolated workspaces, a diff view, and issue and pull request screens.

This session covers the developer inner loop: scope a bug, let an agent fix it in its own git worktree, review the diff, and open a PR. You learn what a session and a workspace are, what Interactive, Plan, and Autopilot each do, and how the app compares with IDE agent mode and the CLI.

In the lab you fix a real bug in a throwaway GitHub repo, run two sessions side by side, and open a real pull request.

Other sessions cover the rest of the app. Session M7-01 tours the app for non-developers and context briefs. Session M3-01 covers canvases and plugins. Session M7-05 covers supervising many child sessions.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain sessions, chats, and workspaces, and how a git worktree isolates parallel work.
  • Choose Interactive, Plan, or Autopilot, and name the failure mode of each.
  • Keep mode, tool permissions, and sandbox settings apart in your head.
  • Use /plan, /review, /rubber-duck, /fork, /spawn, /pr-open, and related commands, and know to check the picker for your version.
  • Hand work to a fresh or child session without losing context.
  • Review an agent's diff, open a PR from the app, and read its checks.
  • Choose between the app, IDE agent mode, and the CLI for a task.

docs.title: You need
docs.text: The GitHub Copilot app, signed in. Git, Python 3.10 or later, and the gh CLI signed in to GitHub. A GitHub account where you can create a private throwaway repo. Without one, you can do Parts 1 to 5 locally.

docs.title: What the app is
docs.text:
A desktop app for directing coding agents.

  • Built on the Copilot CLI. Skills and instructions carry over.
  • Many sessions at once, each on its own branch.
  • Diff view, issues, pull requests, and checks in one place.
  • Runs on This computer or in a Cloud sandbox.

You describe the task. You review the result.

docs.title: App, IDE, or CLI?
docs.text:
App IDE agent mode CLI Works in Own worktree Your open checkout Current folder Parallel Built in Awkward You manage folders Strong at Review, PRs, supervising Editing with you Scripts, quick tasks Weak at One-line fixes Collides with your edits No review UI

Pick by task size and how much you need to review.

docs.title: Chat or session?
docs.text:
Chat Session Has a branch No Yes Edits files No Yes Use it to Think, compare, explain Change and ship

Switching tasks? Start a new session. Old context hurts new work.

docs.title: Workspace: what a worktree is
docs.text:
A git worktree is a second folder for the same repo. It has its own branch and files. It shares history.

git worktree list
Workspace option Meaning New worktree Own folder and branch. Safe in parallel. Current checkout Your folder. One session only.

Two agents in one folder overwrite each other. Two worktrees don't.

docs.title: Worktree traps
docs.text:
• Tracked files only. No .env, no node_modules. Tell the agent how to set up.
  • Disk. Archive finished sessions.
  • Merge conflicts still happen. Isolation stops overwrites, not overlap.
  • One branch, one worktree. Git won't check out a branch twice.

docs.text:
Mode Cost Failure Interactive You are the bottleneck Rubber-stamp approvals Plan Extra review step Plausible plan, wrong problem Autopilot You see results, not steps Runs far on a wrong assumption

Autopilot is for clear problems, not hard ones.

docs.title: Lab: fix a bug and open a PR
docs.text:
You will:

  1. Create a throwaway GitHub repo and issue.
  2. Scope the bug in a chat.
  3. Fix it in a Plan session in a new worktree.
  4. Run a second session in parallel.
  5. Review: diff, tests, /review.
  6. Open the PR, read the check.
  7. Redo a small task in the CLI or IDE. Compare.

Starter: lab/starter. Four failing tests.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-05 lab: Fix a bug in the app and open a PR
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A fixed checkout-pricing repo, a pull request (or a local branch) you reviewed, and a short comparison note

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You fix a pricing bug in a small sample repo. You work in the GitHub Copilot app the way a developer would: scope in a chat, plan in a session, run two sessions side by side, review the diff, and open a PR. Then you do one more small task in the CLI or your IDE and compare.

Everything is real. You use a throwaway GitHub repo you create for this lab, so nothing touches your team's code. The data is synthetic.

Part Work Time 1 Create the throwaway repo and issue 15 min 2 Scope the bug in a chat 10 min 3 Fix it in a Plan-mode session 25 min 4 Run a second session in parallel 15 min 5 Review the result 20 min 6 Open and check the PR 20 min 7 Compare with another surface 15 min

Command names in the app change. If a command below isn't in your picker, type / and look. Check the list in your version and use the closest match.

docs.title: Part 1: Create the throwaway repo and issue
docs.text:
You need Git, Python 3.10 or later, the gh CLI signed in to GitHub, and the Copilot app.

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05
cp -R sessions/session-m2-05-copilot-app-for-developers/lab/starter \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05/checkout-pricing
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05/checkout-pricing
python -m unittest discover -s tests          # 4 failures expected
git init -b main && git add -A && git commit -m "Start"
gh repo create checkout-pricing-lab --private --source . --push
gh issue create --title "Order totals are wrong" --body-file issue-brief.md

In the app, click + next to Sessions and connect the folder (Open local folder) or the GitHub repo (Add GitHub repository).

No GitHub repo? Skip gh repo create and gh issue create. Do everything locally. You can't open a PR in Part 6, so review the branch diff instead.

Checkpoint: Four tests fail. The repo and issue exist, and the app shows the project in the sidebar.

docs.title: Part 2: Scope the bug in a chat
docs.text:
Open Chats (not a project session). A chat has no branch and no worktree, so it can't change your files. Ask:

Here is the issue: <paste issue-brief.md>. Which of these four symptoms
share a root cause? What would you ask the author before coding?

Chats can't read your repo unless you attach files. Use /attach-files or @ to add shop/pricing.py.

Write down one question you would send the issue author. Don't answer it. The rules in the issue are enough.

Checkpoint: You can say which symptoms look like one bug and which look separate.

docs.title: Part 3: Fix it in a Plan-mode session
docs.text:
1. Click + next to Sessions and pick the checkout-pricing project.
  2. Set Environment to This computer.
  3. Set Workspace to New worktree. Keep the base branch main.
  4. Set the mode to Plan. Pick a model. Leave Tool permissions on Ask every time or Assisted.
  5. Reference the issue and prompt:
Fix #1 (type # and pick the issue). Don't edit the tests. Run
python -m unittest discover -s tests before you say you're done.

Read the plan before you approve. Check three things: does it mention all four symptoms, does it say it will leave the tests alone, and does it plan to run the tests? If not, reply in the session and ask it to revise.

Approve the plan and watch. Approve or deny each tool request. Note any command you wouldn't have run yourself.

Checkpoint: The session reports passing tests. You have not merged or pushed anything yet.

docs.title: Part 4: Run a second session in parallel
docs.text:
While you review Part 3, start a second session:

  1. + next to Sessions, same project, Workspace: New worktree, mode Interactive.
  2. Prompt: Add a short "Usage" section to README.md that shows how to call order_total.

Now look at what the app created. In a terminal (the /terminal command opens one in the app):

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05/checkout-pricing
git worktree list
git branch

You should see your original checkout plus two more folders, each on its own branch. Open each folder's git status. The README change appears in only one of them. Your original checkout is untouched.

Two questions to answer in your note:

  • Which files does each session see? Does the second one see the first one's fix?
  • What would have happened if both sessions had edited pricing.py and you merged both?

Checkpoint: You can point to the folder and branch of each session, and git worktree list shows them.

docs.title: Part 5: Review the result
docs.text:
Don't trust the summary. Check the work.

  1. Open the Part 3 session's changes and read the whole diff.
  2. Run the tests yourself, from that session's worktree folder (or with /terminal):

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
3. Run /review on the session. Read its findings. Decide which you accept. 4. Optional: run /rubber-duck and ask it to critique the change. It uses a different model from your session, so it may disagree. 5. Look for these common problems: - The tests changed. - The function signature changed. - A new dependency or unrelated file appeared. - The fix special-cases the test values instead of fixing the rule.

Compare the diff with solution/README.md and solution/shop/pricing.py. Yours doesn't need to match.

If something is wrong, tell the session what to fix and repeat. Don't edit by hand unless it's faster.

Checkpoint: You can name one thing the agent did well and one thing you changed or would change. Tests pass when you run them.

docs.title: Part 6: Open and check the PR
docs.text:
In the Part 3 session, run /pr-open or ask: Open a pull request for these changes. The app creates a branch, pushes it, and opens the PR using the repo's PR template if it has one.

Then check on GitHub (or in the app's Pull requests view):

  • The PR links to the issue. If it doesn't, add Closes #1 to the description.
  • The tests workflow runs and passes.
  • The diff on GitHub matches what you reviewed.

If checks fail, try /pr-fix-checks. If you leave a review comment on the diff, try /pr-resolve-comments. Both need an open PR.

Merge the PR (/pr-merge, the app's merge button, or GitHub). Then open the Part 4 session, ask it to rebase or merge main, and check that the README change still works with the merged fix.

No GitHub repo? Run git log main..HEAD and git diff main in the worktree instead. Skip the merge.

Checkpoint: A PR exists with a passing check, or a local branch with a diff you reviewed.

docs.title: Part 7: Compare with another surface
docs.text:
Do one more small task outside the app, in the Copilot CLI (copilot) or your IDE's agent mode. Use the checkout-pricing folder on a new branch:

Reject negative quantities in order_total with a ValueError. Add a test.

Write a note of five sentences or fewer in comparison.md:

  • Which surface did you use, and how long did the task take?
  • What did you review, and how?
  • What was easier or harder than in the app?
  • When would you pick each one?

See solution/README.md for a sample note.

Checkpoint: comparison.md exists and names one real difference you saw.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. The checkout-pricing repo with the fix merged, or the fix on a local branch.
  2. The PR link, or your git diff main output.
  3. Your answers from Part 4 (two questions) and the /review findings you accepted or rejected.
  4. comparison.md.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text: Delete the throwaway repo when you're done: gh repo delete checkout-pricing-lab (needs the delete_repo scope). Archive or delete the sessions in Settings → Sessions → Manage sessions. That also frees the worktree disk space.

docs.title: Session M2-05 trainer guide: GitHub Copilot app for developers
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text:
Learners leave knowing what a session and a worktree are, how the three modes differ and fail, how to review and ship an agent's work from the app, and when another surface fits better.

Don't tour the app. Session M7-01 does that. Stay on the developer inner loop.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 What the app is, and how it differs from IDE and CLI 0:08 to 0:20 Sessions, chats, and workspaces (worktrees) 0:20 to 0:35 Modes, tool permissions, and sandboxes 0:35 to 0:47 Demo: bug to PR 0:47 to 0:55 Commands, handoff, pros, cons, tips 0:55 to 1:00 Lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Install the app and sign in. Type / in a session and note which commands from this guide appear.
  • Run the lab once with your own throwaway repo. Keep the PR open as a backup.
  • Have git worktree list ready in a terminal for the demo.
  • Make a second small task ready for the comparison (negative quantities).

docs.title: What the app is (0:00 to 0:08)
docs.text:
• A desktop app, built on the Copilot CLI, with GitHub integration. It runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
  • You direct agents. You don't type code. The center of the app is the session.
  • Sessions can run on This computer or in a Cloud sandbox hosted by GitHub.

How it compares. Use one sentence each.

App IDE agent mode CLI Lives in Desktop app Your editor Terminal Works in Its own worktree, or your checkout Your open checkout The current folder Parallel work Built in: many sessions, one worktree each One at a time, in practice Many terminals, you manage folders Strong at Reviewing diffs, issues, PRs, supervising Edit with you, inline, in context Scripts, remote boxes, quick tasks Weak at Heavy for a one-line fix Easy to collide with your own edits You build the review flow yourself

The app and CLI share an engine, so skills, instructions, and many commands carry over.

docs.title: Sessions, chats, and workspaces (0:08 to 0:20)
docs.text:
Chat. A conversation with no branch and no worktree. Use it to think, compare options, or explain a stack trace. It doesn't edit your repo.

Session. An agent working in a repo or folder, with history, a branch, and a diff. Start one when you expect edits, commands, or a PR. Start a new session when you switch tasks. Old context hurts new work.

Workspace. Where the session works. The prompt box offers:

  • New worktree. A separate folder on its own branch.
  • Current checkout. Your existing folder.

What a git worktree is. A worktree is a second working folder for the same repository. It has its own branch and files, and it shares the repo's history. Two worktrees can't have the same branch checked out. Show it live:

git worktree list

Why it matters. Two agents editing one folder overwrite each other and mix up git status. Two worktrees don't. You also keep working in your checkout while an agent runs.

Trade-offs and failure modes:

  • A new worktree has only tracked files. A .env, node_modules, or a virtual environment isn't there. The agent's tests may fail for setup reasons. Tell it how to set up.
  • Worktrees use disk. Archive finished sessions (Settings → Sessions → Manage sessions shows disk use).
  • Isolation stops overwrites, not merge conflicts. Two sessions that change the same lines still conflict at merge.
  • Current checkout is faster but unisolated. Use it for one session on one task.

docs.title: Modes, tool permissions, and sandboxes (0:20 to 0:35)
docs.text:
Three separate settings. Don't let learners mix them up.

Setting Controls Options Mode How the agent works with you Interactive, Plan, Autopilot Tool permissions When it asks before running a tool Ask every time, Assisted, Approve all Sandbox What a tool can reach Local sandbox (/sandbox on or /sandbox off), cloud sandbox

docs.title: The modes
docs.text:
Mode What it does Choose it when Trade-off Failure mode Interactive Suggests changes and waits for your input The task is unclear, or you want to steer You are the bottleneck You approve without reading, or you stall Plan (/plan) Writes a plan. You approve before it edits The change crosses files, or a wrong turn is costly An extra review step A plausible plan you rubber-stamp, and the plan misses the real problem Autopilot (/autopilot) Works on its own: code, tests, retries The task is well defined and tests exist You see the result, not the steps Runs far on a wrong assumption, burns credits, changes more than asked

Autopilot isn't for hard problems. It is for clear problems. A vague goal plus Autopilot gives a confident wrong answer.

Common pairing: Plan to agree the approach, then switch to Autopilot to run it, with Assisted permissions. You can switch modes at any time.

Mode and permissions are different. Autopilot with Ask every time still stops for each tool. Interactive with Approve all still waits for you but runs tools without asking. Approve all (also /allow-all-tools or /yolo) removes your check on each command. Use it only in a sandbox or a throwaway repo.

Sandboxes. A local sandbox limits the filesystem, network, and credentials of tools on your machine. A cloud sandbox runs the whole session on GitHub. They're different technologies with different settings.

docs.title: Demo: bug to PR (0:35 to 0:47)
docs.text:
Use the lab repo. Narrate your choices.

  1. Chat: paste the issue. Ask what's ambiguous. (1 min)
  2. New session, New worktree, Plan. Prompt with the issue. (2 min)
  3. Read the plan aloud. Ask for one revision, such as "don't change the tests". Approve. (3 min)
  4. While it runs, run git worktree list and show the new folder. (1 min)
  5. Open the diff. Run the tests yourself. Run /review. (3 min)
  6. /pr-open. Show the PR and the check on GitHub. (2 min)

Say out loud what you check each time: tests changed? signature changed? new files?

docs.title: Commands, handoff, pros, cons, tips (0:47 to 0:55)
docs.text:
Type / in the app for the current list. The ones this session uses:

Command Use /plan, /interactive, /autopilot Switch mode, optionally with a prompt /review Review the session's changes /rubber-duck Critique by a different model /spar Argue against your approach /security-review Security-focused review of the diff (public preview) /fork, /merge-to-parent Copy a session at the latest turn. Merge it back /spawn Start a focused child session /compact, /clear, /context Shrink, reset, or inspect context /pr-open, /pr-fix-checks, /pr-resolve-comments, /pr-merge PR steps, each needing an open PR or changes /terminal, /sandbox, /rename Terminal, sandbox, naming

Anything the docs don't list or that your picker lacks: type / and check your version's list.

Handing off work. Pick by what you need:

Need Use Try an alternative without losing the current path /fork, then /merge-to-parent or discard Give a side task to a focused agent /spawn Keep going but shorten history /compact Switch task New session. Paste a three-line brief: goal, what's done, what's next Follow from your phone or browser Cloud session, or /remote if your policy allows it

A written brief beats a long history. Name the branch, the failing test, and the decision you made.

Pros

  • Parallel work without folder collisions.
  • Diff, checks, and PR in one place.
  • Starts from an issue with context loaded.
  • Choose autonomy per session.

Cons

  • Heavier than the CLI for a quick edit.
  • Parallel sessions multiply review work. You are the limit.
  • Preview features and commands change.
  • Worktrees need setup and disk.

Tips

  • Put the finish line in the prompt: "tests pass, don't edit tests".
  • Read the plan as hard as you'd read a design.
  • One task per session. Rename sessions with /rename.
  • Use /rubber-duck on plans, not just code.
  • Agent Merge can watch a PR, fix checks, and merge. Try it only in a repo you can afford to break.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Treating the agent's "done" as proof Run the tests yourself Using Autopilot with a vague prompt Plan first, then Autopilot Approve all on a real repo Use Assisted or a sandbox Two sessions in one checkout New worktree for each Agent edits the tests until they pass Say so in the prompt, and read the diff Missing .env or dependencies in a worktree Tell the agent how to set up Letting one session run for days New session per task, with a short brief

docs.title: Lab handoff (0:55 to 1:00)
docs.text: Learners need gh signed in. Point them to the "No GitHub repo" notes in Parts 1 and 6. Remind them to delete the throwaway repo afterwards.

docs.title: Lab answer key
docs.text:
Reference fix: lab/solution/shop/pricing.py. Three root causes: > instead of >=, coupon applied to shipping and shipping decided on the pre-coupon subtotal, and round() on floats (ties round to even). Common agent slips are editing the tests and changing the function signature.

Part 4 answers: each session sees only its own branch, so the second session doesn't have the first fix until you merge. If both edit pricing.py, the second merge conflicts.

docs.title: Session M2-06: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 2: Copilot in Practice

Difficulty: Intermediate

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Repair a small inventory-reconciliation application that doesn't parse, doesn't start, and gives the wrong answer once the startup faults are fixed. Use GitHub Copilot as a debugging partner. Keep each change small and tested.

Restore parsing first, then imports and expected behavior. Add regression tests before you refactor. The reference solution separates file parsing, reconciliation rules, reporting, and the command-line entry point.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• reduce a broken Python program to the first actionable failure;
  • repair syntax and import faults without unrelated changes;
  • use fixtures and expected outputs as a behavioral contract;
  • add regression tests before changing structure;
  • remove duplicated rules and global state;
  • use Python LSP references to find a rule's callers, and tell them apart from duplicated inline rules;
  • approve a CLI /plan before structural changes.

docs.title: Session structure
docs.text: Block Duration Material Trainer content 1 hour Slides and trainer guide Lab 2 hours Repair and refactor lab

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The synthetic application compares warehouse counts with ledger counts. It normalizes SKU values, aggregates duplicate rows, calculates variances, assigns a status and severity, then writes text and JSON reports.

The starter fails in this order:

  1. named syntax errors;
  2. import and startup failures;
  3. deterministic logic defects;
  4. duplicated business rules;
  5. process-wide mutable state;
  6. tangled reconciliation and reporting code.

The supplied fixtures and expected outputs define the intended result.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Marp slides slides.md Lab guide lab/README.md Broken application lab/starter/ Tested reference solution lab/solution/

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Use the repository Dev Container or GitHub Codespaces. For a native setup, use Python 3.11 or later, create a virtual environment, and install the pinned development requirements from the lab directory. You also need GitHub Copilot, the standalone Copilot CLI, and pyright-langserver. Run /lsp test python before the lab. The LSP exercise runs after the parsing and behavior checks pass.

docs.title: Trainer note
docs.text: Don't reveal the source-level fixes at the start. Reveal the failure names and the repair order.

docs.title: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
Copilot in Practice
docs.text: Session M2-06 | Intermediate | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Start from the failure output 8 min Python concepts and failure order 10 min Prepared repair demonstration 12 min Recover behavior from fixtures 12 min Lock behavior with tests 10 min Refactor and lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: The inherited application
docs.text:
The inventory tool should:

  • read warehouse and ledger CSV files;
  • normalize and aggregate SKU quantities;
  • calculate stock variance;
  • write stable text and JSON reports.

It currently does none of this reliably.

docs.title: Python concepts you need
docs.text:
• Import: from .rules import severity_for loads a name from a module in the same package. A missing file or name stops startup.
  • Entry point: python -m inventory_reconciliation runs __main__.py, which calls main() in cli.py.
  • pytest: runs test_* functions with plain assert. A file that can't parse or import stops collection.
  • CSV: every value is a string. Convert and validate quantity.
  • Module-level state: a top-level variable lives as long as the process, so calls can leak into each other.

docs.title: The broken-state contract
docs.text:
Stage Named fault Parsing SYN-01, then SYN-02 Startup IMP-01, then IMP-02 Behavior LOG-01 through LOG-03 Repeatability STATE-01 Design DESIGN-01

Each repaired fault lets execution reach the next failure.

Core (full loop and log entry): SYN-01, IMP-01, LOG-01, LOG-03, STATE-01, DESIGN-01. Quick (repeat a pattern, log if time allows): SYN-02, IMP-02, LOG-02.

docs.title: Start at the lowest blocked layer
docs.text:
parse
  ↓
import
  ↓
start
  ↓
behavior
  ↓
structure

Do not refactor code that Python cannot import.

docs.title: Read the traceback from the bottom
docs.text:
Capture four facts:

  1. exception type;
  2. file and line;
  3. failing source text;
  4. command that produced it.

That is enough to form the first hypothesis.

docs.title: Use Copilot inside a boundary
docs.text:
Explain this SyntaxError using only the shown file and traceback.
Identify the smallest syntax repair.
Do not refactor or change behavior.

The prompt asks for a syntax-only change. Check that the proposal stays in scope.

docs.title: Repair loop
docs.text:
capture failure
  → state one hypothesis
  → make one small change
  → run one narrow check
  → record the result

If the next failure changes, the repair probably moved execution forward.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build

Expected first stop: SYN-01 in cli.py.

docs.title: Narrow checks beat noisy checks
docs.text:
Goal Command Parse package python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation Import entry point python -c "import inventory_reconciliation.cli" Check startup python -m inventory_reconciliation --help Check behavior pytest -q

Use the smallest command that can disprove the current hypothesis.

docs.title: Expected outputs are the contract
docs.text:
SKU     warehouse  ledger  variance  status  severity
AX-100          10      10         0  MATCH   none
BX-200           4       9        -5  SHORT   review
CX-300           0       8        -8  SHORT   urgent

Do not edit the contract to hide a defect.

docs.title: Intended reconciliation rules
docs.text: Rule Expected behavior SKU identity Trim and uppercase Duplicate rows Sum after normalization Missing side Use quantity zero Variance Warehouse minus ledger Output order Sort by SKU Repeated run No prior results retained

docs.title: Classification belongs in one place
docs.text:
Variance Status Severity 0 MATCH none -1 to -5 or 1 to 5 SHORT or OVER review absolute value 6+ SHORT or OVER urgent

The starter's duplicated rules disagree. Keep one implementation.

docs.title: Reproduce each defect with the same fixtures
docs.text:
The same fixtures always expose:

  • overwritten duplicate quantities;
  • ledger-only SKUs that disappear;
  • the wrong urgent threshold;
  • stale results on a second call.

Use these repeatable failures to test each diagnosis.

docs.title: Add tests before changing structure
docs.text:
Keep the fixture-level checks. Add focused tests for:

  • severity at absolute variance 6;
  • negative quantity rejection with row context.

Refactor only after the tests establish the expected behavior.

docs.title: Global state creates delayed failures
docs.text:
RUN_HISTORY = []

def reconcile(...):
    RUN_HISTORY.extend(current_results)
    return RUN_HISTORY

The first call may look correct. The second call exposes the leak.

docs.title: Tangled control flow hides policy
docs.text:
read rows
  + normalize values
  + merge quantities
  + classify variance
  + build output
  + retain state

Separate these jobs so each rule has one implementation.

docs.title: Target design
docs.text:
cli.py
  → parsing.py
  → service.py
  → rules.py
  → reporting.py

The command-line layer coordinates. It does not own business rules.

docs.title: Refactor in small moves
docs.text:
1. Remove process-wide mutable results.
  2. Extract one classification function.
  3. Reuse it from service and reporting.
  4. Extract parsing and aggregation.
  5. Run tests after each move.

Keep public behavior stable.

docs.title: Use Python LSP after the tests are green
docs.text:
.github/lsp.json tells the CLI to start pyright-langserver --stdio for .py files. An LSP answers "where is this defined, who calls it?" from parsed code.

/lsp show           list configured servers
/lsp test python    check that the server starts

/lsp test python proves startup only. It doesn't look up code. Ask for the definition and references of severity_for. Inspect the actual LSP operation and check its locations.

Then read service.py for inline duplicate rules. They may not show up as references to that function.

Approve /plan before structural edits.

docs.title: Review Copilot output like a patch
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Did the change touch only the current fault?
  • Which test proves the claimed behavior?
  • Did a rule move or get copied?
  • Does output order stay deterministic?

Check generated code against tests and fixtures.

docs.title: Lab workflow
docs.text: Part Time Preflight and baseline 10 min Restore parsing and imports 30 min Recover behavior 30 min Add regression tests 20 min Refactor and check 25 min Final output comparison and tests 5 min

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
• repair log with the six core repairs;
  • runnable inventory command;
  • added regression tests;
  • unchanged expected outputs;
  • clean separation of parsing, rules, service, reporting, and CLI;
  • passing pytest -q.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Work in failure order. Log the six core repairs.

Your solution must produce the supplied text and JSON outputs, pass all tests, and return the same result on repeated runs.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-06 lab: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Repair a synthetic inventory-reconciliation application. Recover its intended behavior from fixtures, add regression tests, then refactor without changing the reports.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• a repair-log.md with an entry for each core repair;
  • a command that writes the expected text and JSON reports;
  • at least two new focused regression tests;
  • unchanged files under fixtures/expected/;
  • production code with no process-wide result state or duplicated rules;
  • passing pytest -q output;
  • a Python LSP lookup and an accepted refactor plan.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• GitHub Copilot and the standalone Copilot CLI;
  • Python 3.11 or later;
  • a working Python language server (pyright-langserver).

Use the repository Dev Container or GitHub Codespaces. Copy the starter to a scratch directory so the original stays available:

cp -R sessions/session-m2-06-python-repair-refactor/lab/starter \
  /tmp/session-m2-06-inventory
cd /tmp/session-m2-06-inventory
git init

Use a fresh destination if that folder exists. Read .github/lsp.json before opening the copy in the CLI. Set up pyright-langserver with the LSP setup guide. Session M3-04 isn't a prerequisite. Then check /plan, /lsp show, and /lsp test python (see Python concepts and the LSP config).

Create the environment:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

On Windows PowerShell, activate with:

.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Outside the Dev Container, copy lab/starter/ to a writable folder and run the same commands. Keep the fixture files unchanged.

docs.title: Python concepts and the LSP config
docs.text:
Term What you need to know Import from .rules import severity_for loads one name from rules.py in the same package. A missing file raises ModuleNotFoundError. A missing name raises ImportError. Package entry point python -m inventory_reconciliation runs inventory_reconciliation/__main__.py, which calls main() in cli.py. Python reads cli.py and everything it imports before running anything. pytest Finds tests/test_*.py and runs each test_* function. A plain assert is the check. If a file fails to parse or import, pytest stops during collection, before any test runs. CSV Plain text with a header row. Python's csv module returns every value as a string, so quantity needs an int() conversion and a validity check. Module-level state A variable defined at the top of a module lives as long as the process. A function that appends to it leaks results from one call into the next.

The LSP config. A language server (LSP) answers code questions such as "where is this function defined, and who calls it?" from the parsed code, not from text search. .github/lsp.json tells the Copilot CLI to start pyright-langserver --stdio, Pyright's server, for .py files under the name python. The CLI starts the process, so read the file before you open the copy.

  • /lsp show lists the configured servers.
  • /lsp test python starts a temporary server and checks that it responds. This proves startup only. It doesn't look up any code.
  • A real lookup is a request for definition or references. You run one in Part 5.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The application compares physical warehouse counts with ledger quantities. The starter is broken on purpose. The named faults appear in this order:

SYN-01 → SYN-02 → IMP-01 → IMP-02
       → LOG-01/02/03 → STATE-01 → DESIGN-01

Each fault blocks the next, so fix them in order. You must repair all nine for the tests and reports to pass. Core repairs use the full loop: a Copilot prompt, one check, and one repair-log entry. Quick repairs repeat a pattern you just did. Fix them directly and log them only if time allows.

Core Quick SYN-01, IMP-01, LOG-01, LOG-03, STATE-01, DESIGN-01 SYN-02 (same as SYN-01), IMP-02 (same as IMP-01), LOG-02

docs.title: Behavioral contract
docs.text:
• CSV files have sku and quantity headers.
  • SKU values are trimmed and converted to uppercase.
  • Duplicate rows are summed after normalization.
  • Quantities are whole numbers and can't be negative.
  • A SKU may appear in only one input. The missing quantity is zero.
  • Variance equals warehouse quantity minus ledger quantity.
  • Zero is MATCH; negative is SHORT; positive is OVER.
  • Absolute variance 1-5 is review; 6 or more is urgent.
  • Rows are sorted by SKU.
  • Repeated calls in one Python process return independent results.

The files under fixtures/expected/ are authoritative.

docs.title: Part 1: Capture the baseline (10 minutes)
docs.text:
cp repair-log.md repair-log-working.md
python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build

Expected starter failure: Python stops at SYN-01 in inventory_reconciliation/cli.py.

Record the command, exception type, file and line, one hypothesis, and the next narrow check in repair-log-working.md. Keep each Copilot request to one failure in one file. Don't ask it to repair the whole project.

docs.title: Part 2: Restore parsing and imports (30 minutes)
2.1 Repair SYN-01
docs.text:
Explain the current SyntaxError from this traceback and file. Suggest the
smallest syntax-only repair. Do not refactor or change behavior.

Inspect the suggestion, make the smallest edit, and run:

python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation

Record the result. The next fault is SYN-02.

docs.title: 2.2 Repair SYN-02 (quick)
docs.text:
Repeat the same steps without a log entry. When the package compiles, check imports:

python -c "import inventory_reconciliation.cli"

The next fault is IMP-01.

docs.title: 2.3 Repair IMP-01 (core) and IMP-02 (quick)
docs.text:
For each import failure:

  1. Read the missing module or symbol from the traceback.
  2. Search the package for the intended implementation.
  3. Decide whether the import path or exported name is wrong.
  4. Make one import-only change and re-run the import command.

Log IMP-01. Log IMP-02 only if time allows.

Then run:

python -m inventory_reconciliation --help

Checkpoint: The package parses, imports, and displays command help.

docs.title: Part 3: Recover intended behavior (30 minutes)
docs.text:
pytest -q

The tests should now collect. Use their failures to find the behavior defects, and compare the inputs with fixtures/expected/report.txt and fixtures/expected/reconciliation.json.

Repair these in order:

  1. LOG-01 (core): duplicate normalized SKUs must sum.
  2. LOG-02 (quick): reconcile the union of warehouse and ledger SKUs.
  3. LOG-03 (core): apply the stated severity boundary.
  4. STATE-01 (core): repeated calls must not retain prior results.

After each change, run the narrowest failing test, then the full suite.

The failing test and expected fixture define the behavior. Find the smallest
production-code change for this failure. Do not refactor unrelated code or
edit expected outputs.

Checkpoint: Existing tests pass and generated output matches both expected files.

docs.title: Part 4: Add regression tests (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Add at least two tests before refactoring:

  1. absolute variance 5 is review and 6 is urgent;
  2. a negative quantity raises ValueError with the file and row number.

Keep each test focused. Use temporary files for invalid CSV input. Run pytest -q, then commit or save this green state before changing structure.

docs.title: Part 5: Refactor without behavior changes (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Remove DESIGN-01. Give each file one job:

File Owns parsing.py CSV validation, normalization, aggregation rules.py status and severity classification service.py reconciliation across both inputs reporting.py stable text and JSON rendering cli.py arguments, orchestration, output files

Required changes:

  • remove module-level mutable result state;
  • keep one implementation of status and severity rules;
  • replace nested reconciliation branches with named functions;
  • keep the command arguments and output format;
  • keep deterministic SKU order.

docs.title: Inspect references before planning (5 minutes of this block)
docs.text:
With tests green, ask the CLI:

Use Python language-server operations to locate severity_for and its references.
Report paths and lines. Then inspect service.py for inline classification that
would not appear as a reference to that function. Do not edit files.

Inspect the actual operation or /lsp logs and check its locations against the source. /lsp test python and a plain text search aren't lookups. Record the result in the repair log.

Inline classification can duplicate a rule without calling its function, so track duplicates separately from references. Don't ask for a bulk rename while syntax or behavior checks still fail.

Use Plan mode for the rest of the refactor:

/plan The tests are green. Plan a small refactor that removes global result state and
duplicated classification rules. Preserve the CLI, output files, output order,
and public behavior. Use the checked reference locations and identify inline
duplicates separately. Name the tests that protect each step. Do not implement.

Approve the plan, leave Plan mode, and run pytest -q after each structural move.

docs.title: Part 6: Final check (5 minutes)
docs.text:
rm -rf build
python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build
diff -u fixtures/expected/report.txt build/report.txt
diff -u fixtures/expected/reconciliation.json build/reconciliation.json
pytest -q

On Windows, compare the files in the editor if diff is unavailable.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
• repair-log-working.md with entries for the six core repairs;
  • repaired and refactored source files;
  • the added regression tests;
  • build/report.txt and build/reconciliation.json;
  • terminal output showing all tests pass.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• All nine faults are repaired. The six core ones are in the repair log.
  • Duplicate rows aggregate after SKU normalization.
  • Ledger-only and warehouse-only SKUs appear.
  • Severity changes from review to urgent at absolute variance 6.
  • Negative quantities include file and row context.
  • Repeated service calls don't leak results.
  • Status and severity rules have one implementation.
  • Expected fixture files are unchanged.
  • You inspected the LSP lookup and checked inline duplicates separately.
  • An accepted /plan preceded the structural changes.
  • pytest -q passes and the text and JSON output match.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Action A later fault appears before the named one Restore the starter copy and repeat only the documented small edits pytest cannot be imported Activate .venv and reinstall requirements-dev.txt Package import fails from another directory Run commands from the copied starter root JSON diff shows only formatting changes Use the provided JSON writer settings and final newline A test passes alone but fails in the suite Look for module-level mutable state Copilot proposes a rewrite Reject it and narrow the request to one file Native setup uses the wrong Python Recreate .venv with a Python 3.11+ executable

docs.text: The tested reference implementation is in solution/. Review it after the lab.
