docs.title: Session M2-06 trainer guide: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Delivery objective
docs.text:
Teach learners to repair a deliberately broken inventory-reconciliation application, then improve its design without changing its output. Keep each repair small enough to explain and check.

Each learner finishes with a working command-line application, added regression tests, and a repair log for the six core repairs. File comparisons show that the refactor kept the supplied text and JSON outputs.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00-0:08 Start repairs from the failure output 0:08-0:18 Python concepts, then failures in execution order 0:18-0:30 Demonstrate syntax and import recovery 0:30-0:42 Use fixtures to recover behavior 0:42-0:52 Add regression tests before refactoring 0:52-1:00 Refactor boundaries and hand off to the lab

docs.title: Trainer preparation
docs.text:
1. Open the repository in its Dev Container or a Codespace, with Python 3.11 or later.
  2. Check that GitHub Copilot Chat and inline suggestions work.
  3. Create a private working copy of lab/starter/ and install requirements-dev.txt in it.
  4. Run the starter command and keep the first failure.
  5. Run the solution tests, then keep lab/solution/ closed until the lab review.
  6. Read the supplied .github/lsp.json, prepare pyright-langserver, and check CLI /plan and /lsp test python in the copied repository.

From the session directory:

cd lab/starter
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build

The first failure is SYN-01 in inventory_reconciliation/cli.py. Don't fix later faults in the demo.

docs.title: The repair ladder
docs.text:
Start at the first layer that stops you from checking the next:

Layer Question Check Parse Can Python read every imported file? python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation Import Can the package and entry point load? python -c "import inventory_reconciliation.cli" Start Can the command show help? python -m inventory_reconciliation --help Behavior Does the output match the contract? pytest -q and fixture comparison Structure Can the code change safely? regression tests stay green

Skipping a layer hides the current failure. A syntax error blocks test collection, so tests can't check business logic.

docs.title: Repair loop
docs.text:
1. Capture the exact command and failure.
  2. State one hypothesis.
  3. Ask Copilot for the smallest relevant explanation or change.
  4. Inspect the proposed edit.
  5. Run the narrowest useful check.
  6. Record the result in the repair log.

Learners make the diagnosis. Command output tests each hypothesis. Use the full loop on the six core repairs. SYN-02, IMP-02, and LOG-02 repeat earlier patterns, so learners fix them directly. All nine must be repaired.

docs.title: Prerequisites to cover in the first segment
docs.text:
One minute each, with the slide "Python concepts you need":

  • Imports: ModuleNotFoundError means the file is missing. ImportError means the name is missing.
  • Entry point: python -m pkg runs pkg/__main__.py. Python parses cli.py and its imports first, so one syntax error stops startup.
  • pytest: collects test_* functions. A parse or import failure stops collection, so no test runs.
  • CSV and module-level state: csv gives strings, and a top-level list survives across calls.
  • Pyright LSP: .github/lsp.json makes the CLI start pyright-langserver for .py files. /lsp show lists servers. /lsp test python only proves the server starts. Only a definition or references request looks up code.

docs.title: Controlled starter sequence
docs.text:
The starter uses named faults so learners can compare progress without sharing source-level answers.

Order Fault Tier Surface Intended signal 1 SYN-01 Core cli.py Parser stops at the first malformed function definition 2 SYN-02 Quick service.py The next imported module cannot parse 3 IMP-01 Core cli.py Startup imports a module that does not exist 4 IMP-02 Quick reporting.py Startup imports a symbol that does not exist 5 LOG-01 Core parsing Duplicate SKU rows overwrite earlier quantities 6 LOG-02 Quick reconciliation SKUs present only in the ledger disappear 7 LOG-03 Core rules Severity thresholds do not match the contract 8 STATE-01 Core service Repeated runs leak results through global state 9 DESIGN-01 Core service/reporting Rules are duplicated and control flow is tangled

The first four faults appear in order when learners use the lab's checks. The supplied fixtures expose the behavior defects.

docs.title: 1. Capture the first failure
docs.text: Run the starter command above. Read the traceback from the bottom: file, line, exception type, source line. Ignore every later concern until Python can parse that file.

docs.title: 2. Ask Copilot about one failure
docs.text:
Explain this SyntaxError using only the shown file and traceback. Identify the
smallest syntax repair. Do not refactor or change behavior.

A good repair prompt includes the traceback and names what may change.

docs.title: 3. Check the repair
docs.text:
python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation

The command should expose SYN-02.

docs.title: 4. Log it, then stop
docs.text:
Show one entry in repair-log.md:

Field Example Failure SYN-01 Failure output SyntaxError in cli.py Hypothesis Function header is incomplete Change Small syntax-only edit Check Re-run compile command Result Parser advances to SYN-02

Don't demonstrate the behavior fixes.

docs.title: Behavioral contract
docs.text:
The fixture pair represents two views of stock:

  • warehouse.csv contains physical counts;
  • ledger.csv contains expected counts.

The rules:

  1. Trim surrounding whitespace and uppercase each SKU.
  2. Sum duplicate rows after normalization.
  3. Reject negative quantities with a row-specific error.
  4. Reconcile the union of SKUs from both files.
  5. Calculate variance = warehouse - ledger.
  6. Use MATCH for zero, SHORT below zero, and OVER above zero.
  7. Use severity none for zero, review for absolute variance 1-5, and urgent for absolute variance 6 or more.
  8. Sort report rows by SKU.
  9. Keep repeated runs isolated.

The expected text and JSON files define the result. Learners must not change them to make broken code pass.

docs.title: Regression tests before refactoring
docs.text:
The starter tests cover the fixture-level contract and repeated-run isolation. Learners add at least two focused tests:

  • the boundary between review and urgent;
  • rejection of a negative quantity with file and row context.

Each test names one rule and fails for one reason.

docs.title: Refactoring targets
docs.text:
Keep these five jobs in separate files:

Boundary Responsibility parsing.py Read, validate, normalize, and aggregate CSV data rules.py Classify variance status and severity service.py Reconcile two quantity maps reporting.py Render stable text and JSON output cli.py Parse arguments, call the service, write files

The starter mixes these on purpose. Learners remove the module-level result list, call one rule implementation, and turn nested branches into named functions. No large rewrite: add tests first, then make one structural change at a time.

Spend five minutes of the 25-minute refactor block on a real Python LSP lookup. Ask for the definition and references of severity_for, and check the returned locations in the operation output or /lsp logs. Then inspect service.py for inline copies of the same rule. Those copies may not show up as symbol references. Record both before approving /plan. Don't use LSP diagnostics to skip the syntax and import repairs.

docs.title: Useful Copilot prompts
docs.text:
Repair:

Use the traceback and this file only. Suggest the smallest change that resolves
the current failure. Preserve behavior and do not refactor.

Test:

Write one pytest test for the severity boundary at absolute variance 6. Follow
the existing test style. Do not change production code.

Refactor:

/plan The tests are green. Plan removal of global state and duplicated
classification logic using the checked references and inline duplicates.
Preserve public signatures and output order. Name protecting tests. Do not edit.

Review:

Review the diff for behavior changes. Compare it with the supplied fixtures,
expected outputs, and tests. Call out any unproved assumption.

docs.title: Facilitation notes
docs.text:
• Keep learners on the current failure. Later defects are distractions.
  • Reject changes to expected outputs unless the class first proves the contract is wrong.
  • Ask learners to explain each Copilot suggestion before they accept it.
  • Pair learners when one is stuck for more than eight minutes.

docs.title: Common wrong turns
docs.text: Wrong turn Coaching response Rewrite the application from scratch Return to the first failing command and keep the supplied interface Ask Copilot to "fix everything" Narrow the prompt to one file Change fixtures to match broken output Fixtures are the contract Refactor while imports still fail Restore startup first Remove the repeated-run test Global state often passes once and fails in a process Mock all file reads Keep at least one fixture-level test through the real parser

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Learners finish with a repair log for the core repairs, a working command-line application, at least two added regression tests, unchanged expected-output fixtures, a design with no process-wide result state, and passing pytest output with generated reports. The same inputs must produce the supplied outputs before and after the refactor.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-07: Migrate a legacy Java service to modern .NET
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 2: Copilot in Practice

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Migrate one order-pricing slice from a Java 8-compatible HTTP service to a .NET 10 ASP.NET Core Minimal API. Run the legacy service, trace its request path, record the behavior that must survive, then implement the same contract in .NET and prove parity with shared JSON cases.

The exercise uses synthetic orders and integer-cent arithmetic. It needs no database, cloud service, or production data.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• map a legacy request from HTTP entry point to domain calculation and response;
  • separate observed behavior from incidental Java structure;
  • capture pricing rules in shared contract fixtures;
  • migrate one vertical slice to a .NET 10 Minimal API and keep rounding, validation, shipping, discount, and tax behavior;
  • compare Java and .NET results with repeatable tests;
  • list the next slices instead of planning a full rewrite.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The legacy service prices synthetic orders through POST /orders/price. The rules are small enough to inspect. These details can break a migration:

  • discounts run in a fixed order;
  • all amounts use integer cents;
  • percentage calculations round half up;
  • free shipping uses the discounted merchandise amount;
  • tax applies to discounted merchandise, not shipping;
  • invalid enum-like values and line items return clear errors.

You migrate this slice. Leave the health and sample-order endpoints in Java and record them as backlog items.

docs.title: Session structure
docs.text: Block Duration Work Trainer content 1 hour Migration boundaries, behavior capture, contract tests, .NET mapping, and prepared demo Lab 2 hours Inspect the Java service, implement the .NET slice, and prove parity

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Marp slides slides.md Lab guide lab/README.md Java baseline, fixtures, and .NET scaffold lab/starter/ .NET reference implementation and contract tests lab/solution/

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Use the repository Dev Container or Codespaces. It supplies Java 21, which compiles the legacy source for Java 8, and the .NET 10 SDK. The Maven Wrapper pins Maven 3.9.9, so you don't need a global Maven install. You also need GitHub Copilot.

The lab includes a short native setup route for learners who can't use the container.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
In scope: local HTTP services, synthetic JSON, behavior extraction, one pricing endpoint with validation, calculation, and response handling, package-free .NET contract tests, and a short list of next slices.

Out of scope: databases, messaging, authentication, cloud hosting, a whole-service rewrite, and production performance claims.

docs.title: Migrate a legacy Java service to modern .NET
Preserve behavior one vertical slice at a time
docs.text: Session M2-07 | Copilot in Practice | Advanced | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Define the migration boundary 8 min Read the Java request path 8 min Extract behavior and contract cases 10 min Compare Java and .NET 10 16 min Use Copilot with review gates 10 min Prepared demo and lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: Start with one route
docs.text:
POST /orders/price

The slice includes:

  • request parsing and validation;
  • pricing rules and rounding;
  • response fields and errors;
  • repeatable checks.

The health and sample-order routes stay in Java.

docs.title: A rewrite hides the unknowns
docs.text:
Whole-service rewrite Vertical-slice migration Scope grows before behavior is known One route defines the boundary New code becomes the assumed truth Existing behavior is captured first Cutover checks arrive late Each slice is checked before replacement Java structure leaks into C# Target design follows the contract

Record unknown behavior before expanding the slice.

docs.title: Run the legacy service first
docs.text:
cd lab/starter/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package
java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

Contract fixture tests passed: 5
Legacy order service listening on http://localhost:8080

Check how the service behaves before reading every file.

docs.title: Trace the request path
docs.text:
App.java
  → JsonCodec.readOrderRequest
  → OrderPricingService.price
  → JsonCodec.writeQuote
  → HTTP 200

Errors from validation become HTTP 400 with:

{"error":"..."}

docs.title: Classify what you find
docs.text:
Finding Type Action GOLD means 10% discount External behavior Preserve Coupon runs after tier discount Calculation rule Preserve and test JDK HttpServer Transport choice Replace Java getters Language structure Redesign Unknown throughput Open question Record

Do not translate incidental structure into a requirement.

docs.title: Pricing order is part of the contract
docs.text:
subtotal
  → tier discount
  → SAVE10 coupon
  → shipping decision
  → tax
  → total

Moving one step changes the result.

docs.title: Money stays in integer cents
docs.text:
rounded cents =
(amount in cents × basis points + 5000) / 10000

Examples:

  • SILVER = 500 basis points
  • GOLD = 1000 basis points
  • tax = 825 basis points

No binary floating point.

docs.title: Shipping uses discounted merchandise
docs.text:
Destination Rule Domestic 795 cents Domestic at 5000+ discounted cents Free International 1995 cents

Tax applies to discounted merchandise. Shipping is not taxed.

docs.title: Shared fixtures hold accepted behavior
docs.text:
{"name":"round-half-up",
 "request":{
   "customerTier":"SILVER",
   "destination":"DOMESTIC",
   "couponCode":"SAVE10",
   "items":[{"sku":"SKU-ROUND","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":101}]
 },
 "expected":{"totalCents":888}}

The Java and .NET tests read the same file.

docs.title: What the five cases protect
docs.text:
Case Risk standard-domestic baseline shipping and tax silver-free-domestic-shipping threshold after discount gold-save10-domestic discount order gold-international destination rule round-half-up one-cent drift

Add cases when you discover behavior. Do not invent them after migration.

docs.title: Contract tests cover selected behavior
docs.text:
Shared cases check only the selected successful calculations.

Also review:

  • invalid tiers and destinations;
  • empty orders and bad quantities;
  • unsupported coupons;
  • overflow behavior;
  • method, path, status, and error JSON.

docs.title: Map responsibilities, not classes
docs.text:
Java .NET 10 HttpHandler Minimal API route OrderRequest request records OrderPricingService PricingEngine PriceQuote response record fixture test main contract test executable

The target can be smaller than the source.

docs.title: Java and .NET, side by side
docs.text: Idea Java baseline .NET 10 Minimal API HttpServer, one HttpHandler class per route, body read and written by hand app.MapPost(path, lambda). The framework binds JSON to a record and injects PricingEngine. Vertical slice Route, parsing, rules, errors, and test The same unit moves as a whole JSONL fixtures One case per line, read by a hand-written codec The same file, read with System.Text.Json Basis points (amount × bp + 5000) / 10000 The same integer formula, with checked arithmetic

docs.title: Basis points in one example
docs.text:
1 basis point is 0.01%. SILVER is 500, GOLD is 1000, and tax is 825.

SILVER on 101 cents: (101 × 500 + 5000) / 10000 = 5

Adding 5000 before dividing by 10000 rounds half up. No floating point.

docs.title: The test project must copy the fixture
docs.text:
The Java test gets the fixture path from a system property. A .NET executable runs from bin/, so the file must be copied next to it.

<None Include="../../contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl"
      Link="contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl"
      CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
  • None Include: a file the compiler ignores but the project tracks
  • Link: where it appears under the output folder
  • CopyToOutputDirectory: copy it on build

The test reads it from AppContext.BaseDirectory.

docs.title: The Minimal API boundary
docs.text:
app.MapPost("/orders/price",
    (OrderRequest request, PricingEngine pricing) =>
{
    try
    {
        return Results.Ok(pricing.Price(request));
    }
    catch (ArgumentException exception)
    {
        return Results.BadRequest(new { error = exception.Message });
    }
});

Keep transport code thin.

docs.title: Platform APIs are enough
docs.text:
The target uses:

  • ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs;
  • built-in dependency injection;
  • System.Text.Json;
  • C# records;
  • a console test executable.

Do not add a database, mapper, mediator, or test package.

docs.title: Copilot starts with inspection
docs.text:
Trace POST /orders/price through the Java starter.
Return entry point, parsing, validation, pricing,
response mapping, and tests with file and symbol names.
Do not propose .NET code yet.

The first prompt builds a map. It does not ask for a rewrite.

docs.title: Ask for the behavior rules
docs.text:
Compare the Java pricing code with the shared JSON cases.
List operation order, rounding, shipping threshold,
accepted values, and uncovered behavior.
Do not change files.

Review the answer against code and test output.

docs.title: Bound the implementation prompt
docs.text:
Implement PricingEngine.Price in the .NET 10 scaffold.
Preserve the shared JSON contract.
Use integer cents, checked arithmetic, and platform APIs.
Do not add packages or change the endpoint shape.

Name the limits so you can check Copilot stayed within them.

docs.title: Review generated code before running it
docs.text:
Check:

  • JSON names;
  • calculation order;
  • integer arithmetic;
  • overflow handling;
  • shipping threshold;
  • tax base;
  • added dependencies.

Generated code is a draft.

docs.title: A clean migration can still be wrong
docs.text:
This looks reasonable:

var couponDiscount = Percentage(subtotal, 1000);

The accepted behavior is:

var couponDiscount = Percentage(afterTier, 1000);

One line breaks gold-save10-domestic.

docs.title: Verification has layers
docs.text:
Java fixture tests
        +
.NET fixture tests
        +
same HTTP request to both services
        +
human review of uncovered edges

No single layer proves the whole service.

docs.title: Prepared demo
docs.text:
1. Run the Java contract cases.
  2. Send the gold plus coupon request.
  3. Show the Java request path.
  4. Run a deliberately wrong .NET discount order.
  5. Watch the shared case fail.
  6. restore the accepted code and rerun.

The failing case shows why calculation order matters.

docs.title: Compare test and HTTP results
docs.text:
Java:  Contract fixture tests passed: 5
.NET:  Contract fixture tests passed: 5
HTTP:  matching field values for one shared request

Native alternative: JDK 17 or 21, .NET 10 SDK, Git, and curl.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-07 lab: Migrate one order-pricing slice to .NET 10
docs.text:
Duration: 2 hours

Deliverable: A working .NET 10 order-pricing endpoint, shared contract-test output, and an HTTP parity check. Short migration notes are optional.

docs.title: Lab outcome
docs.text:
Run a Java 8-compatible order service, trace one request through it, and migrate POST /orders/price to an ASP.NET Core Minimal API. The Java and .NET implementations must pass the same JSON contract cases.

Keep the scope narrow. Don't migrate the health or sample-order routes.

Part Work Time 1 Run the Java baseline 15 min 2 Extract behavior and architecture 15 min 3 Review the shared contract 15 min 4 Implement the .NET pricing slice 40 min 5 Add and run contract tests 20 min 6 Compare HTTP behavior 15 min

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
Open the repository in its Dev Container or Codespaces, with GitHub Copilot Chat working. Check:

java -version
dotnet --version
git --version
curl --version
  • Java is available. The container uses Java 21 and compiles the legacy project for Java 8.
  • dotnet --version reports a 10.x SDK.
  • Git and curl are available.

The Maven Wrapper downloads the pinned Maven version on first use.

docs.title: Native setup alternative
docs.text:
Without the container, install JDK 17 or 21, the .NET 10 SDK, Git, and curl or a comparable HTTP client. Check java -version and dotnet --list-sdks.

On macOS or Linux, use ./mvnw. On Windows, use mvnw.cmd. In PowerShell, use Invoke-RestMethod instead of curl. Don't change the target framework or Maven compiler level to fit an older machine.

docs.title: Create a working copy
docs.text:
From the repository root:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07
cp -R sessions/session-m2-07-java-to-dotnet-modernization/lab/starter/. \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07

Complete the lab in the copied folder.

docs.title: Part 1: Run the Java baseline (15 minutes)
docs.text:
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package

Expected test output:

Contract fixture tests passed: 5

Start the service:

java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

Keep that terminal open. In a second terminal:

curl http://localhost:8080/health
curl http://localhost:8080/orders/samples

Send a pricing request:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"customerTier":"GOLD","destination":"DOMESTIC","couponCode":"SAVE10","items":[{"sku":"SKU-RED","quantity":2,"unitPriceCents":1299},{"sku":"SKU-BLUE","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":2499}]}'

Expected field values (JSON spacing may differ):

{
  "subtotalCents": 5097,
  "tierDiscountCents": 510,
  "couponDiscountCents": 459,
  "shippingCents": 795,
  "taxCents": 341,
  "totalCents": 5264
}

docs.title: Without curl
docs.text:
Use the VS Code REST Client, a browser for the two GET routes, or PowerShell:

$body = @{
  customerTier = "GOLD"
  destination = "DOMESTIC"
  couponCode = "SAVE10"
  items = @(
    @{ sku = "SKU-RED"; quantity = 2; unitPriceCents = 1299 }
    @{ sku = "SKU-BLUE"; quantity = 1; unitPriceCents = 2499 }
  )
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 4

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri http://localhost:8080/orders/price `
  -ContentType application/json `
  -Body $body

Checkpoint: The Java tests pass and the service returns the expected pricing fields.

docs.title: Part 2: Extract behavior and architecture (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Optional: cp architecture-notes-template.md migration-notes.md and use it for the tables below.

Read the Java files in this order:

  1. src/main/java/training/orders/App.java
  2. src/main/java/training/orders/JsonCodec.java
  3. src/main/java/training/orders/OrderRequest.java
  4. src/main/java/training/orders/OrderPricingService.java
  5. src/main/java/training/orders/PriceQuote.java
  6. src/test/java/training/orders/ContractFixtureTest.java

Ask Copilot to inspect only this request path:

Trace POST /orders/price through this Java project. Return a table with the entry
point, JSON parsing, validation, pricing calculation, response mapping, and test
evidence. Cite file and symbol names. Do not propose .NET code and do not edit.

Check every row against the files before using it. If you keep notes, fill in the request path and pricing-rule tables.

Record these behaviors:

  • STANDARD, SILVER, and GOLD tier values;
  • SAVE10 coupon behavior;
  • domestic and international shipping;
  • the domestic free-shipping threshold;
  • tax base and rate;
  • integer round-half-up;
  • invalid input behavior;
  • overflow handling.

Java details such as HttpHandler classes, getters, the hand-written JSON codec, and the package layout don't need to survive.

docs.title: Review point 1
docs.text: Explain the route step by step. Say what each step does and which behavior a replacement must preserve.

docs.title: Part 3: Review the shared contract (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Open ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl. Each line is one complete case. Review the five names and expected fields.

Compare OrderPricingService.java with contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl.
List the calculation order, rounding formula, shipping threshold, accepted values,
and behavior that is not covered by the fixtures. Do not edit files.

Check the answer by hand. Calculate the round-half-up case:

subtotal = 101
SILVER discount = round(101 × 5%) = 5
after tier = 96
SAVE10 = round(96 × 10%) = 10
discounted merchandise = 86
shipping = 795
tax = round(86 × 8.25%) = 7
total = 86 + 795 + 7 = 888

Note any behavior no successful fixture covers, such as an invalid tier, empty items, or an unsupported coupon. Don't change the shared fixture yet.

docs.title: Review point 2
docs.text:
Before coding, you should be able to tell a partner:

  • Why is the coupon based on after tier?
  • Why does the free-shipping check use discounted merchandise?
  • Why isn't tax calculated on shipping?
  • Which formula produces round-half-up?

docs.title: Part 4: Implement the .NET pricing slice (35 minutes)
docs.text:
Open ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service/. The scaffold has OrderPricing.Api/Program.cs, Pricing.cs, and OrderPricing.Api.csproj. Program.cs already maps GET /health and POST /orders/price.

Implement only PricingEngine.Price and its private helpers.

Implement PricingEngine.Price in this .NET 10 scaffold.

Source of truth:
- ../legacy-java-order-service/src/main/java/training/orders/OrderPricingService.java
- ../contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl

Requirements:
- preserve the operation order and response fields;
- use integer cents and round-half-up with basis points;
- use checked arithmetic;
- preserve accepted tiers, destinations, coupon behavior, and validation messages;
- use .NET platform APIs only;
- do not add packages;
- do not change Program.cs or the JSON contract.

Return a short plan before editing. After editing, explain how each shared case is
covered.

Review the plan. Reject package additions and contract changes. After Copilot edits the file, inspect it line by line:

  • Tier discount uses the original subtotal.
  • Coupon discount uses the amount after tier discount.
  • Shipping checks the amount after both discounts.
  • Tax uses discounted merchandise only.
  • Percentage calculations add 5000 before dividing by 10000.
  • Arithmetic that can overflow is checked.
  • Empty or unknown coupon values match Java behavior.
  • No package reference was added.

Build:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service/OrderPricing.Api
dotnet build

If the build fails, fix the specific compiler error. Don't weaken nullable checks or change the target from net10.0. If the edit tool fails, type the implementation from the accepted rules.

docs.title: Review point 3
docs.text:
Ask Copilot to review without editing:

Review the Java and C# pricing implementations for behavior drift. Focus on
operation order, rounding, validation, overflow, shipping threshold, tax base,
and response fields. Return findings with file and symbol names. Do not edit.

Check each finding and fix the ones the contract supports. Note rejected suggestions and why they didn't match it.

docs.title: Part 5: Add and run shared contract tests (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Create a package-free console test project:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service
dotnet new console -n OrderPricing.ContractTests --framework net10.0
dotnet add OrderPricing.ContractTests/OrderPricing.ContractTests.csproj \
  reference OrderPricing.Api/OrderPricing.Api.csproj

Update the test project so it copies the shared fixture into its output:

<ItemGroup>
  <ProjectReference Include="../OrderPricing.Api/OrderPricing.Api.csproj" />
  <None Include="../../contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl"
        Link="contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl"
        CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
</ItemGroup>

In OrderPricing.ContractTests/Program.cs, the test executable must:

  1. read every non-empty JSONL line;
  2. deserialize the request and expected quote with System.Text.Json;
  3. call PricingEngine.Price;
  4. compare all six response fields;
  5. throw with the case name and field when a value differs;
  6. print the number of passing cases.
Implement this package-free .NET 10 console project as a contract test runner.
Read contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl from AppContext.BaseDirectory.
Deserialize each line, call PricingEngine.Price, compare every PriceQuote field,
and throw a clear exception with case name, field, expected, and actual.
Do not add a test framework or any package.

dotnet run --project OrderPricing.ContractTests

Expected:

Contract fixture tests passed: 5

Re-run the Java test from the working copy:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test

Both should report five passing cases.

Checkpoint: The Java baseline and .NET replacement read the same fixture file and agree on every response field.

docs.title: Part 6: Compare HTTP behavior (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Keep the Java service on port 8080. Start the .NET API on port 5080:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service
dotnet run --project OrderPricing.Api -- --urls http://localhost:5080

Send the same request to both services:

REQUEST='{"customerTier":"GOLD","destination":"DOMESTIC","couponCode":"SAVE10","items":[{"sku":"SKU-RED","quantity":2,"unitPriceCents":1299},{"sku":"SKU-BLUE","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":2499}]}'

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "$REQUEST"

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:5080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "$REQUEST"

Compare field values. JSON property order and whitespace may differ.

Send one invalid request:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"customerTier":"PLATINUM","destination":"DOMESTIC","couponCode":"","items":[{"sku":"SKU-RED","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":100}]}'

Expect an HTTP 400 response with a clear error.

Optional next slices. In migration-notes.md, list up to three slices to migrate next, such as the sample-order query, health, or error responses. For each, name the Java entry point and the check needed before the Java code goes away. Everything you haven't traced stays in Java.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. The completed .NET 10 PricingEngine.
  2. A package-free .NET contract test executable.
  3. Java and .NET output showing five shared cases passed.
  4. One matching Java and .NET HTTP response, and one .NET HTTP 400 validation example.
  5. Optional: migration-notes.md and a line on any Copilot suggestion you rejected.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Check Permission denied: ./mvnw Run chmod +x mvnw, then retry Maven cannot download on first run Check the network or use the trainer-prepared wrapper cache Port 8080 is in use Set PORT=8081 for Java and update the request URL .NET SDK cannot target net10.0 Use the Dev Container/Codespaces or install .NET 10 Contract test cannot find JSONL Check the None Include path and CopyToOutputDirectory Total differs by one cent Check operation order and round-half-up Domestic shipping is unexpectedly free Check the threshold after both discounts ASP.NET Core chooses another port Pass --urls http://localhost:5080

docs.text: The reference implementation is in solution/. Compare behavior and test results before formatting.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-07 trainer guide: Migrate a legacy Java service to modern .NET

docs.title: Delivery objective
docs.text:
Teach learners to preserve behavior during migration. They inspect a runnable Java service and define the pricing contract before moving one HTTP slice to .NET 10. Then they compare both implementations with the same JSON cases.

Keep the slice narrow: one reviewed route. The rest of the service stays in Java.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 Define the migration boundary 0:08 to 0:16 Read the Java request path 0:16 to 0:26 Extract behavior and contract cases 0:26 to 0:42 Compare Java and .NET 10 0:42 to 0:52 Use Copilot without surrendering decisions 0:52 to 1:00 Prepared demo and lab handoff

docs.title: Trainer preflight
docs.text:
Use the repository Dev Container or Codespaces.

java -version
dotnet --version
cd sessions/session-m2-07-java-to-dotnet-modernization/lab/starter/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package

Expected Java test output:

Contract fixture tests passed: 5

The container should report the .NET 10 SDK. The Java runtime may be newer than Java 8 because Maven compiles the baseline with source and target set to 8.

Prepare two terminals:

# Terminal 1
java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

# Terminal 2
curl http://localhost:8080/health
curl http://localhost:8080/orders/samples

Also build the completed .NET solution:

cd ../../solution/modern-dotnet-order-service
dotnet build
dotnet run --project OrderPricing.ContractTests

After the Maven Wrapper downloads Maven and its plugins, the demo needs no network. The code uses only JDK and .NET platform APIs.

docs.title: 1. Migrate a route, not a codebase
docs.text:
Use the HTTP route as the migration boundary:

POST /orders/price
        |
        v
JSON parsing and validation
        |
        v
Pricing rules
        |
        v
JSON response

This vertical slice includes the entry point, contract, domain logic, failure behavior, and verification. Moving only the calculation class would leave the risky edges behind.

Keep GET /health and GET /orders/samples in Java as backlog candidates. That keeps the boundary clear and the lab inside two hours.

docs.title: 2. Separate contract from structure
docs.text:
The Java classes and JDK HTTP plumbing are implementation choices. The contract is smaller:

  • method and path;
  • request JSON fields and accepted values;
  • calculation order and rounding rule;
  • response JSON fields;
  • status codes and error shape.

Ask learners to classify each finding:

Classification Example Migration treatment External behavior GOLD gives a 10% tier discount Preserve Calculation rule coupon runs after tier discount Preserve and test Transport choice JDK HttpServer Replace with Minimal API Language structure getters and nested item class Redesign in C# Unknown behavior concurrent request limit Record, don't invent

Copilot may reproduce Java structure in C#. Behavior tests establish parity.

docs.title: 3. Use integer money and explicit rounding
docs.text:
The service stores money in cents. Percentage calculations use basis points:

rounded cents = (amount in cents × basis points + 5000) / 10000

This is integer round-half-up for non-negative amounts.

The operation order is fixed:

  1. sum line items;
  2. apply the customer-tier discount;
  3. apply SAVE10 to the remaining merchandise amount;
  4. decide shipping from the discounted merchandise amount;
  5. calculate tax on discounted merchandise;
  6. add discounted merchandise, shipping, and tax.

Changing the order changes the result, and so does floating-point arithmetic. The round-half-up fixture catches both mistakes.

docs.title: 4. Test both implementations with the same fixtures
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl. Each line holds a case name, one request, and the expected response fields.

JSON Lines keeps each case readable and lets the Java 8 baseline read the file without a JSON package. The .NET test executable uses System.Text.Json.

Case Main risk standard-domestic baseline shipping and tax silver-free-domestic-shipping threshold after discount gold-save10-domestic discount order gold-international international shipping round-half-up integer rounding

The fixtures cover shared pricing behavior only. Validation errors and HTTP behavior need focused checks.

docs.title: 5. Compare Java and .NET (16 minutes)
docs.text:
Learners may not know .NET. Walk through five ideas with the side-by-side slides. Open Program.cs from the scaffold next to App.java.

Idea Java baseline .NET 10 Say this Minimal API HttpServer with a handler class per route that reads and writes JSON by hand app.MapPost("/orders/price", ...) in Program.cs The framework binds the JSON body to a record and injects PricingEngine. try/catch maps errors to HTTP 400. Vertical slice Route, parsing, rules, errors, and fixture test The same pieces, in one API project and one test project Migrate all of it together, not only the calculation class. JSONL contract fixtures ContractFixtureTest reads the file path from a contract.fixture system property The test project reads the same file One object per line. Both languages read the same cases, so the fixture, not the C#, defines the result. Basis points Integer formula with + 5000 Same formula with checked arithmetic 1 basis point is 0.01%. SILVER is 500. Work SILVER on 101 cents: (101 × 500 + 5000) / 10000 = 5. None Include and CopyToOutputDirectory Not needed In the test .csproj The test runs from bin/. None Include tracks a non-code file, Link sets its path in the output, and CopyToOutputDirectory copies it on build. The test reads it from AppContext.BaseDirectory. A "cannot find JSONL" error usually means this item is wrong.

Then map the pieces:

Java baseline .NET 10 target Review question App and HttpHandler Minimal API route Are method, path, status, and JSON stable? OrderRequest C# records Do names and null rules match? OrderPricingService PricingEngine Are operation order and overflow checks preserved? PriceQuote response record Are all fields present and in cents? ContractFixtureTest console contract test project Does it read the same fixture file?

The target is one API project and one package-free executable test project. Minimal APIs and System.Text.Json ship with ASP.NET Core and .NET.

Don't add an object mapper, a validation framework, a mediator package, a database abstraction, or a repository interface for fixture data. This slice doesn't need them.

docs.title: Copilot working agreement
docs.text:
Give Copilot a specific route and contract. Don't ask it to infer the business contract.

Inspect:

Trace POST /orders/price through the Java starter. Return a table with the entry
point, parsing, validation, pricing rules, response mapping, and tests. Cite file
and symbol names. Do not propose .NET code yet.

Check behavior:

Compare the Java pricing code with contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl. List the
calculation order, rounding rule, shipping threshold, accepted values, and any
behavior not covered by a fixture. Do not change files.

Implement:

Implement PricingEngine.Price in the .NET 10 scaffold. Preserve the shared JSON
contract exactly. Use integer cents, checked arithmetic, and platform APIs only.
Do not add packages or change the endpoint shape.

Review:

Review the Java and .NET pricing implementations for behavior drift. Focus on
operation order, rounding, validation, overflow, shipping threshold, tax base,
and response fields. Return findings before editing.

docs.title: Reject these patterns
docs.text:
• "Convert this project to .NET."
  • generated packages without a stated need;
  • a new contract because the C# model looks cleaner;
  • decimal or floating-point calculations without a parity decision;
  • tests generated from the .NET implementation instead of the shared fixtures;
  • deleting the Java path before tests and review support the replacement.

docs.title: Step 1: establish the Java behavior
docs.text:
cd sessions/session-m2-07-java-to-dotnet-modernization/lab/starter/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package
java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

Send the gold-save10-domestic request. The response:

{
  "subtotalCents": 5097,
  "tierDiscountCents": 510,
  "couponDiscountCents": 459,
  "shippingCents": 795,
  "taxCents": 341,
  "totalCents": 5264
}

docs.title: Step 2: trace the request
docs.text:
Open in order: App.java, JsonCodec.java, OrderRequest.java, OrderPricingService.java, PriceQuote.java, ContractFixtureTest.java.

The HTTP handler is thin. Most behavior sits in the pricing service and the fixture-backed test.

docs.title: Step 3: show a plausible wrong migration
docs.text:
In a temporary demo copy, change the .NET coupon calculation to use subtotal instead of afterTier, then run:

dotnet run --project OrderPricing.ContractTests

The gold-save10-domestic case fails. Clean C# can still produce the wrong result.

Restore the reference code, run the test again, and show all five cases passing.

docs.title: Step 4: compare HTTP results
docs.text:
dotnet run --project OrderPricing.Api -- --urls http://localhost:5080

Send the same request to ports 8080 and 5080 and compare the JSON field values. This shows one HTTP request and five pricing cases, not full service parity.

docs.title: Review points
docs.text:
Pause the lab at these points.

  1. Request path. Learners identify one HTTP entry point, one parsing boundary, one domain calculation, one response mapping, and one contract test. If they describe only classes, ask which observable behavior each class supports.
  2. Contract before code. Learners explain the round-half-up case without reading the expected value. Ask them to calculate the tier and coupon discounts in order.
  3. Generated change. Before learners accept Copilot output, ask: Did it add packages? Change JSON names? Use floating point? Drop checked arithmetic? Move the shipping threshold? Tax shipping?
  4. Compare test and HTTP results. Require the Java contract test output, the .NET contract test output, and one matching HTTP response.

docs.title: Migration backlog model
docs.text:
Priority Slice Checks before cutover P0 Order pricing Shared contract cases, validation checks, HTTP comparison P1 Sample-order query Response contract and synthetic catalog checks P1 Health and diagnostics Agreed status contract and operational owner P2 Error consistency Status and JSON error matrix P2 Load and concurrency Measured target and repeatable test

Learners may list up to three next slices and what must pass before the Java path goes. This is optional and the lab doesn't require it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
The learner translates every Java class. Return to the route and contract.

The .NET output is off by one cent. Check the operation order and the + 5000 round-half-up step.

Free shipping triggers too early. The threshold uses merchandise after both discounts.

Tax includes shipping. The Java behavior taxes discounted merchandise only.

The generated API adds packages. Remove them unless the learner can name a requirement platform APIs can't meet.

Tests pass because expected values were copied from new code. The shared fixture is the source. Don't regenerate it from the migration.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Learners run and inspect the Java baseline, review the shared contract cases, implement the .NET pricing engine, add package-free contract tests, and compare Java and .NET HTTP responses. Migration notes are optional.

One route must pass the contract and HTTP checks. The rest of the Java service stays until its own slices have contracts and review.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Design a canvas extension for one synthetic delivery-readiness board. Write the contract first, then create the canvas in the GitHub Copilot app. Test a direct update, an agent-requested update, and a rejected update with its recovery. Compare the final canvas with the contract.

A canvas is a shared interactive surface. People use visible controls while an agent calls named agent-callable capabilities on the same state. A plugin can package a canvas with skills or MCP servers. A canvas does not replace the system that owns the work.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Choose a canvas only when visible shared state improves the workflow.
  • Separate canvas state, human actions, and agent-callable capabilities.
  • Write validation rules that reject incomplete state changes.
  • Create a project-scoped or user-scoped canvas and read what it generated.
  • Name the pros, cons, and limits of canvas extensions.
  • Recover from a rejected action without weakening the contract.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• GitHub Copilot app access with the built-in /create-canvas skill.
  • Permission to create files under .github/extensions for project scope. Otherwise use user scope.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. A completed canvas contract.
  2. A canvas created in a sandbox.
  3. Records of a direct, an agent-requested, a rejected, and a recovered change.
  4. A final state that matches the contract.

Optional: the Feature Workbench variant uses synthetic CI results to practice a test-gate decision. Skip it if time is short.

See the curriculum glossary for canvas, capability, plugin, and MCP terms.

docs.title: Define the contract, state, and allowed actions
Today's outcome
docs.text:
Build one delivery-readiness canvas in the Copilot app.

Record:

  • the contract;
  • one direct update;
  • one agent-requested update;
  • one rejected update and its recovery.

You need the Copilot app and the built-in /create-canvas skill. If project scope is unavailable, use user scope.

docs.title: Choose the right customization
docs.text:
Need Use Repository convention Instructions Repeatable procedure Skill Specialist behavior Custom agent External tool or data MCP server Shared interactive artifact Canvas Packaged customizations Plugin

Use a canvas when people and an agent need to inspect or change the same visible state.

Compare with M3-03, M3-04, and M3-05: a skill gives know-how, a custom agent gives a role, an MCP server gives reach. A canvas gives a shared surface.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Term Meaning Canvas extension A shared, interactive panel in the Copilot app for one work artifact: a board, plan, checklist, or dashboard Agent-callable capability A named action the agent can call on the canvas, such as move_card. Each has an input schema Human action A control in the panel: button, card, or filter Plugin A package that can ship a canvas with skills or MCP servers. You install it from Customize > Canvas

People and the agent change the same state. Capabilities are generated from your prompt, and you can ask the agent to add, remove, or revise them.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
A canvas is A canvas is not A visible, shared working surface The system of record Limited to the capabilities you list A way to give the agent broad access Editable by a person and the agent A replacement for review

A capability is the agent's whole reach. If the contract does not list it, remove it. Dependencies and persisted data come with the extension, so read them before you keep it.

docs.title: Canvas anatomy
docs.text:
shared state
  ├─ human actions in the interface
  ├─ agent-callable capabilities
  └─ validation before every change

The contract is a short document you write first. It names all four parts. Copilot generates the extension from the contract, and you check the result against it.

docs.title: Generated files
docs.text:
Scope decides where the extension lives:

Scope Path Project (repository) .github/extensions/<name>/ User ~/.copilot/extensions/<name>/

Docs describe a typical layout. Check what Copilot actually generated.

  • package.json: metadata and dependencies
  • an entry file such as extension.mjs: canvas behavior, capabilities, validation
  • optional JSON under artifacts/: persisted state

Read the entry file against the contract. Check package.json for packages you did not ask for.

docs.title: Worked contract
docs.text: Part Delivery-readiness rule State item, status, review flag, evidence Status planned, in-progress, review, ready Human actions set status, flag review, add evidence Agent capabilities read board, update one named item, list flagged items Validation known item, accepted status, evidence before ready

docs.title: Keep authority narrow
docs.text:
Allowed:

  • read the current board;
  • update one named item;
  • list items flagged for review.

Out of scope:

  • deployment;
  • external writes;
  • credentials;
  • hidden data imports;
  • broad actions such as "manage the project."

docs.title: Prepared demo inputs
docs.text: ID Item Start state Evidence DOC-101 Draft operator guide planned none API-204 Add retry metric in-progress test log WEB-318 Check empty state review preview

docs.title: Demo sequence
docs.text:
1. Optional: run the local scaffolding tests (they check the exercise contract, not Copilot).
  2. Create the canvas from the worked prompt.
  3. Move WEB-318 to ready with a visible control.
  4. Ask the agent to move API-204 to review.
  5. Ask for DOC-101 to move to ready.
  6. Show the rejection, add evidence, and retry.

docs.title: Creation prompt
docs.text:
/create-canvas

Create a delivery-readiness canvas from @prepared-items.json.
Use the contract in @canvas-contract.md.
People can add evidence and update one item.
Copilot can read the board, update one named item, and list review flags.
Reject unknown items or statuses. Require evidence before ready.
Do not connect external systems.

Use project scope when .github/extensions is allowed. Otherwise use user scope.

docs.title: Two paths, one state
docs.text:
Path Result Human control The item visibly changes in the canvas Agent capability The named item changes and the response matches the canvas

If the response and visible state disagree, stop and inspect the artifact.

docs.title: Rejection is part of the design
docs.text:
Request:

Move DOC-101 to ready.

Expected:

Rejected: evidence is required before ready.

The state stays unchanged and the message names the rule.

docs.title: Recovery keeps the rule
docs.text:
1. Add synthetic evidence to DOC-101.
  2. Retry the same transition.
  3. Check that ready is now accepted.
  4. Record the state before, the rejection, the correction, and the state after.

docs.title: Review the generated extension
docs.text:
Check:

  • state fields and defaults;
  • visible actions;
  • agent-callable capabilities;
  • dependencies and persisted data.

Remove anything the contract did not request.

docs.title: About the local tests
docs.text:
lab/starter/src/canvas-contract.mjs and its tests are hand-built scaffolding. They encode this exercise's rules in plain JavaScript.

  • They do not run, test, or imitate Copilot canvas behavior.
  • They give you a fast check of the rules before you generate anything.
  • The real check is the generated canvas against the contract.

docs.title: Pros, cons, and limits
docs.text:
Pros Cons and limits Visible state you can inspect and steer Canvases are new. Behavior and docs may change People and agent share one artifact Generated code needs review like any code State survives turns and handoffs A canvas is not a system of record Capabilities limit what the agent can call Needs the Copilot app. Project scope needs write access to .github/extensions

Stay in chat for a short answer or one draft. Check the current docs before teaching.

docs.title: Source of truth
docs.text:
The canvas is a working artifact, not a system of record.

If another system owns the data, label the canvas as a projection and keep external writes out of scope.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Use one contract and one prepared data set for the full two hours.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-01 lab: Build and review a canvas contract
Objective
docs.text:
Use one synthetic delivery-readiness contract from setup through handoff. Create the canvas in the Copilot app from the contract. Make a visible change and an agent-requested change to the same state. Check that an invalid change is rejected, then recover without changing the rule.

You need the Copilot app and /create-canvas. Use synthetic data only. Canvas extensions are new, so check the current docs if a step differs from what you see.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. Your completed canvas-contract.md.
  2. The generated extension location.
  3. A final state that matches the accepted transitions.

docs.title: Setup (optional)
docs.text:
The local tests are scaffolding: hand-built JavaScript that checks this exercise's rules. They don't test Copilot or the canvas you generate. Run them for a quick sanity check, or skip them.

From the repository root:

cd sessions/session-m3-01-copilot-app-canvases/lab/starter
npm test

Expected result:

tests 4
pass 4
fail 0

Open canvas-contract.md, prepared-items.json, and demo-runbook.md. Copy them to a working folder if you don't want to edit the starter files.

docs.title: Time plan
docs.text: Part Work Time 1 Check the contract 15 min 2 Optional scaffolding tests 5 min 3 Create the canvas 30 min 4 Make two visible state changes 25 min 5 Check rejection and recovery 25 min 6 Inspect and hand off 20 min

docs.title: Part 1: Check the contract (15 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Pick project or user scope.
  2. Check that all data comes from prepared-items.json.
  3. Review every state field, human action, agent capability, and validation rule in canvas-contract.md.

The contract must keep these rules:

  • statuses are planned, in-progress, review, and ready;
  • one update changes one named item;
  • ready requires non-empty evidence;
  • unknown items and statuses are rejected;
  • no external system is connected.

Checkpoint 1: A peer can explain the contract without adding verbal requirements.

docs.title: Part 2: Optional scaffolding tests (5 minutes)
docs.text:
npm test

Map each test in test/canvas-contract.test.mjs to a contract rule. If the tests fail, reset your copy from lab/starter/ or skip this part. The canvas doesn't depend on them.

Checkpoint 2: Your group can name the planned rejection.

docs.title: Part 3: Create the canvas (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Open a Copilot app session and run:

/create-canvas

Create a delivery-readiness canvas from @prepared-items.json.
Use the contract in @canvas-contract.md.
People can add evidence and update one item.
Copilot can read the board, update one named item, and list review flags.
Reject unknown items or statuses. Require evidence before ready.
Do not connect external systems.

Choose project scope (the docs call it repository scope) if you can create files under .github/extensions. Otherwise choose user scope.

Find the generated directory (.github/extensions/<name>/ or ~/.copilot/extensions/<name>/). Expect a package.json and an entry file such as extension.mjs, and possibly JSON state. The exact layout can differ, so write down what you see.

Read the entry file for state, visible controls, and agent-callable capabilities. Check package.json for dependencies you didn't ask for. Ask Copilot to remove anything outside the contract.

Checkpoint 3: The canvas shows all three prepared items and no extra capability.

docs.title: Part 4: Make two visible state changes (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Change A, direct action. Move WEB-318 from review to ready. It succeeds because the item already has evidence.

Change B, agent-requested action. Ask Copilot:

Move API-204 from in-progress to review. Change only that item.

Check that:

  • WEB-318 is ready;
  • API-204 is review;
  • DOC-101 is still planned;
  • the visible state and the response agree.

Checkpoint 4: One human action and one agent request changed the same state without breaking the contract.

docs.title: Part 5: Check rejection and recovery (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Request:

Move DOC-101 to ready.

Expected result:

Rejected: evidence is required before ready.

DOC-101 stays planned. Now add this synthetic evidence:

docs://operator-guide-review

Retry the same status change. It succeeds.

Record the state before the request, the rejection text, the evidence you added, and the final accepted state.

If the first request succeeds, stop. Restore the validation rule and repeat the case.

Checkpoint 5: Recovery corrected the data and kept the rule.

docs.title: Part 6: Inspect and hand off (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Swap canvases with another group. Inspect:

  • artifact location and scope;
  • state and defaults;
  • visible human actions;
  • agent-callable capabilities;
  • rejection and recovery records;
  • dependencies and persisted data.

Fix contract mismatches, then compare the final state with ../solution/final-state.json.

Checkpoint 6: The canvas matches the contract.

You're done when another person can identify the extension scope, the fixed contract, the starting state, both accepted changes, and the rejected change with its recovery.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Issue Response Project scope is blocked Use user scope. Generated actions exceed the contract Remove them before testing. State and agent response disagree Stop and inspect the shared artifact. Local tests fail before edits Restore the starter files, or skip Part 2. ready accepts empty evidence Fix the rule before review.

The worked contract and final state are in ../solution/.

docs.title: Optional variant: Feature Workbench
docs.text:
Optional. Skip it unless you finish early or your trainer assigns it.

  1. Open starter/feature-workbench-contract.md.
  2. Load the synthetic checks from starter/feature-workbench-sample.json.
  3. Decide whether FEAT-204 should pass the test gate.
  4. Record the required check that blocks the decision.
  5. Compare your review with solution/feature-workbench-solution.md and solution/feature-workbench-final-state.json.

The canvas may propose pass, hold, or rerun. A human reviewer records the final decision. Don't connect a live CI system, merge code, or trigger deployment.

docs.title: Session M3-01: Trainer guide
docs.text:
00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide Enable timer shortcut (T)

Teaching time: 60 minutes

Lab handoff: ../lab/README.md

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Teach learners to define a canvas contract and explain each action. Show a rejected update, then check whether the final state matches the contract.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
1. Check that you have Copilot app access and the built-in /create-canvas skill.
  2. Decide on project scope (.github/extensions) or user scope.
  3. Optional: run the scaffolding tests (see 0:24 to 0:28):
cd sessions/session-m3-01-copilot-app-canvases/lab/starter
npm test
  1. Open prepared-items.json, canvas-contract.md, and demo-runbook.md.
  2. Keep ../lab/solution/demo-evidence.md ready in case the live run is delayed or unavailable. If /create-canvas is missing, use this prepared manual demo and say so.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment What learners show 0:00 to 0:03 Outcome Deliverables understood 0:03 to 0:08 Choose the right customization Canvas decision explained 0:08 to 0:16 Terms and boundaries Canvas, plugin, capability defined 0:16 to 0:24 Contract and generated files State, actions, capabilities, validation 0:24 to 0:28 Prepared inputs and scaffolding Items understood 0:28 to 0:40 Live or prepared demo Two visible state changes 0:40 to 0:46 Rejection and recovery Rule preserved through recovery 0:46 to 0:50 Generated extension review Keep, revise, or remove 0:50 to 0:56 Pros, cons, and limits Fit decision 0:56 to 1:00 Lab handoff Roles and checkpoints clear

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:03: Outcome
docs.text:
Frame the session: "We are designing one shared artifact. Judge it by its visible behavior, not by a polished chat response."

Show the deliverables and say whether you'll run the live or prepared demo.

docs.title: 0:03 to 0:08: Choose the right customization
docs.text:
Use the decision table from the slides:

  • instructions state conventions;
  • a skill describes a repeatable procedure;
  • a custom agent supplies specialist behavior;
  • an MCP server connects tools or data;
  • a canvas gives people and an agent one interactive artifact;
  • a plugin can package a canvas with other customizations.

Tie back to M3-03 to M3-05: a skill gives know-how, a custom agent gives a role, an MCP server gives reach. A canvas gives a shared surface.

Use a canvas when state must stay visible across several actions or a handoff. Stay in chat for a short answer or one draft.

Checkpoint: Ask, "What breaks if this stays in chat?" A good answer names lost visibility, direct control, or saved state for handoff.

docs.title: 0:08 to 0:16: Terms and boundaries
docs.text:
Define four terms, using the slides:

  • Canvas extension: a shared, interactive panel in the Copilot app for one work artifact.
  • Human action: a control in the panel.
  • Agent-callable capability: a named action the agent can call on the canvas. Copilot generates capabilities from your prompt. You can ask it to add, remove, or revise them.
  • Plugin: a package that can ship a canvas with skills or MCP servers. Some featured canvases need a plugin installed from Customize > Canvas.

Then state the boundaries. A capability is the agent's whole reach on that canvas, so the contract lists only what is needed. A canvas is not the system of record. Generated code and dependencies need review.

Checkpoint: Ask, "Which capability would you refuse to expose, and why?"

docs.title: 0:16 to 0:24: Contract and generated files
docs.text:
Open ../lab/starter/canvas-contract.md and walk through it:

  1. State: id, item, status, reviewFlag, and evidence.
  2. Human actions: add evidence, set a status, set the review flag.
  3. Agent capabilities: read the board, update one named item, list flagged items.
  4. Validation: reject unknown IDs, unknown statuses, and ready without evidence.
  5. Boundary: synthetic data, no external systems.

Teaching test: Every action must fit in one sentence. A broad verb such as "manage" needs a smaller action.

Then explain what Copilot generates from the contract. Scope sets the location: .github/extensions/<name>/ (project) or ~/.copilot/extensions/<name>/ (user). The docs describe a typical layout: package.json for metadata and dependencies, an entry file such as extension.mjs for behavior and capabilities, and optional JSON under artifacts/ for state. Layouts vary, so check what appears.

docs.title: 0:24 to 0:28: Prepared inputs and scaffolding
docs.text:
Open prepared-items.json. Point out the three starting states and which item lacks evidence. Optionally run:

cd sessions/session-m3-01-copilot-app-canvases/lab/starter
npm test

The tests are scaffolding. Hand-built code in src/canvas-contract.mjs encodes this exercise's rules so learners can check them quickly. They don't run, test, or imitate Copilot canvas behavior. The real check is the generated canvas against the contract. The rules they encode:

  • an item with evidence can move to ready;
  • an agent-requested named update changes the same state model;
  • DOC-101 cannot move to ready without evidence;
  • adding evidence allows the retry.

docs.title: Live demo
docs.text:
/create-canvas

Create a delivery-readiness canvas from @prepared-items.json.
Use the contract in @canvas-contract.md.
People can add evidence and update one item.
Copilot can read the board, update one named item, and list review flags.
Reject unknown items or statuses. Require evidence before ready.
Do not connect external systems.

After generation:

  1. inspect the files and declared capabilities;
  2. remove fields or actions outside the contract;
  3. use a visible control to move WEB-318 from review to ready;
  4. ask Copilot to move API-204 from in-progress to review;
  5. compare the visible board with the agent response.

docs.title: Prepared demo
docs.text:
Open ../lab/solution/demo-evidence.md and ../lab/solution/final-state.json. Trace the same two changes and tell learners these are prepared examples, not a live app call.

If the canvas isn't ready by 0:36, switch to the prepared demo. Keep the rejection, recovery, and review segments.

docs.title: 0:40 to 0:46: Rejection and recovery
docs.text:
Request:

Move DOC-101 to ready.

Expected:

  • the update is rejected;
  • the message names the missing evidence rule;
  • DOC-101 stays planned.

Add the synthetic evidence docs://operator-guide-review, then retry. The same transition now succeeds, the rule is unchanged, and the change record shows the state before, the rejection, the correction, and the state after.

If the generated canvas accepts the first request, pause and restore the rule. An accepted unsafe update is a failed demo.

docs.title: 0:46 to 0:50: Inspect the extension
docs.text: Check generated files and dependencies, state fields and persisted data, visible human actions, agent-callable capabilities, and validation messages. Remove generated features the contract didn't request.

docs.title: 0:50 to 0:56: Pros, cons, and limits
docs.text:
Pros Cons and limits Visible state you can inspect and steer Canvas extensions are new; behavior and docs may change People and agent share one artifact Generated code needs review like any code State survives turns and handoffs Not a system of record Capabilities limit what the agent can call Needs the Copilot app; project scope needs write access to .github/extensions

Ask: "Would you use a canvas or chat for this task?" Check current docs before teaching: the /create-canvas skill, the two scopes, and the file layout come from GitHub's canvas extension docs.

docs.title: 0:56 to 1:00: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Assign four roles. One person may hold two in a small group: contract writer, app operator, contract tester, reviewer.

Point to the six lab checkpoints. The same three prepared items stay in use for the whole lab.

Close with: "Keep the contract fixed while you test the implementation. If the implementation needs broader authority, review the contract first."

docs.title: Common failures
docs.text: Failure Recovery /create-canvas is missing Use the prepared demo. Project scope is not allowed Use user scope. Generation takes too long Stop and show the prepared demo record. Extra capabilities appear Remove them. Agent response and visible state differ Stop and inspect the artifact. ready succeeds without evidence Fix the rule and rerun the rejection. A learner proposes real work data Use the supplied synthetic input.

docs.title: Optional: Feature Workbench
docs.text:
Skip this unless learners finish early or the audience is CI-focused. It reuses the same method with a narrower decision: may synthetic feature work pass a test gate?

  • ../lab/starter/feature-workbench-contract.md
  • ../lab/starter/feature-workbench-sample.json
  • ../lab/solution/feature-workbench-solution.md
  • ../lab/solution/feature-workbench-final-state.json

Learners review three synthetic CI checks, see a gate decision rejected when a required check fails, then add the evidence that allows a retry. People may acknowledge a result and request a gate evaluation. The agent may propose pass, hold, or rerun. A human reviewer records the decision. The workbench never deploys, merges, or calls a live CI service. The worked solution holds FEAT-204 because integration-tests failed.
