docs.title: Session M3-05: Agent Skills
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Agentic Workflows Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-04 Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file that teaches Copilot one repeatable workflow. Copilot loads it only when your request matches its description.

You learn what skills are and how they differ from instructions, prompt files, custom agents, and MCP servers. Then you write one with the skill-creator skill, test it live in the Copilot CLI, and fix it from what you see. You finish with the pros, cons, and traps of skills.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain what a skill is, where it lives, and when Copilot loads it.
  • Choose between a skill, instructions, a prompt file, a custom agent, and an MCP server.
  • Use skill-creator to interview, draft, and revise a skill.
  • Build an interview skill (grill-me) that pressure-tests a plan.
  • Compare skills with custom agents and MCP servers, and pick the right one.
  • Write a description that triggers when it should and stays quiet when it shouldn't.
  • Test a skill live with a matching, a non-matching, and an ambiguous prompt.
  • Judge a skill from someone else before you install it.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
The standalone Copilot CLI from Session M2-01 with skills support, and Git.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Starter project lab/starter/release-notes-project/ Reference skill lab/solution/release-notes/SKILL.md Expected output lab/solution/expected-output.md

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• Skill anatomy: SKILL.md, frontmatter, scripts, references
  • Where skills load from: project and personal locations
  • Skills vs instructions, prompt files, custom agents, and MCP
  • Writing the description, the body, and bundled files
  • skill-creator: interview, draft, test prompts
  • Pros, cons, and tips
  • Trusting third-party skills

docs.title: Write one, test it, fix it
docs.text: Session M3-05 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time What a skill is 10 min Skill, agent, or MCP server? 15 min Writing a good skill 10 min Demo: skill-creator 12 min Pros, cons, and tips 8 min Lab handoff 5 min

docs.title: What a skill is
docs.text:
A folder with a SKILL.md file. Copilot loads it when your request matches its description.

.github/skills/release-notes/
├── SKILL.md          # required: frontmatter + instructions
├── references/       # optional: read when needed
└── scripts/          # optional: run, not read
  • Project skills: .github/skills, .claude/skills, .agents/skills
  • Personal skills: ~/.copilot/skills, ~/.agents/skills

An open standard. Works in the CLI, the Copilot app, cloud agent, and IDE agent mode.

docs.title: How Copilot uses one
docs.text:
1. You send a request.
  2. Copilot compares it with each skill's description.
  3. On a match, it loads SKILL.md into context.
  4. It follows the instructions and can use files in the folder.

Or call one yourself: Use the /release-notes skill for this.

The description is the trigger. Get it wrong and nothing else matters.

docs.title: Skill or something else?
docs.text:
Need Use Rule that always applies Repository instructions One saved prompt you run by hand Prompt file A workflow Copilot picks up when relevant Skill A persona with its own tools and scope Custom agent Live access to a system MCP server

Rule of thumb: instructions are always on. Skills load on demand.

docs.title: Skill vs custom agent vs MCP server
docs.text:
Skill Custom agent MCP server Gives Copilot Know-how A role Reach Is Markdown, plus optional files Markdown with tools and model A running server Loads On demand When picked or delegated When configured Risk Wrong trigger Too many tools Credentials, data

They combine. An agent can use skills. A skill can teach Copilot to use an MCP server well.

docs.title: Example: grill-me
docs.text:
A skill that interviews you about a plan.

  • Reads your file first, so it doesn't ask what you already wrote.
  • One question at a time, with a recommended answer.
  • Stops when a colleague could build from the plan.
  • Ends with decisions and open questions.

Not every skill makes a file. Some change how Copilot works with you.

docs.title: More examples
docs.text: Skill What it does release-notes Writes changelog entries in your format. grill-me Interviews you before you plan. skill-creator Helps you write and test skills. pdf, docx, xlsx Bundle scripts that read and write files.

docs.title: Frontmatter
docs.text:
---
name: release-notes
description: Write release notes or a CHANGELOG entry from merged PRs.
  Use when the user asks for release notes, a changelog entry, or
  "what shipped". Don't use for commit messages or PR descriptions.
---
  • name: lowercase with hyphens, same as the directory
  • description: what it does and when to use it
  • Optional: allowed-tools, argument-hint, user-invocable, disable-model-invocation, license. Check the current docs

docs.title: Write the description
docs.text:
Weak: Helps with releases.

Better: says what, when, and when not.

  • List the words people actually use.
  • Add a "Don't use for…" line next to look-alike tasks.
  • Be a little pushy. Skills tend to undertrigger.

docs.title: Write the body
docs.text:
• Use imperative steps: "Read the top two entries."
  • Explain why a rule matters. The model generalizes better from reasons than from shouting.
  • Show a short example of the output.
  • Say what to do when input is missing: ask.
  • Keep SKILL.md short. Move long templates to references/.

docs.title: Bundle files
docs.text:
SKILL.md        → "Group PRs using references/format.md"
references/    → loaded only when the step needs it
scripts/        → run for deterministic work

Scripts need allowed-tools to run without a prompt. Don't pre-approve shell unless you've read every script and trust the source.

docs.title: skill-creator
docs.text:
A skill that helps you write skills.

  1. Interviews you: purpose, triggers, output, edge cases.
  2. Drafts SKILL.md and bundled files.
  3. Suggests test prompts.
  4. Revises from what you saw.

Its eval and description-optimizer scripts call the claude CLI. Skip them. Test by hand.

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Repeatable: same workflow every time.
  • On demand: loaded only when relevant, unlike always-on instructions.
  • Shareable: commit it, review it, version it.
  • Portable: an open standard across Copilot surfaces.
  • Bundles files: templates, references, scripts.

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Triggering is probabilistic. It can miss or misfire.
  • Failures are quiet. No error when it doesn't load.
  • Skills collide. Overlapping descriptions confuse selection.
  • They go stale like any doc.
  • Third-party skills are code. Scripts can run.
  • Support differs by surface. Check yours.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start from a real task you've done by hand.
  • Test three prompts: should trigger, shouldn't, ambiguous.
  • Run each twice. Variance is normal.
  • Fix one thing at a time, then rerun.
  • If it's one always-on rule, write instructions instead.
  • Delete skills nobody uses.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
1. Run a baseline with no skill.
  2. Install skill-creator.
  3. Create release-notes with it.
  4. Test three prompts live.
  5. Fix what failed.
  6. Build grill-me and interview yourself about idea.md.
  7. Decide: skill, custom agent, or MCP server?
  8. Review one third-party skill.

Submit your test results, both skills, and decisions.md.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-05 lab: Write, test, and fix a skill
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A working release-notes skill, your live test results, an interview skill, and a decision table

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Your team writes changelog entries by hand and each one looks different. You will write a skill that produces them in the project's format, using skill-creator to do most of the drafting.

Part Work Time 1 Baseline: no skill 10 min 2 Install skill-creator 10 min 3 Create the skill 25 min 4 Test it live 20 min 5 Fix it 15 min 6 Example: an interview skill 25 min 7 Skill, custom agent, or MCP server? 10 min 8 Review a third-party skill 5 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need Git and the standalone Copilot CLI from Session M2-01 with skills support. Use the synthetic project in this lab.

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05
cp -R sessions/session-m3-05-agent-skills/lab/starter/release-notes-project \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/release-notes-project
git init -q && git add -A && git commit -qm "Start"

The project has three files: CHANGELOG.md with the team's format, merged-prs.md with PRs merged since the last release, and idea.md, a rough plan you will use in Part 6.

docs.title: Part 1: Baseline without a skill
docs.text:
Start copilot in the project and ask:

Write release notes for the PRs in merged-prs.md.

Save the answer as baseline.md. Compare it with the entries in CHANGELOG.md.

Checkpoint: You can name at least two differences, such as missing sections, internal PRs included, or a different tone.

docs.title: Part 2: Install skill-creator
docs.text:
skill-creator is a skill that helps you write skills. It lives in anthropics/skills.

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/anthropics/skills ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/skills
mkdir -p ~/.copilot/skills
cp -R ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/skills/skills/skill-creator ~/.copilot/skills/

Restart copilot, or run /skills reload. Then run:

/skills info skill-creator

You should see its description and location. A skill in ~/.copilot/skills is personal: it works in every project.

Read the first 60 lines of its SKILL.md before you use it. Note how it tells Copilot to work: interview first, then draft, then test.

docs.title: Part 3: Create the skill
docs.text:
Ask Copilot to use it. Keep the request short and let skill-creator interview you:

Use /skill-creator to create a project skill called release-notes in
.github/skills/. It should turn a list of merged PRs into a changelog entry
in this project's format.

Answer its questions with these facts:

  • The entry matches the top entries of CHANGELOG.md.
  • Group PRs by label. Leave out chores, dependency bumps, and docs typos.
  • Breaking changes go under Upgrade notes.
  • If the version or date is missing, ask for it.
  • It must not trigger for commit messages or PR descriptions.

When skill-creator offers formal evals, decline. Its eval and description-optimizer scripts call the claude CLI, which you don't use here. You will test by hand in Part 4.

Read what it wrote.

.github/skills/release-notes/
├── SKILL.md
└── references/format.md      # may differ

Checkpoint: SKILL.md starts with name and description frontmatter. The directory name matches name. Compare it with solution/release-notes/SKILL.md.

docs.title: Part 4: Test it live
docs.text:
Run /skills reload, then /skills info release-notes. Start a fresh session. Try three prompts and note what happens for each:

# Prompt You expect 1 Write release notes for the PRs in merged-prs.md. Version 2.4.0, dated 2026-10-21. The skill loads. The entry matches the format. 2 Write a commit message for the CSV export change. The skill stays out. 3 What changed recently? Unclear. Record what you see.

Also try naming the skill: Use the /release-notes skill for merged-prs.md.

Skill selection can vary between runs. Run prompt 1 twice. Record whether it loaded both times.

Compare prompt 1 with solution/expected-output.md.

Checkpoint: You have a result for each prompt and know which ones the skill got wrong.

docs.title: Part 5: Fix it
docs.text:
Use what you saw in Part 4. Fix one problem at a time and rerun the failing prompt.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Skill didn't load for prompt 1 Description lacks the words you used Add trigger phrases: "release notes", "changelog entry", "what shipped" Skill loaded for prompt 2 Description is too broad Add "Don't use for commit messages or PR descriptions" Output ignores a rule Rule is buried or vague Move it up, state it as an instruction, and say why it matters SKILL.md is long Everything is in one file Move the entry template to references/format.md and link it from SKILL.md Skill invents a version No "ask first" rule Add one

You can ask skill-creator to apply a fix, or edit the file yourself. Run /skills reload after each change.

Checkpoint: Prompts 1 and 2 behave as expected on two runs each. Save the final skill under .github/skills/release-notes/.

docs.title: Part 6: Example: an interview skill
docs.text:
Not every skill produces a file. Some change how Copilot works with you. A popular example is grill-me: you give Copilot a rough plan, and it interviews you until the gaps are gone.

  1. Ask skill-creator:

Create a skill called grill-me. When I share a plan or idea, it should interview me one question at a time, recommend an answer for each question, and finish with a summary of decisions and open questions.

  1. Save it under .github/skills/grill-me/ and run /skills reload.
  2. Start a fresh session and run: Grill me on idea.md.
  3. Answer at least eight questions. Notice that Copilot reads idea.md first and doesn't ask what the file already says.
  4. Compare your skill with solution/grill-me/SKILL.md. Which instructions did yours miss?

Then try the same idea without the skill: Review idea.md and tell me what's missing. Copilot will probably return a list of gaps. Compare the two experiences.

Why a skill works here. The interview rules ("one question at a time", "recommend an answer", "stop when a colleague could build it") are exactly the kind of instruction you forget to type. The skill stores them. Use the same pattern for design reviews, incident retros, or a spec before you start a /plan.

Checkpoint: You have a working grill-me skill and a summary from your interview of idea.md.

docs.title: Part 7: Skill, custom agent, or MCP server?
docs.text:
A skill, a custom agent, and an MCP server solve different problems. Sessions M3-03 and M3-04 cover MCP servers and custom agents in depth.

Skill Custom agent MCP server What it is Instructions, plus optional scripts and files A persona with its own prompt, tools, and model A process that exposes tools and data Gives Copilot Know-how: how to do a task A role: who is doing the task Reach: access to a system Loads On demand, when the description matches When you pick it or Copilot delegates When the server is configured Needs code? No, a Markdown file No, a Markdown file Yes, a server Main risk Triggers at the wrong time Too much tool access Credentials and data leaving the machine

They combine. A custom agent can use skills. A skill can tell Copilot how to use an MCP server's tools well.

For each task, choose the best home: repository instructions, a skill, a prompt file, a custom agent, an MCP server, or nothing. Write one sentence for each choice in decisions.md.

Task Your choice "Use 2-space indentation in this repo." Produce release notes in the team format when asked. Query the issue tracker for open bugs. A reviewer persona with read-only tools. A one-off question about a stack trace. A weekly report that always starts from the same template and script. Interview me about a plan before I write a spec.

Compare with a neighbor and discuss where you differ.

docs.title: Part 8: Review a third-party skill
docs.text:
Open github/awesome-copilot skills and pick one skill. Read its SKILL.md and any scripts. Answer in decisions.md:

  • What does the description promise?
  • Does it run scripts or ask for allowed-tools? Would you approve that?
  • Would you install it? Why or why not?

Don't install it into this project.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. .github/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md and any bundled files.
  2. .github/skills/grill-me/SKILL.md and your interview summary for idea.md.
  3. Your prompt 1, 2, and 3 results, plus what you changed to fix them.
  4. decisions.md with the seven choices and your third-party review.

docs.text: Learners leave knowing what a skill is, when to write one, how to write one with skill-creator, and what can go wrong.

docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:10 What a skill is 0:10 to 0:25 Skill, agent, or MCP server? 0:25 to 0:35 Writing a good skill 0:35 to 0:47 Demo: skill-creator 0:47 to 0:55 Pros, cons, and tips 0:55 to 1:00 Lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Install skill-creator in ~/.copilot/skills (see lab Part 2) and run /skills info skill-creator.
  • Copy the starter project to a scratch folder and run the lab once. Keep the reference skill in lab/solution/release-notes/ open for comparison.
  • Pick a second demo task you can finish in 10 minutes (a commit-message or PR-template skill works).

docs.title: What a skill is (0:00 to 0:10)
docs.text:
• A skill is a folder. SKILL.md is required and must be named exactly that.
  • Frontmatter needs name and description. name is lowercase with hyphens and matches the directory.
  • Project skills live in .github/skills, .claude/skills, or .agents/skills. Personal skills live in ~/.copilot/skills or ~/.agents/skills.
  • Copilot picks a skill from the description. It then loads SKILL.md and can use other files in the folder. You can also name it: Use the /name skill.
  • It's an open standard used by several tools. Support differs by surface. Check the docs for the one you teach on.

Show: /skills list, /skills info <name>, /skills reload.

docs.title: Skill, agent, or MCP server? (0:10 to 0:25)
docs.text:
Ask the room to sort five tasks, then reveal the table.

Need Use Rule that always applies Repository instructions One saved prompt you run by hand Prompt file Workflow Copilot should pick up when relevant Skill Persona with its own tools and scope Custom agent Live access to a system MCP server

Key line: instructions are always on, skills load on demand.

Skill vs custom agent vs MCP server. Use one sentence each: a skill gives Copilot know-how, a custom agent gives it a role, an MCP server gives it reach. Link back to M3-03 (MCP) and M3-04 (custom agents) rather than re-teaching them. Stress that they combine: an agent can load skills, and a skill can describe how to use an MCP server's tools.

Example: grill-me. Show the slide, then run it live on idea.md: Grill me on idea.md. Let it ask three questions, answer them, and stop. Point out that it reads the file first and recommends an answer. The takeaway: skills can shape how you work with Copilot, not only what it produces. The finished skill is in lab/solution/grill-me/SKILL.md.

Answer key for lab Part 7:

Task Best home 2-space indentation Instructions: always applies Release notes in team format Skill Query issue tracker for open bugs MCP server Read-only reviewer persona Custom agent One-off stack trace question Nothing Weekly report from template and script Skill, with the script bundled Interview me about a plan Skill (grill-me). A custom agent also works if you want a fixed persona with restricted tools.

Accept other answers if the reasoning holds. Prompt file is a fair answer for the release notes if the team runs it by hand every time.

docs.title: Writing a good skill (0:20 to 0:32)
docs.text:
Description. It decides whether the skill loads. - Say what it does and when to use it. - List the words people actually say. - Add "Don't use for…" for look-alike tasks. - Skills tend to undertrigger, so lean specific and a bit pushy.

Show a weak and a better description side by side.

Body. - Imperative steps. - A reason for each non-obvious rule. - A short output example. - An "ask if missing" rule instead of guessing. - Keep it short. Move long templates to references/ and link them.

Scripts and tools. Files in the skill folder are available to Copilot. allowed-tools pre-approves tools. Warn that pre-approving shell removes the confirmation step, so only do it after reading every script and trusting its source.

docs.title: Demo: skill-creator (0:32 to 0:44)
docs.text:
Build your second demo skill live. Narrate the loop.

  1. Prompt: Use /skill-creator to create a project skill called <name> in .github/skills/.
  2. Let it interview you. Answer in one line each.
  3. Decline formal evals. Its eval and description-optimizer scripts call the claude CLI.
  4. Read the draft out loud. Point at the description.
  5. /skills reload, then test one matching and one non-matching prompt.
  6. If it misfires, change the description and retest.

Say what you'd edit by hand. The tool drafts; you own the result.

docs.title: Pros, cons, and tips (0:44 to 0:54)
docs.text:
Pros: repeatable, loaded on demand, shareable through git, portable across surfaces, can bundle templates and scripts.

Cons: - Triggering is probabilistic and can miss or misfire. - Failures are quiet. Nothing errors when it doesn't load. - Overlapping descriptions collide. - Skills go stale. - Third-party skills can run scripts. - Support differs by surface.

Tips: - Start from a task you've done by hand. - Test three prompts: should trigger, shouldn't, ambiguous. Run each twice. - Fix one thing at a time. - If it's one always-on rule, write instructions instead. - Delete skills nobody uses.

docs.title: Lab handoff (0:54 to 1:00)
docs.text: Open lab/README.md. Walk through the eight parts. Tell learners to run the baseline first so they can see what the skill changes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Directory name differs from name Make them match File is skill.md or Skill.md Rename to SKILL.md Skill doesn't show up /skills reload, then /skills info <name> Description is "helps with X" Add triggers and a "don't use for" line Everything in one long SKILL.md Move templates to references/ Learner tries the skill-creator eval scripts Skip them. Test by hand

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: You learn the parts of a GitHub Actions workflow first, then use one Node.js application, copilot-webapp, for three tasks: generate and lint CI with Copilot, design a staged deployment, and repair broken workflow files. Validating a local JavaScript action is optional. Every decision traces back to the same scripts, tests, build output, and health endpoint.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Name the parts of a workflow: trigger, job, step, runner, action, artifact, needs, permissions, secrets, and environments.
  • Generate CI with Copilot from repository facts, then check it with actionlint and local commands.
  • Design staging and production jobs without a live deployment.
  • Repair workflow syntax and behavior from exact failures.
  • Decide when a reusable workflow or custom action is worth it.
  • Spot common YAML mistakes in review.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
Node.js 20 or later, GitHub Copilot (CLI or agent mode in your editor), and actionlint. Repository and GitHub Actions access are optional: the lab runs locally.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Application starter lab/starter/webapp/ Reference workflows and action lab/solution/

docs.title: DevOps & infrastructure | Intermediate
docs.text: Session M4-01 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Time Topic 0:00 to 0:15 Workflow anatomy 0:15 to 0:23 Reusable workflows, custom actions, common mistakes 0:23 to 0:35 Generate and fix CI with Copilot and actionlint 0:35 to 0:45 Design deployment 0:45 to 0:55 Repair workflow failures 0:55 to 1:00 Review and lab handoff

docs.title: Anatomy of a workflow
docs.text: Part What it is Workflow A YAML file in .github/workflows/ Trigger The on: block. Decides who can start a run Job Steps on one runner. Parallel unless needs: orders them Runner A fresh machine, such as ubuntu-latest Step One run: command or one uses: action Action Reusable code a step calls

docs.title: Anatomy: data, access, and gates
docs.text:
Part What it is Artifact Files a job uploads. Jobs don't share a disk needs Job order. A failed job skips its dependents Permissions What the job's GITHUB_TOKEN can do. Set the minimum Secrets Stored values, read as ${{ secrets.NAME }} Environment A named target such as production. Holds secrets and can require reviewers

The environment's required reviewers are the deployment gate.

docs.title: Start with repository facts
docs.text:
copilot-webapp already defines the contract:

npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/app.js

The workflow calls these commands. It doesn't invent another build, artifact path, or runtime.

docs.title: When to reuse
docs.text:
Option Use it when Reusable workflow (workflow_call) Several repositories run the same pipeline Composite or JavaScript action (action.yml) One step needs real code, or you want to test it locally Neither One repository, one pipeline

An action that never fails hasn't shown it enforces anything. Test a passing and a failing run.

docs.title: Common YAML mistakes
docs.text:
• Indentation that changes what counts as a step.
  • Typos that stay valid YAML: refs/head/main never matches.
  • Old runner labels and action versions.
  • No actions/checkout, so the job has no code.
  • A secret name that doesn't match the stored one.
  • No permissions: block.
  • Secrets used directly in a step's if:.

A linter finds some of these. You find the rest by reading the spec.

docs.title: Generate CI from the application
docs.text:
Read package.json, tests, and scripts/build.js. Create ci.yml for pull requests
and pushes to main. Use Node.js 20, npm ci, existing lint, test, and build scripts,
npm caching, contents: read, and a seven-day dist artifact.

Check the draft with actionlint and the application's own commands:

actionlint ci.yml
npm test && npm run lint && npm run build

docs.title: Copilot edits, the linter decides
docs.text:
In Copilot CLI (copilot) or agent mode:

  1. Prompt: generate ci.yml from the repository.
  2. Run actionlint ci.yml yourself.
  3. Paste the exact message back: "Fix this with the smallest change."
  4. Rerun actionlint and the npm commands.

Example: runs-on: ubuntu-18.04 gives an "unknown label" message on one line. The fix changes that line.

docs.title: Deployment stays a design exercise
docs.text:
build → staging → production

The workflow references environments and secrets. Production reviewers are set in repository settings. Placeholder commands must not imply a deployment ran.

docs.title: Syntax and behavior fail differently
docs.text:
broken-ci.yml doesn't parse. actionlint points at steps:, but the cause is the step list below it: the first step is indented less than the rest.

broken-deploy.yml parses. actionlint reports only the stale runner. The bad Git ref, the wrong secret name, and the missing checkout need the spec and a careful read.

Get the output before the repair.

docs.title: Tie each repair to a failure
docs.text:
Observation: the parser fails near Setup Node.js.
Change: align the step indentation.
Proof: parse the file again.

For behavior faults, cite the deployment spec or repository facts, then check the repair.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Generate and lint CI, design deployment, and repair failures on copilot-webapp. The custom action is optional.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-01 lab: Three workflow tasks on one application
docs.text: Deliverable: ci.yml, cd.yml, and a repaired broken-deploy.yml for copilot-webapp

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You use the same application for every part. Copilot writes and fixes the YAML. actionlint and the application's own commands tell you whether it worked.

Part Work Time Setup Baseline and actionlint 10 min 1 Generate CI with Copilot, then lint and fix it 35 min 2 Design staged deployment 35 min 3 Repair the broken deploy workflow 30 min 4 Review the three files 10 min Optional Validate the JavaScript action 15 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need GitHub Copilot and Node.js 20 or later. Repository access is optional. Unless the instructor says otherwise, don't push, run Actions, install an external action, or use a deployment target. Everything here runs locally. Use no real credentials or deployment endpoints.

Use Copilot CLI (copilot, started in this session directory) or agent mode in your editor. Either works.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run commands from this session directory unless a command changes directory.

node --version
cd lab/starter/webapp
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/app.js
cd ../../..

Expected: Node 20 or later, seven passing tests, lint and build succeed, and dist/app.js exists.

Install actionlint. It checks workflow syntax, expressions, runner labels, and action inputs.

# macOS or Linux with Homebrew
brew install actionlint

# Any Linux or macOS shell: downloads the binary into the current directory
bash <(curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rhysd/actionlint/main/scripts/download-actionlint.bash) 1.7.12

On Windows, use winget install rhysd.actionlint or go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@v1.7.12. If you downloaded the binary, run it as ./actionlint below.

Check it works:

actionlint -version

If you can't install it, check syntax only and note that you skipped expression and runner checks:

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' path/to/workflow.yml

docs.title: Part 1: Generate CI, then lint and fix it
docs.text:
Goal: see what Copilot gets right from repository facts, and what a linter catches that you'd miss.

Ask Copilot:

Read lab/starter/webapp/package.json, the tests, and scripts/build.js. Create
lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml for pushes to main and pull requests.
Use ubuntu-latest and Node.js 20, npm ci, the existing lint, test, and build scripts,
npm caching, permissions: contents: read, and a dist/ artifact kept for 7 days.
Don't add dependencies or deployment steps.

Check the result in two ways:

actionlint lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml
cd lab/starter/webapp && npm ci && npm test && npm run lint && npm run build && test -f dist/app.js; cd ../../..

actionlint prints nothing when the file is clean. If it reports problems, paste the exact output back to Copilot and ask for the smallest fix. Don't ask it to rewrite the file.

If Copilot's first draft is clean, break it on purpose and fix it. Change runs-on: ubuntu-latest to ubuntu-18.04, run actionlint, and read the message. Then ask Copilot to fix it from that message.

Compare with lab/solution/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml. Check each of these in your file:

  • every run: command exists in package.json;
  • the upload path: is the directory the build creates;
  • permissions: is set, so the job token can only read contents;
  • the trigger covers pull requests, so the workflow runs on code from forks and branches. Know who can start it.

Checkpoint: Write down one thing actionlint caught or one thing you corrected in Copilot's draft, and why the workflow uploads dist/.

docs.title: Part 2: Design staged deployment
docs.text:
Goal: wire jobs together with needs, environments, and secrets, without deploying anything.

Read lab/starter/deployment-spec.md. Ask Copilot to create lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/cd.yml that:

  • builds the same application and uploads the artifact;
  • deploys to staging first, then to production with needs:;
  • references the staging and production GitHub Environments and the secrets the spec names;
  • runs two health checks;
  • describes rollback without calling a real endpoint;
  • sets permissions: at the top and widens it only on a job that needs it.
actionlint lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/cd.yml
grep -nE 'environment: (staging|production)|needs:|permissions:' \
  lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/cd.yml

Expected: no actionlint output, and the grep shows both environments, job ordering, and a permissions block.

Compare with lab/solution/workflows/cd.yml. Repository settings configure production reviewers. The workflow only names the production environment. Answer these:

  1. Which jobs would you move into a reusable workflow (workflow_call) if three repositories deployed the same way? Which stay local?
  2. Which secrets are environment secrets and which are repository secrets?
  3. What stops production from running if staging health checks fail?

Checkpoint: Write down the secret names, the production gate, the health-check behavior, and the rollback steps. No deployment ran.

docs.title: Part 3: Repair the broken deploy workflow
docs.text:
Goal: fix a workflow that parses but behaves wrongly, using the linter's output and the repository's facts.

lab/starter/broken-workflows/broken-deploy.yml targets copilot-webapp. Don't read the solution first.

actionlint lab/starter/broken-workflows/broken-deploy.yml

actionlint reports the stale runner label. It doesn't report everything. Ask Copilot to review the file against lab/starter/deployment-spec.md and list problems before it changes anything. Then check its list against these four:

Problem Where to look Runner ubuntu-18.04 no longer exists actionlint output refs/head/main should be refs/heads/main, so the deploy job never runs the if: line DEPLOY_KEY isn't the secret name in the spec deployment-spec.md No checkout step, so npm ci has no package.json the build job

Copy the file to lab/starter/broken-workflows/repaired-deploy.yml, apply the fixes, and run actionlint again. Compare with lab/solution/fixed-workflows/fixed-deploy.yml.

Then do the same for the CI file, which doesn't parse:

actionlint lab/starter/broken-workflows/broken-ci.yml

The parse error points at steps:. The cause is the first step, which is indented less than the rest. Fix it, update actions/checkout, add permissions:, and use npm ci in place of npm install. Compare with lab/solution/fixed-workflows/fixed-ci.yml.

Checkpoint: For each change, name the output or repository fact behind it. Reject a Copilot rewrite that changes lines you can't tie to a problem.

docs.title: Part 4: Review the three files
docs.text:
Read ci.yml, cd.yml, and the repaired deploy file as a reviewer. For each, find the trigger, the token permissions, every uses: reference, every secret, and every artifact. Write a short note for any line you wouldn't merge.

Local checks don't show that a production deployment is safe.

docs.title: Optional: Validate the custom action
docs.text:
Do this if you finished early. It shows when a custom action is worth writing: the logic is JavaScript, other repositories will reuse it, and you want to test it without a runner.

Copy the dependency manifests into the starter action, install, and run it against the application:

cp lab/solution/custom-action/package.json \
  lab/solution/custom-action/package-lock.json lab/starter/custom-action/
npm ci --prefix lab/starter/custom-action
cd lab/starter/webapp
: > ../custom-action/summary.md
env INPUT_THRESHOLD=0 'INPUT_REPORT-FORMAT=markdown' \
  GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY="$PWD/../custom-action/summary.md" \
  node ../custom-action/src/main.js
test -s ../custom-action/summary.md
cd ../../..

Expected: passed: true, exit code 0, and a written summary.

Now the failing case:

cd lab/starter/webapp
action_status=0
env INPUT_THRESHOLD=101 'INPUT_REPORT-FORMAT=json' \
  node ../custom-action/src/main.js || action_status=$?
printf 'Action exit code: %s\n' "$action_status"
test "$action_status" -eq 1
cd ../../..

Expected: the action reports a score below 101 and exits with code 1. Complete the action's metadata and implementation in lab/starter/custom-action/ first, then compare with lab/solution/custom-action/.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. ci.yml and cd.yml for copilot-webapp, both clean under actionlint.
  2. The repaired deploy and CI workflows, with each change tied to a message or fact.
  3. Your notes from the checkpoints.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-01 trainer guide: One application through GitHub Actions
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Teach the parts of a workflow first. Then use copilot-webapp start to finish: Copilot generates CI, actionlint and local commands check it, and learners design a staged deployment and repair broken workflows. The JavaScript action is a short demo and an optional lab part.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text:
Time Segment 0:00 to 0:15 Workflow anatomy 0:15 to 0:23 Reusable workflows, custom actions, and common YAML mistakes 0:23 to 0:35 Generate and fix CI with Copilot and actionlint 0:35 to 0:45 Design staging and production jobs 0:45 to 0:55 Diagnose workflow failures 0:55 to 1:00 Review and lab handoff

The timings match slides.md. Stop a live tool response at the end of its segment and use the prepared solution.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Run the application tests, lint, and build.
  • Install actionlint and run it on lab/starter/broken-workflows/ so you know the output.
  • Keep the supplied broken workflows unchanged.
  • Install the solution action dependencies and prepare the threshold-0 and threshold-101 runs for a short demo.
  • Don't configure a deployment target.

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:15: Workflow anatomy
docs.text:
Put lab/solution/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml on screen and label each part as you meet it:

  • Workflow: the YAML file in .github/workflows/.
  • Trigger: the on: block. It decides who can start the run.
  • Job: a group of steps on one runner. Jobs run in parallel unless one lists needs:.
  • Runner: the machine, such as ubuntu-latest. Each job gets a fresh one.
  • Step: one run: command or one uses: action.
  • Action: reusable code that a step calls, such as actions/checkout.
  • Artifact: files a job uploads so another job or a person can get them. Jobs don't share a disk.
  • needs: ordering and failure propagation between jobs.
  • Permissions: what the job's GITHUB_TOKEN can do. Set the minimum.
  • Secrets: values stored in GitHub and read as ${{ secrets.NAME }}. They are masked in logs.
  • Environments: named targets such as staging and production. They can hold secrets and require reviewers before a job starts. That is the deployment gate.

Then run the baseline:

cd lab/starter/webapp
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/app.js

Tie each workflow step to a repository fact. dist/ is a valid artifact path because the build creates it.

docs.title: 0:15 to 0:23: Reuse and common mistakes
docs.text:
Reusable workflow (on: workflow_call): a whole workflow that other workflows call as a job. Use it when several repositories repeat the same pipeline. Don't use it for one repository.

Custom action (action.yml): a single step packaged for reuse. Use a JavaScript or composite action when the logic needs real code, or when you want to test it locally. Show the optional lab's threshold-0 and threshold-101 runs in two minutes. An action that never fails hasn't shown it enforces anything.

Common YAML mistakes, with one example each from the broken files:

  • Indentation that changes what is a step. broken-ci.yml fails to parse.
  • Typos in values that stay valid YAML: refs/head/main never matches.
  • Old runner labels and old action versions.
  • Missing actions/checkout, so the job has no code.
  • Secret names that don't match what is stored.
  • No permissions: block, so the token gets the default scope.
  • ${{ }} expressions in the wrong place, for example secrets inside if: on a step.

docs.title: 0:23 to 0:35: Generate and fix CI with Copilot
docs.text:
Demo in Copilot CLI (or agent mode). Start copilot in the session directory and send:

Read package.json, tests, and scripts/build.js in copilot-webapp. Create ci.yml
for pull requests and pushes to main. Use Node.js 20, npm ci, the existing lint,
test, and build scripts, npm caching, contents: read, and a seven-day dist artifact.
Do not add dependencies or deployment steps.

Then lint outside Copilot:

actionlint lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml

If the draft is clean, change runs-on to ubuntu-18.04, run actionlint again, and paste the message into Copilot with "Fix this with the smallest change." Show that the message points at one line and the fix touches one line. Then rerun the local commands. A valid workflow can still call a missing script or upload a path that doesn't exist.

docs.title: 0:35 to 0:45: Deployment design
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/deployment-spec.md. Ask learners to find the trigger, environments, secret names, health checks, and rollback rule before generating YAML.

Review the design without deploying it. Repository settings enforce production reviewers, and the endpoints are placeholders.

docs.title: 0:45 to 0:55: Diagnose failures
docs.text: Run actionlint on broken-ci.yml. It reports the parse error at steps:, but the cause is the step list below it: the first step is indented less than the rest. Run it on broken-deploy.yml: it reports the runner label and nothing else. Use that to show what a linter can't know: the ref typo is valid, the secret name is valid, and a missing checkout is valid YAML. Each repair needs a source: the linter, the deployment spec, the Git ref format, or the checkout requirement.

docs.title: 0:55 to 1:00: Review and handoff
docs.text:
Review triggers and token permissions, action references, secret references and environment gates, and artifact contents and retention.

Learners keep notes at each lab checkpoint. Their workflow files should agree with the actionlint and application results.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Valid YAML only proves the file parses. Run the application commands and review what the workflow does.

Why one application? Learners use the same repository facts for each decision instead of rebuilding a project per exercise.

Does Copilot replace actionlint? No. Copilot drafts and fixes. actionlint and the application's commands decide whether the result is right.

Why test an action failure? An action that always exits successfully hasn't shown it enforces the threshold.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-02: Infrastructure as code with Copilot
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: DevOps & Infrastructure with Copilot Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-02, M4-01 Duration: 2 hours 30 minutes (1 hour trainer content + 1 hour 30 minutes lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means you describe networks, servers, and storage in files, and a tool builds them. The files can be reviewed, repeated, and scanned.

You learn Terraform's vocabulary in plain words, the networking terms you need, and how to prompt Copilot for IaC. You see where Copilot is weak: invented arguments, old provider versions, insecure defaults. Then you build one VPC with two subnets and a bucket, run init, validate, and plan, scan it with Trivy, and fix a finding. You finish by writing the same resources in Bicep. No cloud account needed.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain what IaC is and why teams use it.
  • Define resource, variable, output, module, provider, state, and plan.
  • Explain VPC, CIDR, subnet, and security group.
  • Write a Copilot prompt with architecture, constraints, naming, and variables instead of literals.
  • Run fmt, init, validate, and plan, and read the plan.
  • Spot invented arguments, outdated syntax, and insecure defaults in Copilot's output.
  • Scan Terraform with Trivy and fix a finding.
  • Write the same resources in Bicep and build them with az bicep build.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
GitHub Copilot, Terraform 1.5 or later, Trivy, and the Azure CLI with Bicep. No cloud account or credentials. Internet access for the first init and scan.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Starter project lab/starter/ Reference module lab/solution/modules/baseline/ Reference Bicep lab/solution/bicep/main.bicep

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• What IaC is and why
  • Terraform: resource, variable, output, module, provider, state, plan
  • Networking: VPC, CIDR, subnet, security group
  • Prompting Copilot for IaC, and repository instructions
  • Where Copilot is weak
  • Static scanning with Trivy
  • Bicep compared with Terraform
  • Pros, cons, tips, and common mistakes

docs.title: Prompt it, check it, scan it
docs.text: Session M4-02 | 2 hours 30 minutes

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time What IaC is and why 8 min Terraform in plain words 12 min Networking terms you need 5 min Prompting Copilot for IaC 12 min Where Copilot is weak 8 min Demo: prompt, plan, scan 10 min Bicep, pros and cons, handoff 5 min

docs.title: What IaC is
docs.text:
Infrastructure as code: you describe servers, networks, and storage in files. A tool builds them.

  • Review it: infrastructure changes go through pull requests.
  • Repeat it: the same files give the same setup, every time.
  • Undo it: git history is your change log.
  • Scan it: tools read the files before anything exists.

Clicking in a portal gives you none of these.

docs.title: Terraform in plain words
docs.text: Word Means Resource One thing to create: a VPC, a bucket Variable An input, so values aren't hardcoded Output A value the code shows or passes on Module A folder of resources you call like a function Provider The plugin that talks to a cloud (AWS, Azure) State Terraform's record of what it built Plan A preview of changes. Nothing changes yet.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
fmt → init → validate → plan → (review) → apply
Command Does fmt Fixes style init Downloads providers, loads modules validate Checks syntax and references. No cloud call. plan Shows what would change apply Changes the cloud. Not in this lab.

docs.title: State, in one slide
docs.text:
Terraform keeps a state file: what it built, and the IDs.

  • plan compares your code with state, then proposes the difference.
  • State can contain secrets. Don't commit it.
  • Teams store it remotely, with locking.
  • Lose it and Terraform no longer knows what it owns.

docs.title: Networking terms
docs.text:
• VPC: your private network in AWS.
  • CIDR: an address range, like 10.0.0.0/16.
  • Subnet: a slice of the VPC, in one zone.
  • Private subnet: no direct route from the internet.
  • Security group: a firewall for resources. Rules say who may connect, on which port.
  • 0.0.0.0/0: every address on the internet.

docs.title: Our lab architecture
docs.text:
VPC 10.0.0.0/16
├── private subnet 10.0.0.0/24  (zone a)
├── private subnet 10.0.1.0/24  (zone b)
└── S3 bucket: private, versioned, encrypted

Small on purpose. You read all of it.

docs.title: Prompting Copilot for IaC
docs.text:
Give it five things:

  1. Architecture: what exists and how it connects
  2. Constraints: private, encrypted, no public access
  3. Naming and tags: ${var.name_prefix}-<purpose>
  4. Variables, not literals: "hardcode nothing that belongs in a variable"
  5. Limits: "no apply", "only arguments in provider 5.x"

Then read the plan. The plan is the review point.

docs.title: Weak and strong
docs.text:
Weak

Make me a VPC and a bucket in AWS.

Strong

Module modules/baseline: one VPC from var.vpc_cidr, two private subnets
from cidrsubnet, one bucket with public access blocked, versioning, and
encryption. Name ${var.name_prefix}-<purpose>. Tag with var.tags.
No hardcoded values. Do not run apply.

docs.title: Put the rules in instructions
docs.text:
Repeat yourself once, in .github/copilot-instructions.md.

- Use hashicorp/aws ~> 5.0.
- Variables need a description and a type.
- Never write secrets into .tf files.
- Do not run terraform apply.

Copilot reads it on every request. The lab starter has one.

docs.title: Where Copilot is weak
docs.text:
Problem Example Invented arguments A resource argument that doesn't exist Old versions Pins an old provider; uses retired bucket syntax Insecure defaults 0.0.0.0/0, public buckets, no encryption Hardcoded values CIDRs and names inline Plausible but wrong Valid code, wrong architecture

validate catches the first. Scanning catches the third. You catch the rest.

docs.title: Scan before you plan
docs.text:
Trivy reads Terraform files and reports misconfigurations. No cloud account.

trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL .

AWS-0107 (HIGH): Security group rule allows unrestricted
ingress from any IP address.

Alternatives: Checkov, TFLint (a linter for provider-specific mistakes). Pick one for CI.

docs.title: Demo
docs.text:
1. Prompt Copilot with the five parts.
  2. fmt, init, validate, plan.
  3. Ask for "SSH from anywhere".
  4. trivy config. Read the finding.
  5. Fix with a variable. Scan again.

docs.title: Bicep in one slide
docs.text:
Azure's IaC language. Same ideas, different words.

Terraform Bicep variable param resource resource output output Provider and state Azure handles both 
az bicep build --file main.bicep

docs.title: Pros and cons
docs.text:
Pros Cons Fast first draft Confident wrong answers Knows the syntax Outdated versions Explains plans and errors Insecure shortcuts Converts between tools Doesn't know your org's rules

Tip: let Copilot draft. Let plan and a scanner judge.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Prompting for "a VPC" with no constraints
  • Accepting the code without reading the plan
  • Committing .terraform/, state files, or plans
  • "Fixing" validate by deleting the failing line
  • Treating a clean scan as proof of a safe design

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: One module, one scan, one Bicep file. 90 minutes, no cloud account.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-02 lab: A VPC and a bucket with Copilot
docs.text: Duration: 90 minutes Deliverable: A baseline Terraform module that passes terraform validate, a saved plan, a clean trivy scan for HIGH and CRITICAL findings, and a Bicep file that builds

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You build a small AWS setup with Copilot: one VPC (a private network), two subnets, and one S3 bucket. You run init, validate, and plan. You never run apply, and you need no AWS account.

Part Work Time 1 Read the starter 10 min 2 Build the module with Copilot 20 min 3 Run fmt, init, validate, plan 15 min 4 Catch what Copilot got wrong 10 min 5 Add an admin rule, scan, fix 20 min 6 The same thing in Bicep 10 min 7 Decide 5 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • GitHub Copilot in the Copilot CLI or your IDE's agent mode
  • Terraform 1.5 or later
  • Trivy (for example brew install trivy)
  • The Azure CLI with Bicep for Part 6 (az bicep install)

Check them with terraform version, trivy --version, and az bicep version.

Terraform and Trivy download a provider and a rule set on first run, so you need internet access. Everything else runs locally.

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m4-02
cp -R sessions/session-m4-02-iac-with-copilot/lab/starter ~/copilot-labs/session-m4-02/iac
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m4-02/iac
git init -q && git add -A && git commit -qm "Start"

docs.title: Part 1: Read the starter
docs.text:
Read the files before you prompt.

File What it is main.tf Provider setup and one module call. The provider block skips credential checks so plan works offline. variables.tf Variables: the inputs, with defaults. outputs.tf Outputs: values the root shows after a run. modules/baseline/ Empty. Copilot fills it in Part 2. .github/copilot-instructions.md Terraform rules Copilot reads on every request.

Answer in your own words:

  1. Which file sets the CIDR block (the address range) of the VPC?
  2. How does the module get its inputs? Where do its outputs go?
  3. What do the instructions forbid?

Checkpoint: You can say what a resource, variable, output, and module are, using this project as the example.

docs.title: Part 2: Build the module with Copilot
docs.text:
Start copilot in the project, or open agent mode. Give it the architecture, the constraints, and the naming. Do not say "make me a VPC".

Write the Terraform module in modules/baseline. The root main.tf already calls it.

Architecture:
- One VPC using var.vpc_cidr
- Two private subnets, one per zone in var.zones. Derive their CIDRs from the VPC CIDR with cidrsubnet. No public IPs.
- One S3 bucket for application data

Constraints:
- Bucket: block all public access, enable versioning, enable server-side encryption.
- Name every resource ${var.name_prefix}-<purpose>. Tag every resource with var.tags.
- Define the module's variables in variables.tf and its outputs in outputs.tf.
  The outputs are vpc_id, subnet_ids, and bucket_name, as the root outputs.tf expects.
- Hardcode nothing that belongs in a variable.
- Use only arguments that exist in the hashicorp/aws 5.x provider. Say so if you are unsure.
- Do not run terraform apply.

Read the diff before you accept it. Look for hardcoded CIDRs, names, or zones, and for arguments you do not recognize.

Checkpoint: The module has main.tf, variables.tf, and outputs.tf. You know which variable feeds each resource.

docs.title: Part 3: Run the Terraform workflow
docs.text:
Run these in order:

terraform fmt -recursive
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=tfplan
  • fmt fixes style.
  • init downloads the AWS provider and loads the module.
  • validate checks syntax and references. It does not call AWS.
  • plan shows what Terraform would create.

If validate fails, paste the error into Copilot and ask for a fix. Check that the fix does not just delete the failing line.

Read the plan. Find your VPC, two subnets, and the bucket settings. terraform show tfplan prints it again.

Checkpoint: validate passes. The plan ends with Plan: N to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. You can explain each resource in it.

A plan is a prediction. validate and plan do not catch a wrong CIDR, an unwanted cost, or a setting that is legal but unsafe.

docs.title: Part 4: Catch what Copilot got wrong
docs.text:
Copilot's Terraform often looks right and is not. Check your module:

Problem How to check Invented argument validate fails with Unsupported argument. Old style Bucket settings written inside aws_s3_bucket (acl, versioning, server_side_encryption_configuration blocks). In provider 5.x they are separate resources. Hardcoded value Search for quoted 10., eu-west, or a literal bucket name. Missing tags or names Read terraform show tfplan against the naming rule. Old provider version Compare the version line in main.tf with the provider docs. The lab pins ~> 5.0 on purpose, so a newer major version is not a Copilot mistake.

If you find a problem, name it when you ask Copilot to fix it. If you find none, ask:

Which arguments in modules/baseline/main.tf are you least sure exist in
hashicorp/aws 5.x? Check each against the provider docs.

Re-run terraform validate after every fix.

Checkpoint: You fixed at least one problem or checked each row and found it clean. validate still passes.

docs.title: Part 5: Add an admin rule, scan, fix
docs.text:
Admins need SSH to future servers. Ask Copilot for the quick version:

Add a security group named ${var.name_prefix}-admin to modules/baseline, in the VPC.
Allow SSH (port 22) in from anywhere so admins can connect from home.

Scan it:

trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL .

Trivy reads the .tf files. It needs no init and no cloud account. Expect AWS-0107 (HIGH): unrestricted ingress from any IP address. Older Trivy versions may also report AWS-0132: the bucket isn't encrypted with a customer-managed key. Rule IDs and severities change between Trivy versions, so fix what your run reports.

Ask Copilot to fix each finding:

Fix this trivy finding. Add a variable ssh_allowed_cidrs with a description and a
default of ["10.0.0.0/16"]. Use it in the security group. Show me the diff.

<paste the finding>

If your run reports AWS-0132, ask for an aws_kms_key with key rotation, used in the bucket's encryption rule.

Run until clean:

trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .
terraform validate && terraform plan -out=tfplan

Then run trivy config . with no filter. LOW and MEDIUM findings remain, such as bucket logging and VPC flow logs. For each, decide: fix now, accept for the lab, or fix later.

Checkpoint: The HIGH and CRITICAL scan exits with code 0. validate and plan pass. The SSH range is a variable, not a literal.

docs.title: Part 6: The same thing in Bicep
docs.text:
Bicep is Azure's IaC language. Ask Copilot for the Azure equivalent of your module in one file:

Write bicep/main.bicep with the Azure equivalent of the baseline module:
one virtual network with two subnets (cidrSubnet from a vnetCidr parameter) and one
storage account with public blob access off, HTTPS only, and TLS 1.2.
Use parameters with @description for names, region, and CIDR. Add tags.

Build it:

az bicep build --file bicep/main.bicep --stdout > /dev/null && echo "Bicep builds"

az bicep build compiles Bicep to an ARM template and reports errors. It needs no Azure login.

Answer in one sentence each:

  1. Which Terraform concept matches param, resource, and output?
  2. What did you not write in Bicep that Terraform needed? (Hint: provider setup.)

Checkpoint: az bicep build succeeds. You can name one thing both tools share and one that differs.

docs.title: Part 7: Decide
docs.text:
Write short answers:

  1. Which prompt rule prevented the most mistakes?
  2. What will you always check by hand after Copilot writes IaC?
  3. What would you run in CI so nobody has to remember?

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Keep in your lab folder:

  • modules/baseline/ that passes terraform validate
  • tfplan from terraform plan -out=tfplan
  • A passing trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 . run
  • bicep/main.bicep that builds with az bicep build
  • Your answers from Part 7

Compare with lab/solution/ last. Your resources can differ if the checks pass.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-02 trainer guide: Infrastructure as code with Copilot
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Learners leave knowing what IaC is, what the Terraform words mean, how to prompt Copilot for IaC, where Copilot goes wrong, and how a static scan catches some of it.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 What IaC is and why 0:08 to 0:20 Terraform in plain words, including state 0:20 to 0:25 Networking terms 0:25 to 0:37 Prompting Copilot for IaC 0:37 to 0:45 Where Copilot is weak 0:45 to 0:55 Demo: prompt, plan, scan 0:55 to 1:00 Bicep, pros and cons, lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Install Terraform 1.5+, Trivy, and the Azure CLI with Bicep. Run terraform version, trivy --version, az bicep version.
  • Copy lab/starter to a scratch folder and run the lab once. Keep lab/solution/ open for comparison.
  • Run terraform init and trivy config . once before the session. Both download files on first use.
  • Leave AWS credentials unset. The starter's provider block makes plan work without them.
  • Do not commit .terraform/ or .terraform.lock.hcl from scratch runs into this folder.

docs.title: What IaC is and why (0:00 to 0:08)
docs.text:
• IaC means infrastructure described in files and built by a tool.
  • Four reasons: review, repeat, undo, scan. Ask who has debugged a setup nobody remembers clicking.
  • Terraform works across clouds. Bicep is Azure-only.

docs.title: Terraform in plain words (0:08 to 0:20)
docs.text:
Use the lab starter as the example. Open each file and point at the word.

Word Plain meaning Where to see it Resource One thing to create modules/baseline/main.tf in the solution Variable An input variables.tf Output A value shown or passed on outputs.tf Module A folder you call like a function module "baseline" in main.tf Provider Plugin for a cloud required_providers State Terraform's record of what it built Created by apply, not by plan in this lab Plan Preview of changes terraform plan

State needs its own two minutes. Say: Terraform compares your code to state and plans the difference. State can hold secrets, so it stays out of git. Teams use remote state with locking. This lab never applies, so no state file appears.

Walk through fmt, init, validate, plan, and say that apply is where money starts.

docs.title: Networking terms (0:20 to 0:25)
docs.text: Define in one sentence each: VPC, CIDR, subnet, private subnet, security group, 0.0.0.0/0. Draw the lab architecture on a slide or board. Show that cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 1) is 10.0.1.0/24.

docs.title: Prompting Copilot for IaC (0:25 to 0:37)
docs.text:
Teach the five parts: architecture, constraints, naming and tags, variables not literals, limits. Show the weak and strong prompts side by side. Run the weak one if time allows and list what it hardcodes.

Show .github/copilot-instructions.md from the starter. Rules you repeat in every prompt belong there.

Say: the plan is the review point. Copilot drafts. You read the plan.

docs.title: Where Copilot is weak (0:37 to 0:45)
docs.text:
Weakness What to say Invented arguments It writes arguments that sound right. validate catches them. Old provider and syntax Older examples dominate. In AWS provider 5.x, bucket versioning and encryption are separate resources. Insecure defaults It writes what works fast: open ingress, no encryption. Hardcoded values Literals are shorter than variables. Wrong architecture Valid code does not mean the right design.

Ask it: "Which arguments are you least sure about?" It often names real doubts. Treat the answer as a lead, not proof.

docs.title: Demo: prompt, plan, scan (0:45 to 0:55)
docs.text:
1. Prompt with all five parts in the starter. Read the diff aloud.
  2. Run terraform fmt -recursive, init, validate, plan.
  3. Prompt: "Add a security group named ${var.name_prefix}-admin that allows SSH from anywhere."
  4. Run trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL .. Read AWS-0107.
  5. Ask Copilot to fix it with a variable. Scan again.

Copilot's output varies. If your run is already clean, the SSH prompt still produces the finding. Fall back to the solution if a prompt misfires.

docs.title: Scanner options
docs.text:
Tool Notes Trivy (trivy config) Reads .tf files directly. Also scans containers. Used in the lab. Checkov Python-based, many policies, can scan plans. TFLint Linter. Finds invalid instance types and provider-specific mistakes. Not a security scanner.

Trivy rule IDs and severities change between releases. Say "check the output you see".

docs.title: Bicep comparison (0:55 to 1:00)
docs.text: Show lab/solution/bicep/main.bicep next to the Terraform module. Map param to variable, resource to resource, output to output. Run az bicep build --file main.bicep --stdout. Bicep needs no provider block and no state file because Azure Resource Manager tracks deployments.

docs.title: Lab answer key
docs.text:
Part Expected 1 CIDR is in variables.tf. Inputs come from the module call. Outputs return to the root outputs.tf. No secrets, no apply. 3 Plan: 9 to add with the solution. Your count varies with how Copilot splits resources. 4 Common catches: bucket settings inline, hardcoded CIDRs, missing tags, old provider pin. 5 AWS-0107 on open SSH. Older Trivy versions also report AWS-0132 on bucket encryption without a customer-managed key. Fix with ssh_allowed_cidrs and aws_kms_key. 6 az bicep build passes. Terraform variable maps to param. No provider block or state in Bicep.

LOW and MEDIUM findings left in the solution: bucket access logging (AWS-0089) and VPC flow logs (AWS-0178). Use them to discuss accepting a risk versus fixing it.

docs.title: Pros, cons, and tips
docs.text:
Pros

  • Fast first drafts of standard resources
  • Explains plans and errors in plain language
  • Converts between Terraform and Bicep

Cons

  • Invents arguments and picks old versions
  • Writes insecure shortcuts when you ask for quick
  • Does not know your organization's naming, tagging, or network rules

Tips

  • Put rules in .github/copilot-instructions.md.
  • Ask for variables up front.
  • Run validate and a scan after every change.
  • Name the finding when you ask for a fix. Paste the scanner output.
  • Pin provider versions and read the changelog before you upgrade.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Prompting for "a VPC" with no constraints
  • Accepting code without reading the plan
  • Committing .terraform/, state files, or plans
  • "Fixing" validate by deleting the failing line
  • Trusting a clean scan as proof of a safe design
  • Using the lab's dummy provider credentials outside the lab

docs.text:
Check the current docs before the session.

  • Terraform language documentation
  • Terraform AWS provider
  • Trivy misconfiguration scanning
  • Bicep documentation
  • Repository custom instructions for Copilot

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-03: CI/CD debugging & agentic remediation
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: DevOps & Infrastructure with Copilot Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-02, M4-01 Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A failed pipeline is a puzzle with a log attached. Copilot can read the log and suggest a cause. It can be wrong. You treat its answer as a hypothesis and prove it with a rerun.

In the lab you push a small sample repo to a throwaway GitHub repository. It holds three broken workflows. You watch them fail in real GitHub Actions, diagnose each with Copilot, fix, push, and rerun until they pass. You also fix two code scanning alerts and review the patches.

You learn what is a real Copilot feature here and what is just a good habit. The session names the features exactly: Explain error, the Copilot CLI, the Copilot cloud agent, and Copilot Autofix for code scanning.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Name the parts of a pipeline: trigger, job, step, runner, context, secret, and artifact.
  • Recognize five failure classes: dependency, environment or secret or permission, flaky test, matrix, and cache.
  • Read a real failed run with gh run view --log-failed.
  • Use Copilot (CLI, Explain error, cloud agent) to propose a cause, then prove or reject it with a rerun.
  • Handle a second failure that appears only after the first fix.
  • Say which "agentic" remediation features exist and what each one does.
  • Review a security patch for scope and for behavior it might break.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• GitHub Copilot in the Copilot CLI (Session M2-01), the GitHub CLI (gh) signed in, Git, and Node.js 20 or later.
  • A personal GitHub account that can create repositories and run Actions. A public throwaway repo is easiest, because Copilot Autofix is free for public repositories.
  • A paid Copilot plan for the cloud agent step. Part 3 has a CLI path if you don't have one.

Use only the synthetic sample repo. Delete the throwaway repo when you finish.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Sample repo with broken workflows lab/starter/ci-lab-repo/ Fixed workflows lab/solution/fixed-workflows/ Fixed server and its test lab/solution/secure-src/ Generated lockfile lab/solution/package-lock.json

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• Pipeline anatomy: trigger, job, step, runner, context, secret, artifact
  • Failure classes and how each looks in a log
  • gh run list, gh run view --log-failed, gh run rerun --failed
  • Explain error, Copilot CLI, and cloud agent for diagnosis
  • A diagnosis is a hypothesis: prove it with a rerun
  • Autofix, agentic autofix, and the cloud agent: what each one is
  • Reviewing a security patch
  • Pros, cons, tips, and common mistakes

docs.title: A diagnosis is a hypothesis. A rerun is the proof.
docs.text: Session M4-03 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Pipeline anatomy 10 min Failure classes 12 min Copilot as a diagnostician 10 min Demo: a real failed run 12 min What "agentic" really means 8 min Pros, cons, tips, lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: Pipeline anatomy
docs.text:
trigger  ->  workflow  ->  job (on a runner)  ->  step
push, PR     .github/      ubuntu-latest         uses: / run:
             workflows/
  • Trigger: the event that starts a run.
  • Job: steps that share one runner (a fresh VM).
  • Step: one action or shell command.
  • Context: data like github.ref and secrets.NAME.
  • Artifact: a file a job saves for later jobs or download.

Jobs don't share files unless you upload an artifact.

docs.title: Five failure classes
docs.text:
Class Typical log clue Dependency npm ci can't find or match the lockfile Environment, secret, permission empty variable, Resource not accessible by integration Flaky test passes on rerun, no code change Matrix one version fails, others cancelled Cache lockfile not found, stale restore

Find the first red step. Later errors are often side effects.

docs.title: Read a real run
docs.text:
gh run list --limit 5
gh run view <run-id> --log-failed
gh run rerun <run-id> --failed

Works in the same terminal where Copilot CLI runs.

docs.title: Three ways to ask Copilot
docs.text:
Where Use it for Explain error on a failed check or run page A quick read of one failure Copilot CLI in your clone Read logs, reproduce locally, edit, rerun Cloud agent Hand off a fix as an issue and review its pull request

Check current docs: Explain error is described for failed checks and the run summary page.

docs.title: Hypothesis, then proof
docs.text:
1. Quote the first failing line.
  2. Ask for a cause and what would disprove it.
  3. Reproduce the command locally.
  4. Make the smallest fix.
  5. Push and read the new run.

A green run proves the fix. A plausible explanation doesn't.

docs.title: One failure can hide another
docs.text:
run 1: secret empty        -> fix: add the secret
run 2: 403 on label create -> fix: add issues: write

Fix one cause per push. Read the next log fresh.

docs.title: What "agentic" really means
docs.text:
Feature What it does Copilot Autofix One suggested fix for a CodeQL alert. You apply it. Free for public repos. Agentic autofix Assign a default-branch alert to Copilot. It validates the fix and opens a draft PR. Must be enabled per repo. Cloud agent Works an issue you assign to Copilot and opens a PR

None of them merges for you. You review the PR.

docs.title: Review a security patch
docs.text:
• Does it fix the cause or only the alert?
  • Does it change behavior for valid input?
  • Is there a test that fails without the fix?
  • Did it touch unrelated files?

Make the alert disappear and break the feature? That's a failed fix.

docs.title: Pros, cons, tips
docs.text:
Pros: fast first reading of long logs; suggests the right file to open; drafts the fix.

Cons: guesses when the log is thin; can "fix" by deleting the check; sees only what you give it.

Tips: give it the failed log, not the whole log; ask for one cause at a time; keep fixes on a branch.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Push a broken sample repo, watch it fail, and fix it with Copilot.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-03 lab: Fix real failing GitHub Actions runs
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A throwaway repo with three fixed workflows and all runs green, two reviewed security fixes, and a short note on each Copilot diagnosis you proved or rejected

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You push a small Node app with three broken workflows to a new GitHub repository. The runs fail for real. You diagnose each one with Copilot, fix it, and rerun.

Part Work Time 1 Create the repo and watch it fail 15 min 2 Dependency and cache failure 20 min 3 Matrix failure 20 min 4 Two-stage secret and permission failure 20 min 5 Fix code scanning alerts and review the patch 30 min 6 Reruns and clean up 15 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need the Copilot CLI, gh signed in (gh auth status), Git, and Node.js 20 or later. Everything is synthetic. Don't put real secrets in the repo or in a prompt.

Use a public repo so Copilot Autofix works for free. In a private repo, Autofix needs GitHub Code Security. Check current docs.

Keep lab/solution/ closed until you finish a part.

docs.title: Part 1: Create the repo and watch it fail
docs.text:
Copy the starter out of the curriculum repo and push it. Run this from the curriculum repo root.

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m4-03
cp -R sessions/session-m4-03-cicd-debugging-autofix/lab/starter/ci-lab-repo/. \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m4-03/ci-lab
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m4-03/ci-lab
git init -q -b main && git add -A && git commit -qm "Start"
gh repo create ci-lab-m4-03 --public --source=. --push

Pick a different repo name if it's taken. Now watch the runs:

gh run list --limit 10
gh run watch

Expect these results in a minute or two:

Workflow Expected Build Fails Test on several Node versions Fails Label good builds Fails CodeQL Passes (alerts come later)

Open one run in the browser with gh run view --web. Find the trigger, the job, the runner, and the failed step. Write each in one line in your notes.

Checkpoint: three red runs, one per workflow.

docs.title: Part 2: Dependency and cache failure
docs.text:
Start with Build. Read the failure yourself first.

gh run list --workflow build.yml --limit 1
gh run view RUN_ID --log-failed

Write down the first failing line. Then start Copilot in the clone:

copilot

Read the failed log of the latest Build run with `gh run view --log-failed`.
Give me the most likely cause and one thing that would disprove it.
Don't change any files yet.

Treat the answer as a hypothesis. Test it locally before you fix anything:

ls package-lock.json
npm ci

Then ask Copilot for the smallest fix on a branch, and read the diff.

Fix the cause on a new branch called fix/build. Change only what's needed.

Push the branch, open a pull request, and watch the checks:

git push -u origin fix/build
gh pr create --fill
gh pr checks --watch

Checkpoint: the Build check is green. Other checks may still be red.

Name the failure class. Two apply here.

docs.title: Part 3: Matrix failure
docs.text:
Look at Test on several Node versions. Open the run page. One leg is red and the others are cancelled.

Try Explain error. In the pull request, open the menu (the three dots) next to the failed check in the merge box and choose Explain error. Or click the failed check and use the button at the top of the run summary page. If you don't see it, check current docs. It may be off for your account.

Does its answer explain why Node 18 fails but 20 and 22 don't? If it doesn't, say what is missing.

Now fix it with the cloud agent if your plan includes it.

  1. Open an issue in your repo: "Matrix job fails on Node 18".
  2. Paste the first failing line into the issue.
  3. Assign the issue to Copilot.
  4. Wait for the pull request. Read the diff and the checks.

No cloud agent? Fix it in the CLI session instead:

The matrix workflow fails on Node 18. Check package.json and the code, then propose
the smallest correct fix. Don't change the test to hide the failure.

You have two options: remove Node 18 from the matrix, or change the code to run on 18. Check engines in package.json before you choose.

Merge the fix after its checks pass.

Checkpoint: every matrix leg is green, and you can say why the fix was right.

docs.title: Part 4: Two-stage secret and permission failure
docs.text:
Open Label good builds. The first failure is a missing secret. Ask Copilot for the cause and what would disprove it.

Read the failed log of the latest "Label good builds" run. What is the most
likely cause? Don't edit files. Tell me what I'd need to change outside the repo.

A secret isn't in the code, so a file fix can't solve it. Add a synthetic value:

gh secret set DEPLOY_TOKEN --body "synthetic-not-a-real-token"
gh run rerun --failed
gh run watch

The run fails again at a different step. That's the second failure. Read the new log and repeat: hypothesis, local reasoning, smallest fix.

Let Copilot propose the change. Reject any fix that uses write-all. The step needs one permission. Push on a branch, open a pull request, and read the checks.

Checkpoint: Label good builds is green. Your notes say which change fixed which failure.

docs.title: Part 5: Fix code scanning alerts and review the patch
docs.text:
src/server.js has two deliberate vulnerabilities. CodeQL analyzed main in Part 1. Open the Security tab of your repo (it may be labeled Security and quality), then Code scanning. If there are no alerts yet, wait a few minutes and refresh. The alerts you get depend on CodeQL's current rules.

For one alert, open its page and use Generate fix (Copilot Autofix). Read the suggested change. It's a suggestion, not a commit.

Review it before you apply it:

  • Does it fix the cause or only the alert?
  • Does valid input still work?
  • Did it touch other files?

For the second alert, use the Copilot CLI:

Explain the second code scanning alert in src/server.js. Then fix it with the
smallest change and add a test that fails without the fix.

Check both fixes with the reference test. Copy it into your repo and run it. Replace the path with where your curriculum clone lives.

cp /path/to/curriculum/sessions/session-m4-03-cicd-debugging-autofix/lab/solution/secure-src/security.test.js test/
npm test

Both security tests should pass.

Optional: try agentic autofix. It must be enabled for your repository, and it only handles alerts on the default branch. Assign an alert to Copilot. It starts an agent session, checks its fix with CodeQL, and opens a draft pull request. It uses AI credits and Actions minutes. Compare its patch with the Autofix suggestion.

Checkpoint: both vulnerabilities are fixed, tests pass, and you can say what each fix protects.

docs.title: Part 6: Reruns and clean up
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes:

  1. A rerun turned a run green with no code change. What does that tell you?
  2. Why is "rerun until green" a bad fix?
  3. Where did Copilot's first diagnosis miss or go too far?

Then delete the repo:

gh repo delete ci-lab-m4-03 --yes

If gh asks for the delete_repo scope, run gh auth refresh -s delete_repo first. Or delete the repo from its Settings page.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Keep this before you delete the repo:

  1. gh run list output showing the latest runs green.
  2. Your notes for each of the three workflows: failure class, Copilot's diagnosis, what you tested, and the fix.
  3. One line for each security fix: the alert and what the patch does.

docs.text:
