  • Fixed workflows and secure server

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-03 trainer guide: CI/CD debugging & agentic remediation
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Learners leave able to read a real failed Actions run, ask Copilot for a cause, and prove the cause with a rerun. They also know exactly which "agentic" fixes GitHub ships, and which are only habits.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:10 Pipeline anatomy 0:10 to 0:22 Failure classes 0:22 to 0:32 Copilot as a diagnostician 0:32 to 0:44 Demo: a real failed run 0:44 to 0:52 What "agentic" really means 0:52 to 1:00 Pros, cons, tips, lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Create your own throwaway repo from lab/starter/ci-lab-repo/ and run it once, so you know what the failures look like today. Action versions and runner images change.
  • Check that Explain error appears on your failed run page. Docs say it opens from a failed check in the PR merge box or from the run summary page.
  • Check that Autofix shows a Generate fix button on a CodeQL alert in your repo. Wait a few minutes for CodeQL to finish.
  • Keep lab/solution/ closed in the room.

docs.title: Pipeline anatomy (0:00 to 0:10)
docs.text:
Draw the chain: trigger, workflow, job, step. Then add the runner, context, and artifact.

  • A runner is a fresh virtual machine. Nothing from the last run is there, except what a cache restores.
  • A context is data GitHub gives a workflow, like github.ref or secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN.
  • An artifact is how jobs pass files to each other.

Open build.yml from the starter repo and have learners name each part.

docs.title: Failure classes (0:10 to 0:22)
docs.text:
Class What happened Typical clue Usual fix Dependency Lockfile missing or out of sync npm ci error Commit the lockfile Environment, secret, permission Missing secret or too little GITHUB_TOKEN access Empty variable; 403 Resource not accessible by integration Add the secret or the permission Flaky test Test depends on time, order, or network Passes on rerun Fix the test, don't rerun until green Matrix One version or OS fails One leg red, others cancelled Fix the code or drop an unsupported leg Cache Wrong key or missing lockfile Cache or lockfile error Fix the key or the path

Two points to stress:

  • The first red step is the cause. Later red is often fallout.
  • A rerun that turns green is not a fix. It hides a flaky test.

docs.title: Copilot as a diagnostician (0:22 to 0:32)
docs.text:
Three entry points, each with a different job:

Entry point Strength Limit Explain error One click on a failed check or run page Reads the log, can't run your code Copilot CLI Reads logs with gh, runs commands locally, edits files Needs your permission for each command Cloud agent Works alone from an issue and opens a PR Slower; you review a PR, not a chat

A diagnosis is a hypothesis. Show the habit:

  1. Quote the first failing line.
  2. Ask Copilot for the most likely cause and what would disprove it.
  3. Reproduce the failing command locally if you can.
  4. Make the smallest fix.
  5. Push and read the new run.

docs.title: Demo: a real failed run (0:32 to 0:44)
docs.text:
Use your own throwaway repo.

  1. gh run list. Point at the three red runs.
  2. Pick Build. Run gh run view <id> --log-failed and read the error aloud.
  3. Start copilot in the clone and ask: "Read the failed log of the latest Build run with gh run view --log-failed. Give me the most likely cause and what would disprove it. Don't change files."
  4. Ask the room: do we believe it? Reproduce: run npm ci locally. It fails with the same lockfile message.
  5. Let Copilot fix it. Show the diff. Push. Watch gh run watch.
  6. Open Label good builds. Fix the first failure (empty secret), push, and let learners see the second failure appear (403).

Say aloud when Copilot is wrong. If it isn't, ask it to defend the answer against another cause.

docs.title: What "agentic" really means (0:44 to 0:52)
docs.text:
"Agentic" is a word people use loosely. These are the features that exist. Check the docs before the session, because they change.

Feature What it does Needs Explain error Chat about one failed run Copilot access Copilot cloud agent You assign an issue (or a code scanning alert) to Copilot. It works in a GitHub Actions environment and opens a pull request. Paid Copilot plan Copilot Autofix One suggested fix for a CodeQL alert. You review and apply it. Public repo, or a private repo with GitHub Code Security. No Copilot subscription. Agentic autofix Assigning an alert to Copilot runs an agent session that explores, fixes, re-runs CodeQL, and opens a draft PR. Default-branch alerts only. Enabled for the repository. No Copilot license needed. Uses AI credits and Actions minutes.

What is not a feature: a Copilot that watches your pipeline and fixes it by itself. Learners can build loops with the CLI or a workflow, but that is their own automation. Nothing merges without a human.

docs.title: Pros, cons, and tips (0:52 to 0:58)
docs.text:
Pros

  • Reads a 2,000-line log in seconds and points at the first real error.
  • Knows common errors: lockfiles, permissions, version mismatches.
  • Drafts the fix and the commit.

Cons

  • Guesses when the log is thin or the cause is outside the repo, such as a missing secret.
  • Can "fix" by deleting a test, loosening a permission, or adding continue-on-error.
  • Sees only the logs and files you give it. It doesn't see your org settings.

Tips

  • Give it gh run view --log-failed, not the whole log.
  • Ask for one cause at a time.
  • Ask what would disprove the diagnosis.
  • Work on a branch. Open a PR so checks run before main.
  • Reproduce locally before you push, when the failure isn't environment-only.
  • Pin permissions. Start with contents: read and add only what a step needs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Rerunning until green. That hides flaky tests.
  • Accepting the first diagnosis. Check it with a rerun.
  • Fixing three things in one push. You can't tell which one worked.
  • Broadening permissions. permissions: write-all fixes a 403 and creates a risk.
  • Pasting real secrets into a prompt. Use synthetic values in the lab.
  • Treating "alert gone" as "fixed". Read the patch and run the tests.
  • Expecting agentic autofix to be on by default. A repository admin must enable it, and an organization owner may have to allow it first.

docs.title: Lab handoff (0:58 to 1:00)
docs.text: Learners create their own repo and delete it at the end. Remind them: public repo for Autofix, no real secrets, and one fix per push.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Workflow Class Cause Fix Build Dependency and cache No package-lock.json, and cache: npm needs one Run npm install, commit the lockfile Test on several Node versions Matrix toSorted needs Node 20; engines says 20 or later Remove Node 18 from the matrix Label good builds Secret, then permission DEPLOY_TOKEN empty, then GITHUB_TOKEN lacks issues: write gh secret set, then add issues: write CodeQL alerts Security Reflected XSS and path traversal in src/server.js Escape output; resolve and check the path

Accept a different fix for the matrix case if the learner changes the code to run on Node 18 and engines agrees.

docs.title: Session M5-01: Brady's Squad: Human-led AI teams
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Specification-Driven Frameworks Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 and M3-02 to M3-05 Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Squad is an open-source tool by Brady Gaster. It gives you a team of AI specialists (a lead, developers, a tester, a scribe) that live in your repository as files. You talk to one coordinator. It splits the work, starts the specialists in parallel, and writes down what the team learned.

You learn what Squad is, how a team is built (charters, routing, shared decisions, per-agent history), and how it runs inside the Copilot CLI. You then install the real tool, point it at a small API, give it a multi-part task, and watch it work. You also learn when a team of agents beats one agent, and when it only costs more.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain what a human-led AI team is and what the coordinator, agents, and Scribe do.
  • Read a charter, a routing table, and a decision file, and say what each controls.
  • Install Squad, create a team, and run it with copilot --agent squad.
  • Watch a team split a task, then review and steer it as the human.
  • Find what Squad wrote in .squad/ and tell product-defined files from your own choices.
  • Explain what Ralph does and run a real triage pass over GitHub issues.
  • Judge when a team beats a single agent, and when it costs more (overhead, edit conflicts, tokens).

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• GitHub Copilot and the standalone Copilot CLI from Session M2-01
  • Git and Node.js 22.5 or later for the npm install (other install methods don't need Node.js)
  • GitHub CLI (gh), signed in, for Part 7 (Ralph)
  • A throwaway GitHub repository for Part 7

Squad changes quickly. Where a step depends on the version, the lab says: check the Squad README for your version.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Starter project lab/starter/squad-project/ Reference solution lab/solution/ Squad README bradygaster/squad

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• What Squad is: coordinator, specialists, Scribe, Ralph
  • Charters, routing, and casting
  • Shared decisions and personal history in .squad/
  • How Squad runs in the Copilot CLI and VS Code
  • Parallel work, conflicts, and cost
  • Ralph: the work monitor, in a chat session and with squad watch
  • Team of agents or one agent?

docs.title: Install it, run it, read what it wrote
docs.text: Session M5-01 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time What Squad is 10 min Charters, routing, shared memory 15 min How it runs, and Ralph 10 min Demo: a live run 15 min Team or one agent? 7 min Lab handoff 3 min

docs.title: What Squad is
docs.text:
An open-source tool by Brady Gaster. Not a GitHub product.

  • A team of AI specialists that live in your repo as files
  • You talk to one coordinator
  • It starts specialists in parallel, each with its own context
  • A Scribe records decisions. Ralph watches the work queue
  • You review and merge. The human stays accountable

docs.title: The team
docs.text:
Role Job Coordinator Reads your request, routes it, starts agents Lead Triages, reviews, unblocks Developers, tester Do the work in their area Scribe Merges decisions into one file Ralph Monitors issues, PRs, and CI

Roles are proposed from your repo. You accept or change them.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
.squad/
├── team.md          # roster
├── routing.md       # who handles what
├── decisions.md     # shared rules, read by all
├── agents/<name>/
│   ├── charter.md   # job description
│   └── history.md   # what this agent learned
├── casting/         # persistent names
└── orchestration-log/

Commit it. Anyone who clones gets the team.

Check the Squad README for your version. File names move.

docs.title: Charters and routing
docs.text:
Charter: what an agent owns, what it doesn't handle, how it works.

Routing: a table the coordinator reads first.

Pattern Owner src/** Developer tests/** Tester docs/** Writer

Order: named request, then path rule, then skill match. No match? The lead triages.

docs.title: Shared and personal memory
docs.text:
Shared Personal File decisions.md agents/<name>/history.md Read by Every agent That agent Holds Team rules and choices Project knowledge for one role

Say "always" or "never" and it becomes a team rule.

It is Markdown in git. You can read it, diff it, and fix it.

docs.title: Product format or your choice?
docs.text:
Squad defines: the folder layout, roster, routing, charters, decisions.

Your run chooses: agent names, routing rows, decision wording, error formats.

A sample .squad/ file is an example. Don't copy it as a requirement.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
npm install -g @bradygaster/squad-cli@latest
squad init
copilot --agent squad
  • Copilot CLI is the main interface. VS Code: pick the Squad agent.
  • squad is for setup and checks: init, doctor, upgrade, watch
  • The coordinator checks dependencies, runs independent work in parallel, dependent work in order

docs.title: Ralph, the work monitor
docs.text:
Form What it does In a chat session Checks GitHub for more work after each batch squad watch Polls on a timer. Triage only, or --execute GitHub Actions heartbeat Triages labeled issues between sessions

Needs gh access. Triages from routing.md.

Weak routing means weak triage.

docs.title: Demo
docs.text:
1. squad init
  2. copilot --agent squad, describe the project
  3. Edit the proposed roster, accept
  4. Give a multi-part task
  5. Watch who starts, who waits
  6. Review. Add a directive
  7. Read decisions.md and orchestration-log/

docs.title: A team can help
docs.text:
• Parts are independent: docs, tests, separate modules
  • Roles need different context
  • Work spans many sessions and needs memory
  • A backlog needs triage

docs.title: A team costs
docs.text:
• Tokens. Each agent loads its own context, plus the coordinator.
  • Overhead. Splitting and collecting takes time. Small tasks get slower.
  • Conflicting edits. Two agents, one file.
  • Review load. More output, plus memory files.
  • Memory drift. Stale decisions mislead every agent.

Start with one agent. Add a team when you hit a ceiling you can name.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using a team for a one-minute task
  • Splitting work that edits the same file
  • --yolo on a repo you care about
  • Never reading decisions.md
  • Ralph without gh access or a good routing table
  • Trusting docs over your installed version

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Part Work 1 to 2 Install Squad, create the team 3 to 4 Give a four-part task, review, steer 5 Read .squad/ 6 Same task with one agent. Compare 7 Ralph on real issues

Use the sample project and a throwaway repo for Ralph.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-01 lab: Run a real Squad team
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A Squad team in a sample repo, one finished multi-part task, your notes on what the team did and cost, and a Ralph triage run

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You install Squad, create a team for a small Express API, and give it one task with four parts. You watch the team split the work, steer it, and read the files it wrote. Then you compare against a single agent and try Ralph on real GitHub issues.

Part Work Time 1 Install Squad and set up the project 10 min 2 Create the team 15 min 3 Give the team a task 30 min 4 Review and steer 15 min 5 Read what Squad wrote 10 min 6 Same task, one agent 20 min 7 Ralph on real issues 20 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Squad installs in the sample project only. Use a scratch folder. Use synthetic data only.

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m5-01
cp -R sessions/session-m5-01-squad-orchestration/lab/starter/squad-project \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m5-01/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m5-01/squad-project
npm install && npm test
git init -q && printf 'node_modules/\n' > .gitignore
git add -A && git commit -qm "Start" && git branch -M main

The tests should pass.

docs.title: Part 1: Install Squad
docs.text:
The Squad README lists several install methods. With Node.js 22.5 or later, use npm:

npm install -g @bradygaster/squad-cli@latest
squad --version

Other methods (Homebrew, WinGet, an install script) are in the Squad README. Check the Squad README for your version if the command or the Node.js requirement has changed.

Create the Squad files:

squad init

squad init is safe to run again. Read its output. It may ask questions. Answer them from the project: a small Node.js and Express API with Jest tests. The README also describes squad init --preset default, which starts with a ready-made team. Skip the preset in this lab. You want to see the team being proposed.

squad doctor
git status --short

squad doctor checks your setup. git status shows what init added. Squad owns the coordinator file and templates. Your team's state goes in .squad/.

Checkpoint: .squad/ exists and squad doctor reports no blocking problem.

docs.title: Part 2: Create the team
docs.text:
Start the Copilot CLI with the Squad agent:

copilot --agent squad --yolo

--yolo lets Squad run its many tool calls without asking each time. That is acceptable here because the project is a disposable sample. Don't use it on a real repository until you understand what Squad runs. In VS Code you can pick the Squad agent in Copilot Chat instead.

Tell the coordinator what you are building:

This is a small Express API with a users resource and Jest tests. Set up the team.

Squad scans the repo and proposes a roster: a lead, one or more developers, a tester, and a Scribe. Each member gets a name from a themed "universe". That is casting: names persist, so the same person returns in every session.

Change something before you accept. For example, ask it to drop a role you don't need, or rename a member. Then say yes.

Open the files it wrote. File names depend on your Squad version, so check the README if one is missing.

ls -R .squad | head -50

Read three of them:

  • .squad/team.md is the roster.
  • .squad/routing.md says who handles what. Look for rules tied to src/ and tests/.
  • One agent's charter.md says what that agent owns, what it does not handle, and how it works.

Checkpoint: You can answer from the files: Who reviews work? Who owns tests/? What does the lead's charter forbid?

docs.title: Part 3: Give the team a task
docs.text:
Commit the new team first, then work on a branch so you can compare later.

git add -A && git commit -qm "Add Squad team"
git switch -c squad-run

In the Squad session, paste this task:

Do these four things in this repo:
1. Validate POST /api/users: reject a malformed email and a name over 100 characters with 400.
2. Add a tasks resource: GET /api/tasks (optional ?status=todo|doing|done), POST /api/tasks
   (title required, at most 100 characters), PATCH /api/tasks/:id (change status), and
   DELETE /api/tasks/:id. Status is todo, doing, or done.
3. Add tests for both changes.
4. Document the new endpoints in README.md.

The task has parts that can run in parallel (docs, tests) and parts that touch the same file (items 1 and 2 both change src/routes/api.js). That is on purpose.

Watch the session. As it runs, write down:

  • Which agents the coordinator started, and in what order.
  • What it ran in parallel and what it ran one after another.
  • Whether any two agents touched the same file.
  • Whether anyone asked you a question or stopped for review.

Don't interrupt unless the team is stuck. Expect this to take several minutes. A multi-agent run is slower to read than a single-agent run, even when it finishes sooner.

Checkpoint: The session reports the work as done, and you have your notes on who did what.

docs.title: Part 4: Review and steer
docs.text:
You stay in charge. Review the result like a pull request.

git diff main --stat
npm test

Open src/routes/api.js and check that both the user validation and the tasks routes are present. Compare the README with the real endpoints.

Pick one thing you would change and steer the team in the same session. Examples:

  • "Return errors as { error, field } everywhere."
  • "Always write tests before changing a route."
  • "Fix the README. It lists an endpoint that doesn't exist." (Only if it's true for your run.)

Squad treats a phrase like "always" or "never" as a directive: a rule saved for the whole team. Try one, then check that it was saved (Part 5).

Run npm test again.

Checkpoint: Tests pass, and you steered the team at least once.

docs.title: Part 5: Read what Squad wrote
docs.text:
Commit the run and look at what changed under .squad/:

git add -A && git commit -qm "Squad run"
git diff HEAD~1 --stat -- .squad

Open these. If one is missing, check the Squad README for your version.

File Ask .squad/decisions.md and .squad/decisions/inbox/ Which decisions did agents record? Is your directive here? .squad/agents/<name>/history.md What did one agent learn about this project? .squad/orchestration-log/ What did the coordinator start, and why? .squad/log/ Is there a session record?

Now separate what the product requires from what this run chose. Squad defines the folder layout, the roster, routing, charters, and decisions. The agent names, the routing rows, the decision wording, and the error format are this run's choices. Don't copy them into another project as if they were required.

Check the cost. The Squad CLI documents squad cost, but also says hosts that run the coordinator themselves, such as the Copilot CLI, don't write its usage ledger. Use the Copilot CLI's own usage view (check the current Copilot CLI docs for the command) and note the total for the run.

Checkpoint: You can point to one decision, one history entry, and one orchestration entry, and say which agent wrote each.

docs.title: Part 6: Same task, one agent
docs.text:
Run the identical task with plain Copilot on a fresh branch. The team's .squad/ folder is already committed, and plain Copilot ignores it.

git switch main && git switch -c single-agent
copilot --yolo

Paste the same four-part task. Record wall-clock time and the usage total.

Then compare the two branches:

git diff squad-run single-agent --stat -- src tests README.md

Fill in this table in notes.md:

Squad One agent Time to finish Usage (tokens or requests) Tests pass Both routes edits present in api.js README matches the code What you had to fix yourself

Answer in two sentences each: Where did the team help? Where did it cost more than it gave? A four-part task on one small API is a weak case for a team. Say what size of task would change your answer.

Checkpoint: notes.md has the table and your two answers.

docs.title: Part 7: Ralph on real issues
docs.text:
Ralph is the work monitor. He is on every roster. He reads GitHub issues, triages them using routing.md, and can start agents on them. He needs the gh CLI. The Squad docs say the default token may lack the scopes to read and write issues and labels, so you may need a personal access token. Check the Squad README for your version before you sign in.

Use a throwaway repository, not a real one. Push the project and create three issues:

git switch squad-run
gh repo create squad-lab-m5 --private --source . --push
gh issue create --title "Add pagination to GET /api/users" --body "Support ?page and ?limit."
gh issue create --title "Add a README section on running tests" --body "Short section in README.md."
gh issue create --title "Return JSON for unknown routes" --body "A 404 JSON error instead of the HTML default."

Squad triages issues that carry the squad label. Add it to all three:

gh label create squad --color 0E8A16 2>/dev/null; for n in 1 2 3; do gh issue edit $n --add-label squad; done

Triage only. Run one pass of watch mode without executing anything:

squad watch --interval 1

Leave it for a minute or two, then stop it with Ctrl+C. Look at the issues: Ralph should assign each one a squad:<member> label based on routing.md. Flags change between versions. Run squad watch --help if one of these fails.

Execute one. Pick one small issue (the README one). Ask Ralph in the Squad session:

Ralph, show me what everyone is working on.
Ralph, assign and start the README issue only.

Or run squad watch --execute and stop it after one issue. Don't leave it polling. Read what it did: the comment on the issue, the branch or PR, and the new entries in .squad/.

Checkpoint: All three issues have a squad:<member> label, and you can explain how Ralph chose the member.

When you finish, stop squad watch and delete the throwaway repository.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. The squad-project repo with squad-run and single-agent branches.
  2. notes.md with your Part 3 observations, the comparison table, and your two answers.
  3. A list of three .squad/ files you read and one thing each told you.
  4. Your Ralph result: the labels it assigned, and what it did on the issue you started.

Compare your code against solution/. Your files and names will differ. Behavior should match.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-01 trainer guide: Brady's Squad
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Learners leave knowing what Squad really is, how a team is defined and remembered, what Ralph does, and when a team of agents is worth its cost.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:10 What Squad is 0:10 to 0:25 Charters, routing, and shared memory 0:25 to 0:35 How it runs, and Ralph 0:35 to 0:50 Demo: a live run 0:50 to 0:57 Team or one agent? 0:57 to 1:00 Lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Install Squad and the Copilot CLI. Run the whole lab once. Check the Squad README for your version: install method, file names, and flags change.
  • Keep a finished squad-run project to fall back on. A live run takes minutes and can stall.
  • Open bradygaster/squad and its docs/ folder. Read "What is Squad?", "Memory & Knowledge", "Parallel Work & Models", and "Ralph".
  • Prepare a throwaway GitHub repo with three squad-labeled issues for the Ralph demo.
  • Warn learners about Node.js 22.5 or later for the npm install.

docs.title: What Squad is (0:00 to 0:10)
docs.text:
• Squad is an open-source tool that gives you a human-led team of AI specialists. Brady Gaster maintains it. It is not a GitHub product, so say so.
  • The team lives in your repo as files, in .squad/. Commit them and anyone who clones gets the team.
  • You talk to a coordinator. It reads your request, applies routing, and starts specialists as separate sub-agents with their own context.
  • A Scribe records decisions. Ralph watches the work queue. Both are on every team.
  • It is not "a chatbot wearing hats". Each specialist has its own context window and its own memory file.
  • Humans stay accountable. Squad drafts and coordinates. You review and merge.

Ask: "What would you want a team to do that one agent can't?" Collect answers. Come back to them at 0:50.

docs.title: Charters, routing, and shared memory (0:10 to 0:25)
docs.text:
Show each file from a real project.

File Job team.md Roster. Who is on the team. routing.md Who handles which kind of work. agents/<name>/charter.md Identity, what the agent owns, what it doesn't handle. agents/<name>/history.md What this agent learned about your project. Only that agent reads it. decisions.md Shared rules and choices. Every agent reads it before working. decisions/inbox/ Where agents drop new decisions. The Scribe merges them. casting/ Persistent names from a themed universe.

Teach these points:

  • Charter = a job description. Narrow charters make routing predictable.
  • Routing = a table. Named request beats path rule beats skill match. If nothing matches, the lead triages. You can always name an agent.
  • Shared decisions keep agents from re-arguing settled questions. Personal history lets an agent get better at its own area.
  • Directives: say "always" or "never" and Squad saves it as a team rule.
  • Memory is plain Markdown in git. You can read it, diff it, and fix it.
  • Context cost: a long decisions.md and long histories get loaded into every spawn. squad nap compresses them.

Say clearly: the folder layout and roles come from Squad. The names, routing rows, and decision text are your team's. Learners confuse a sample file with a required format.

Version note: docs and README have differed on some names (for example history.md or context.md). Tell learners to trust what their version wrote.

docs.title: How it runs, and Ralph (0:25 to 0:35)
docs.text:
• Interface: copilot --agent squad in the Copilot CLI is the recommended way. In VS Code, pick the Squad agent in Copilot Chat. The squad command is for setup and checks (init, upgrade, doctor, watch). Its interactive shell is deprecated.
  • squad init writes the files. Copilot then loads the coordinator as a custom agent.
  • Parallel work: the coordinator checks dependencies, starts independent agents in the background, and runs dependent ones in order. A reviewer gate runs before the result returns.
  • --yolo skips tool approvals. Explain why the lab allows it and why a real repo shouldn't.
  • Ralph has three forms:
  • In a chat session, Ralph checks GitHub for more work after each batch.
  • squad watch polls on a timer. Without --execute it only triages. With it, it starts Copilot sessions.
  • A GitHub Actions heartbeat triages labeled issues between sessions.
  • Ralph needs gh and a token that can read and write issues and PRs. Check the Squad docs for the current scope advice.
  • Ralph triages from routing.md. A weak routing table means weak triage.

docs.title: Demo: a live run (0:35 to 0:50)
docs.text:
1. In an empty sample repo, run squad init. Show the folder.
  2. copilot --agent squad --yolo. Say what you're building. Show the proposed roster. Rename one member. Accept.
  3. Open routing.md and one charter. Read three lines aloud.
  4. Give a multi-part task. Use the lab task or something similar with a shared file.
  5. While it runs, narrate: who started, who waits, who is writing to decisions/inbox/.
  6. Review as a human. Run the tests. Say "always return errors as { error }" and show the directive land in decisions.md.
  7. Show orchestration-log/ and one history.md.

If the run stalls, switch to the finished project and walk its files. Tell learners you did.

docs.title: Team or one agent? (0:50 to 0:57)
docs.text:
Reveal the answers to the 0:00 question.

A team helps when A single agent is better when Parts are independent (docs, tests, separate modules) The task is small or tightly coupled Roles need different context or tools One file or one idea carries the task Work spans many sessions and needs memory It is a one-off You want a standing review gate You'd read all of it anyway A backlog needs triage (Ralph) You have two issues

What a team costs:

  • Tokens. Every specialist starts with its own context and reads decisions.md and its history. More agents mean more input tokens, and the coordinator adds its own.
  • Coordination overhead. Splitting, routing, and collecting takes time. Small tasks finish slower.
  • Conflicting edits. Parallel agents can overwrite the same file. Routing says "split only independent deliverables." When your task isn't independent, don't split it.
  • Review load. You read several agents' output plus their memory files.
  • Memory drift. Stale decisions mislead every agent. Prune them.

Rule of thumb: start with one agent. Add a team when you hit a ceiling you can name.

docs.title: Lab handoff (0:57 to 1:00)
docs.text: Show the lab parts. Point at Part 6 (single-agent comparison) and say it's the point of the lab. Remind learners to use the throwaway repo for Ralph and to delete it.

docs.title: Lab timing and tips
docs.text: Part Common snag 1 Node.js below 22.5. Use another install method. 2 Learners skip the roster tweak. Make them change one thing. 3 The run takes long. Tell learners to read routing.md while they wait. 4 The team skipped the shared-file conflict. Ask which agent edited api.js. 5 A file name differs. Ask learners to list .squad/ and use what is there. 6 Usage numbers are hard to find. Accept request counts or wall-clock time. 7 gh token lacks scope. Check the Squad docs, then use a PAT.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
• Part 2 questions: reviewer and ownership are in routing.md and charters. Learners cite their own files.
  • Part 4: a correct run has both api.js changes, passing tests, and a README that matches. See lab/solution/README.md.
  • Part 6: expect the team to cost more and to take longer on this size of task. Some runs show fewer README or test misses from the team. Don't force a winner.
  • Part 7: each issue should get a squad:<member> label that fits routing.md.

docs.title: Pros, cons, and tips
docs.text:
Pros

  • Memory persists in git and carries across sessions.
  • Charters and routing make roles visible and editable.
  • Parallel work saves time on independent parts.
  • Decisions are written down where everyone, including humans, can read them.

Cons

  • Higher token and request use.
  • Slower on small tasks.
  • Newer tool that changes quickly. File names and flags move.
  • More output to review.
  • Needs good routing. A vague table sends work to the wrong agent.

Tips

  • Keep the team small. Three to five specialists is plenty.
  • Write narrow charters, with "I don't handle" lines.
  • Give each agent its own files in the task.
  • Review decisions.md like code. Delete what's stale.
  • Run squad nap when histories grow.
  • Use squad doctor when something breaks.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a sample .squad/ file as the required format.
  • Using a team for a task one agent finishes in a minute.
  • Splitting work that edits the same file.
  • Running --yolo on a repository you care about.
  • Never reading decisions.md, then wondering why agents behave oddly.
  • Expecting Ralph to work without gh access or without a useful routing.md.
  • Leaving squad watch --execute running.
  • Assuming the docs match your installed version.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-02: Spec Kit: Specification-driven development
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Specification-Driven Frameworks

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-01 to M3-05

Duration: 3 hours 30 minutes (1 hour trainer content, 2 hours 30 minutes lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use Spec Kit to turn one feature request into tested code. You initialize an existing Python project, create the Spec Kit artifacts, implement an archive operation, and run convergence review. If you have time, an optional second cycle adds a restore requirement to the living specification.

The lab uses Spec Kit's real project model:

  • .specify/memory/constitution.md stores project principles.
  • specs/<feature>/spec.md stores requirements and user stories.
  • plan.md, supporting design files, and tasks.md drive implementation.
  • /speckit-analyze checks artifact consistency.
  • /speckit-converge compares the implementation with the accepted artifacts.
  • /speckit-github-taskstoissues converts the generated task list into GitHub Issues (optional). It comes from Spec Kit's opt-in GitHub extension. specify init doesn't install it, so run specify extension add github first.

specify init generates the Copilot skills. Each skill is a folder under .github/skills/ with instructions for one slash command, so /speckit-plan runs the instructions in .github/skills/speckit-plan/.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Initialize Spec Kit in an existing repository and inspect the generated files.
  • Write testable requirements before choosing an implementation.
  • Turn the accepted specification into a plan and dependency-ordered tasks.
  • Implement the change in stages and use convergence to find missing work.
  • Explain constitution, convergence, and idempotent in your own words.
  • Optional: convert generated tasks into GitHub Issues.
  • Optional: evolve a living specification and update the plan, tasks, and code to match.
  • Explain which files come from Spec Kit and which records belong to the team.

docs.title: You need
docs.text: Python 3.10 or later, Git, uv, and GitHub Copilot. The optional issue-conversion part also needs a GitHub training repository where you can create issues. For disconnected environments, prepare the official air-gapped package before the session.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
This session uses Spec Kit v1.4.0, the latest release on 12 November 2026. Check github/spec-kit releases before the session. If you change the tag, run the lab once first, because command names and generated files change between releases.

export SPECKIT_TAG='v1.4.0'
uv tool install specify-cli --force \
  --from "git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@${SPECKIT_TAG}"
specify version

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/ Slides slides.md Lab lab/ Starter project lab/starter/archive-task/ Reference result lab/solution/archive-task/

docs.title: Make the work clear before asking an agent to build it
docs.text: Session M5-02 | 3 hours 30 minutes

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Why specification-driven development 6 min Spec Kit project and artifact model 12 min Requirements and clarification 12 min Planning, checklists, tasks, and analysis 12 min Implementation and convergence 10 min Installation, demonstration, and lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: A feature request is a starting point
docs.text:
Users need to remove completed tasks from their normal working list without deleting task history.

This sounds clear until implementation starts:

  • Does "remove" mean hide, archive, or delete?
  • What happens when the same task is archived twice?
  • Can callers still retrieve archived tasks?
  • What result should an unknown task ID produce?

Code should not be where these decisions first appear.

docs.title: Resolve decisions before implementation
docs.text: Code-first path Specification-driven path The agent fills gaps while coding The team resolves gaps before planning Tests inherit hidden assumptions Acceptance scenarios state expected behavior Scope additions appear as code Non-goals make additions visible Review starts with implementation details Review starts with requirements and test results

docs.title: What Spec Kit provides
docs.text:
Layer Purpose CLI scaffolding Initializes templates, scripts, memory, and an agent integration Agent skills Guide constitution, specification, planning, implementation, and review Feature artifacts Keep requirements, design decisions, tasks, and checks reviewable

The tool supplies a workflow. The team still owns each product and technical decision.

docs.title: Initialize an existing project
docs.text:
specify init --here --force --integration copilot

Review the generated diff before using the workflow:

.specify/
├── memory/constitution.md
├── scripts/
└── templates/

.github/skills/
└── speckit-*/

--force allows initialization in a non-empty directory. It is not permission to accept every generated change without review.

docs.title: Two artifact scopes
docs.text:
Project-wide Feature-specific .specify/memory/constitution.md specs/<feature>/spec.md Shared scripts and templates plan.md and design files Agent integration files checklists/ and tasks.md

The constitution applies across features. Each feature gets its own specification, design, tasks, and review trail.

docs.title: Four terms and one file layout
docs.text:
Term Meaning Constitution The project's rules. Planning and review check against them Convergence Compare code, tests, and artifacts. Add tasks for any gap. Repeat until none are left Idempotent Doing it twice has the same result as doing it once Skill A folder in .github/skills/ holding the instructions for one command

/speckit-plan runs the instructions in .github/skills/speckit-plan/. Edit the folder and the command changes.

docs.title: The full workflow
docs.text:
Constitution
    ↓
Specify → Clarify
    ↓
Plan → Checklist → Tasks
    ↓
Analyze
    ↓
Implement ⇄ Converge

Clarify, checklist, and analyze are review gates. Use them when the request is ambiguous or risky.

docs.title: Constitution: rules for how the project works
docs.text:
/speckit-constitution

A useful principle is testable:

Weak principle Reviewable principle Write high-quality code Every accepted behavior has a focused automated test Keep things simple Use the Python standard library unless the plan records an approved exception Avoid regressions Existing create and list tests must remain in the suite

If a principle cannot affect a plan or review, delete it.

docs.title: Specify behavior, not implementation
docs.text:
/speckit-specify

spec.md should answer:

  • Who needs the behavior?
  • What outcome do they need?
  • Which scenarios test the behavior?
  • What is outside scope?
  • Which requirements are measurable?

Avoid class names, database choices, package names, and file paths at this stage.

docs.title: Write scenarios a reviewer can challenge
docs.text:
Given an active task
When the caller archives its ID
Then the task keeps its ID and title
And the default list no longer returns it

Given an unknown task ID
When the caller archives it
Then the store returns a clear not-found result

Good scenarios expose decisions. "Archive works correctly" does not.

docs.title: Clarify before choosing a design
docs.text:
/speckit-clarify

For the archive feature, clarification must settle:

Question Accepted decision Archive twice? Return the same archived task Unknown ID? Raise TaskNotFoundError Default list? Exclude archived tasks Historical access? Support include_archived=True Title during archive? Preserve it unchanged

Record clarification decisions in the specification so future readers have one place to check the agreed behavior.

docs.title: Plan: decide how the feature will work
docs.text:
/speckit-plan

The plan can now choose implementation details:

  • Python 3.10 or later;
  • standard library only;
  • in-memory dictionary storage;
  • an archived Boolean on each task;
  • changes limited to src/task_store.py and its tests.

The specification owns behavior. The plan owns the technical approach.

docs.title: Supporting design files have a purpose
docs.text:
Artifact Question it answers research.md Which choices were made, and which alternatives were rejected? data-model.md Which entities, fields, rules, and state transitions exist? contracts/ Which external interfaces must consumers follow? quickstart.md How can a reviewer check the planned behavior?

Not every feature needs every optional artifact. Keep the files that help someone implement or review the change.

docs.title: A checklist reviews requirement quality
docs.text:
/speckit-checklist

A requirements checklist asks questions such as:

  • Is repeated archive behavior defined?
  • Is the default list behavior defined?
  • Does the specification define an unknown-ID result?
  • Are existing behaviors protected?

Checking an item means a reviewer found the requirement clear. It does not mean the code has been implemented or tested.

docs.title: Tasks turn design into executable work
docs.text:
/speckit-tasks

Each task needs a place in the dependency order, a source requirement, and an exact file:

T001 [US1] Add archive state to new tasks in src/task_store.py
T002 [US1] Implement archive_task(task_id) in src/task_store.py
T003 [US1] Test default list filtering in tests/test_task_store.py
T004 [US2] Test repeated archive requests in tests/test_task_store.py

"Implement the feature" is not a task breakdown.

docs.title: Analyze artifacts before implementation
docs.text:
/speckit-analyze

Analysis looks across spec.md, plan.md, and tasks.md for:

  • a requirement with no implementation task;
  • a task with no source requirement;
  • a plan choice that contradicts accepted behavior;
  • ambiguous or inconsistent terminology;
  • missing coverage for a user story.

The command is read-only. Fix each issue in the artifact that owns the decision, then analyze again.

docs.title: Implementation follows the accepted tasks
docs.text:
/speckit-implement

Before you start: review the checklist, fix the analysis findings, and commit the artifacts.

Tie tests and code to the user stories in spec.md. The original prompt alone is not enough.

docs.title: Compare implementation with accepted artifacts
docs.text:
/speckit-converge

Implementation
      ↓
Compare code, tests, spec, plan, and tasks
      ↓
Converged ───────────────→ Review or pull request
      ↓ gaps found
Append tasks → Implement → Test → Converge again

Convergence never rewrites requirements to match the code. It adds the tasks that close the gap.

docs.title: specify check is not compliance validation
docs.text:
specify check

Use it to inspect the local Spec Kit environment and available tools.

It does not check whether the implementation meets the specification. Use tests, review, /speckit-analyze, and /speckit-converge to compare the accepted artifacts and implementation.

docs.title: Optional: living specifications evolve accepted behavior
docs.text:
When requirements change, update the current feature artifacts in order:

spec.md
  ↓
plan.md
  ↓
tasks.md
  ↓
/speckit-analyze
  ↓
/speckit-implement
  ↓
/speckit-converge

Do not leave a restore requirement only in code or an issue if spec.md remains the contract.

docs.title: Optional: convert tasks into GitHub Issues
docs.text:
/speckit-github-taskstoissues

Each issue keeps its task ID, dependencies, and file paths. Issues distribute the work. They are not a second requirements source.

The command comes from Spec Kit's opt-in GitHub extension. Install it with specify extension add github, or skip this step.

docs.title: Install Spec Kit
docs.text:
Install a pinned release. This session uses v1.4.0, the latest on 12 November 2026. Check the releases page before you teach:

export SPECKIT_TAG='v1.4.0'
uv tool install specify-cli --force \
  --from "git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@${SPECKIT_TAG}"
specify version

Disconnected environments need the official air-gapped package prepared on a connected machine.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
Show one deliberate gap:

  1. Implement archive filtering.
  2. Omit the include_archived=True test.
  3. Run the existing unit tests.
  4. Run /speckit-converge.
  5. Inspect the task it appends.
  6. Add the missing test and converge again.

This shows that passing tests and satisfying the specification are different.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
You will:

  1. Run the starter tests.
  2. Initialize Spec Kit in the Python project.
  3. Specify and clarify task archiving.
  4. Create the plan, checklist, and tasks.
  5. Analyze before implementation.
  6. Implement in stages and run the unit tests.
  7. Converge until the artifacts and code agree.

Optional, with time left: convert tasks into GitHub Issues, and add restore behavior through the living specification.

The lab ends with working code, passing tests, and a final convergence result.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-02 lab: Implement and evolve a feature with Spec Kit
docs.text:
Duration: 2 hours 30 minutes

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-01 to M3-05

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Add task archiving to a small Python project. You implement it in stages and use convergence review to find missing work.

Parts 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 take about 1 hour 45 minutes. Parts 4 and 7 are optional. Do them with the time that remains.

Part Work Time 1 Prepare and initialize the project 15 min 2 Specify and clarify archive behavior 25 min 3 Plan, check, create tasks, and analyze 25 min 4 Optional: convert tasks to GitHub Issues 15 min 5 Implement in stages and run tests 25 min 6 Converge the archive implementation 15 min 7 Optional: evolve the living specification (restore) 30 min

docs.title: Terms you will see
docs.text:
• Constitution: the project's rules, in .specify/memory/constitution.md. Spec Kit reads it when it plans and reviews. A rule that can't change a plan or a review doesn't belong there.
  • Convergence: /speckit-converge compares the code, tests, spec, plan, and tasks. If something is missing, it adds tasks to tasks.md. You implement them and run it again until it reports Converged.
  • Idempotent: doing it twice has the same result as doing it once. Archiving an archived task succeeds and changes nothing.
  • Skills and commands: specify init writes one folder per command under .github/skills/, such as .github/skills/speckit-plan/. Typing /speckit-plan makes Copilot follow the instructions in that folder. Edit the folder and the command changes.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need Python 3.10 or later, Git, GitHub Copilot, and uv. Part 4 also needs a GitHub training repository where you can create issues. For a disconnected environment, the instructor prepares the official Spec Kit air-gapped package beforehand.

docs.title: Part 1: Prepare and initialize the project (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Copy the starter into the instructor-provided GitHub training repository:

cp -R sessions/session-m5-02-spec-kit/lab/starter/archive-task/. <training-repository>/
cd <training-repository>
git add .
git commit -m "Start Spec Kit archive-task lab"
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

The two starter tests should pass. Read feature-request.md, but do not open change-request.md yet.

Install Spec Kit v1.4.0. If your instructor gave you a different tag, use that one:

export SPECKIT_TAG='v1.4.0'
uv tool install specify-cli --force \
  --from "git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@${SPECKIT_TAG}"
specify version

Initialize the current repository:

specify init --here --force --integration copilot

Review the generated files:

git status --short
find .specify -maxdepth 3 -type f | sort
find .github -maxdepth 3 -type f | sort

Checkpoint: .specify/memory/constitution.md and the .github/skills/speckit-* folders exist.

docs.title: Part 2: Specify and clarify archive behavior (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Create the project constitution:

/speckit-constitution

Create principles for this training project:
- preserve existing create and list behavior;
- use only the Python standard library;
- require tests for every accepted behavior;
- keep requirements separate from implementation choices.

Open .specify/memory/constitution.md. Check that you can use each principle to judge a plan, implementation, or review.

Create the feature specification:

/speckit-specify

Use feature-request.md as the source. Add task archiving without changing create
or list behavior. Keep the specification technology-neutral.

Inspect specs/<feature>/spec.md. Check that it contains prioritized, independently testable user stories and measurable acceptance scenarios.

Clarify the missing decisions:

/speckit-clarify

Focus on repeated archive requests, unknown task IDs, whether archived tasks stay
in the default list, and whether task titles may change during archive.

The specification should settle these decisions:

  • archiving an active task succeeds;
  • archiving an already archived task is idempotent;
  • an unknown task ID produces a clear not-found result;
  • the default list excludes archived tasks;
  • callers can request archived tasks explicitly;
  • archiving does not change the title.

Checkpoint: spec.md defines behavior without choosing classes, file names, or storage structures.

docs.title: Part 3: Plan, check, create tasks, and analyze (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Create the implementation plan:

/speckit-plan

Use Python 3.10+ and the standard library. Extend src/task_store.py and
tests/test_task_store.py. Keep storage in memory. Do not add packages.

Review plan.md, research.md, data-model.md, and quickstart.md. Remove any dependency, service, or infrastructure that the accepted feature does not need.

Generate and review a requirements-quality checklist:

/speckit-checklist

Check archive state transitions, list filtering, not-found behavior, and
regression protection for existing create and list behavior.

Mark an item complete only when its requirement is clear in spec.md. A checked requirements item does not mean the implementation exists.

Create tasks and analyze the artifacts:

/speckit-tasks
/speckit-analyze

Fix each material finding in the artifact that owns the decision. Run /speckit-analyze again until the specification, plan, and tasks agree.

Checkpoint: each implementation task names an exact file and traces to an accepted user story.

docs.title: Part 4 (optional): Convert tasks to GitHub Issues (15 minutes)
docs.text:
/speckit-github-taskstoissues comes from Spec Kit's opt-in GitHub extension. specify init doesn't install it. From the project root, run:

specify extension add github

If the extension isn't available, skip this part. Parts 5 and 6 don't depend on it.

Commit and push the artifacts so far:

git add .specify .github specs
git commit -m "Specify task archive behavior"
git push

Convert the generated task list into GitHub Issues:

/speckit-github-taskstoissues

Create issues from the unchecked tasks in tasks.md. Preserve task IDs, user-story
references, dependencies, and file paths.

Open the created issues. Each should carry a task ID and its dependencies, and add nothing that isn't in spec.md.

docs.title: Part 5: Implement in stages and run tests (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Use Spec Kit to implement one set of tasks at a time. Do not implement everything in one agent run.

First implement the primary archive behavior:

/speckit-implement

Implement only the tasks for the primary archive user story. Stop before repeated
archive and unknown-ID behavior.

Run the tests:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

Then implement the remaining archive tasks:

/speckit-implement

Implement the remaining archive tasks, including repeated requests, unknown IDs,
and final verification.

Run the full suite again. Existing create and list tests must still pass.

docs.title: Part 6: Converge the archive implementation (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Run convergence review:

/speckit-converge

If convergence appends a new phase to tasks.md:

  1. inspect each appended task and its source reference;
  2. run /speckit-implement for the appended convergence tasks;
  3. rerun the unit tests;
  4. run /speckit-converge again.

Repeat until Spec Kit reports Converged. When it finds no remaining work, it leaves tasks.md unchanged.

docs.title: Part 7 (optional): Evolve the living specification (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Do this part only if Parts 1 to 6 are finished and converged. A living specification is one you update when requirements change, then bring the plan, tasks, and code back in line.

Open change-request.md. Add restoring archived tasks to the accepted behavior.

Use the documented living-spec sequence:

  1. Update the specification:
/speckit-clarify

Update the current feature for change-request.md. Define restore success,
repeated restore, unknown IDs, and default-list behavior after restore.
  1. Update the technical plan:
/speckit-plan

Revise the current plan for restore behavior. Keep the existing Python,
standard-library, in-memory design.
  1. Regenerate the task list and analyze it:
/speckit-tasks
/speckit-analyze
  1. If you did Part 4, convert only the new unchecked restore tasks into issues:
/speckit-github-taskstoissues

Create issues only for new restore tasks that do not already have an issue.
Preserve their task IDs and dependencies.
  1. Implement, test, and converge:
/speckit-implement
/speckit-converge

The final suite should cover restore the way it covers archive: ID and title preserved, repeated requests idempotent, unknown IDs raise TaskNotFoundError, and restored tasks return to the default list. If convergence appends work, repeat the implement and converge loop.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. A constitution, a specification, a plan, and tasks for archive behavior.
  2. Working archive behavior with passing tests.
  3. A final Converged result.
  4. Optional: GitHub Issues from the task list, and restore behavior with its own Converged result.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-02 trainer guide: Spec Kit
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Show the complete Spec Kit loop on one small change: request, specification, plan, tasks, implementation, tests, and convergence. Learners should know which files Spec Kit creates and which decisions the team still owns. The lab's required parts stop at convergence. Issue conversion and the restore cycle are optional.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text:
Time Segment 0:00 to 0:06 Why specification-driven development 0:06 to 0:18 Spec Kit project and artifact model 0:18 to 0:30 Requirements and clarification 0:30 to 0:42 Planning, checklists, tasks, and analysis 0:42 to 0:52 Implementation and convergence 0:52 to 1:00 Installation, demonstration, and lab handoff

The timings match the agenda in slides.md. Keep the first five segments moving so the demonstration and lab handoff get the last eight minutes.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Install Spec Kit v1.4.0 (latest on 12 November 2026) and check the releases page for newer ones. If you change the tag, rerun the lab first.
  • Check that /speckit-github-taskstoissues exists in your install. It comes from the opt-in GitHub extension (specify extension add github). If it doesn't, tell learners to skip Part 4.
  • Prepare an initialized copy of the archive-task starter. Run its tests first so learners see the baseline.
  • Check that the training repository allows issue creation.

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:06: Why specification-driven development
docs.text:
Slides: Spec Kit: Specification-Driven Development, Agenda, A feature request is a starting point, and Resolve decisions before implementation

  1. Read the archive request aloud. Ask learners how many decisions hide inside the word "remove." Use the four questions on the slide. Don't answer them yet.
  2. Compare the two paths. Specification-driven development moves decisions earlier. It doesn't add documents for their own sake.

docs.title: 0:06 to 0:18: Spec Kit project and artifact model
docs.text:
Slides: What Spec Kit provides, Initialize an existing project, Two artifact scopes, Four terms and one file layout, and The full workflow

  1. Separate the three layers. The CLI creates the project structure, the generated skills guide the workflow, and the feature artifacts hold the work.
  2. Show initialization as a reviewed change. Explain --here, --force, and --integration copilot, then show the generated diff. --force allows initialization in a non-empty directory. It doesn't accept every generated file.
  3. Distinguish scopes. The constitution applies to the project. The specification, plan, design files, checklists, and tasks belong to one feature.
  4. Define the four terms. Constitution, convergence, idempotent, and skill. Say that /speckit-plan runs the instructions in .github/skills/speckit-plan/. Open that file so learners see a command is just a Markdown instruction file.
  5. Walk through the workflow once. Clarification, checklist review, and analysis are optional gates for ambiguity or risk.

Check: Learners can say where project principles live and where feature behavior lives.

docs.title: 0:18 to 0:30: Requirements and clarification
docs.text:
Slides: Constitution: rules for how the project works, Specify behavior, not implementation, Write scenarios a reviewer can challenge, and Clarify before choosing a design

  1. Make constitution principles testable. A useful principle changes planning, implementation, or review.
  2. Keep spec.md technology-neutral. It defines the user, outcome, scenarios, non-goals, and measurable requirements. Class names, storage, packages, and paths belong later.
  3. Use scenarios to test decisions. Walk through the active-task and unknown-ID examples. Each Given/When/Then statement lets a reviewer challenge one behavior.
  4. Resolve the archive questions. Reveal the accepted decisions after learners see the ambiguity. Clarification updates spec.md.

docs.title: 0:30 to 0:42: Planning, checklists, tasks, and analysis
docs.text:
Slides: Plan: decide how the feature will work, Supporting design files have a purpose, A checklist reviews requirement quality, Tasks turn design into executable work, and Analyze artifacts before implementation

  1. Move technical choices into the plan. Python version, storage, fields, and file paths belong in plan.md, not spec.md.
  2. Explain each supporting file by the question it answers. Not every feature needs every optional artifact.
  3. Separate requirement review from implementation status. A checked checklist item means the requirement is clear. It doesn't mean the code exists.
  4. Read the sample tasks as a dependency sequence. Point out the task ID, user-story reference, action, and exact file. "Implement the feature" is too broad to assign.
  5. Explain analysis as a read-only check. Fix a finding in the artifact that owns the decision, then analyze again. Don't edit code to hide a spec contradiction.

Check: Ask which artifact owns an ambiguous behavior, a storage choice, and a missing implementation step. Answers: spec.md, plan.md, tasks.md.

docs.title: 0:42 to 0:52: Implementation and convergence
docs.text:
Slides: Implementation follows the accepted tasks, Compare implementation with accepted artifacts, specify check is not compliance validation, Living specifications evolve accepted behavior, and Convert tasks into GitHub Issues

  1. Set the implementation gate. Review the checklist, fix the analysis findings, and commit the artifacts.
  2. Explain convergence. It compares implementation, tests, specification, plan, and tasks. When it finds a gap, it adds work. It doesn't rewrite accepted requirements to match the code.
  3. Correct the specify check misconception. It checks the local Spec Kit environment, not implementation compliance, security, performance, or coverage.
  4. Show how accepted behavior changes (optional in the lab). Restore behavior starts in spec.md. Analysis, implementation, and convergence then bring plan, tasks, code, and tests back in line.
  5. Show task-to-issue conversion (optional in the lab). Issues keep the task IDs, dependencies, and file paths. They are not a second requirements source.

docs.title: 0:52 to 1:00: Installation, demonstration, and lab handoff
docs.text:
Slides: Install Spec Kit, Prepared demonstration, and Lab handoff

  1. Install a pinned release. The lab uses v1.4.0. A disconnected environment needs the official air-gapped package prepared beforehand.
  2. Run the convergence demo. Prepare an implementation that hides archived tasks by default but has no test for include_archived=True. Run the existing tests, then /speckit-converge. Inspect the appended task, add the missing test, rerun the suite, and converge again.
  3. Hand off. Learners initialize the project, define archive behavior, plan, implement in stages, and converge. Learners who finish early convert tasks to issues and add restore behavior. Reveal change-request.md only then.

Final message: Passing tests and satisfying the accepted specification are different things.

docs.title: Generated files and commands
docs.text:
After specify init, show the generated files before running any agent command:

.specify/
  memory/constitution.md
  scripts/
  templates/
.github/
  skills/speckit-*/

Copilot skill names generated by the current integration:

/speckit-constitution
/speckit-specify
/speckit-clarify
/speckit-plan
/speckit-checklist
/speckit-tasks
/speckit-analyze
/speckit-implement
/speckit-converge
/speckit-github-taskstoissues

Another integration may use different invocation syntax. Teach the workflow and let the generated files define the syntax.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why not ask an agent to build it immediately? A specification exposes missing decisions while they are cheap to change.

Can the tool define the process? No. The team owns the process and reviews its outputs.

docs.title: Overview
